en: Śrīḥ.
The Compendium of Indicators (Jñāpakasaṃgraha)
First Chapter:

*Ai-u-ṇ* |1| The letter *a* is taught as being wide-open (*vivṛta*) even during the stage prior to grammatical operation; in this regard, the rule for restoration, *a a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68), serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). May that certain mass of compassion bestow welfare upon us—he who dwells on the peak of Mount Vṛṣa, the venerable Śrīnivāsa, who excels the wish-fulfilling tree in granting the desired fruits to those who take refuge in him, and who is served day after day by throngs of supplicants approaching him. [Salutations] to those proficient in many systems of thought, who are ever intent on the welfare of their disciples.

I bow my head in reverence to the gurus, the foremost among those of great spiritual power. (2) The *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* was composed by the wise Nāgeśabhaṭṭa; it was previously published in the Andhra script by Pārthasārathi. (3) At the command of that wise man, I now commence its commentary—concise in words but rich in meaning, which delights the hearts of the learned. (4) By this pretext, [I shall provide] a thorough examination of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts through the intellect... [of the author]. (5)

That purity which arises is the supreme fruit of this work. In this regard, the venerable Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of grammar, semantics, and epistemology (*padavākyapramāṇa*), having begun to compose a treatise titled *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*—which compiles those statements established by indicators (*jñāpaka*) found here and there in the *Mahābhāṣya*, excluding the *Paribhāṣās*—first states the following rule: "The vowel *a* is open (*vivṛta*)."

Regarding the statement by the author of the Vārttika that in the sūtra *aiuṇ*, the vowel *a* should be taught as being *vivṛta* (open) for the sake of including the vowel *ā*, a challenge is raised: "Is this purpose being stated by the author of the Vārttika for something already established by the author of the sūtra himself, or is the teaching of *a* as *vivṛta* something not yet done that the author of the Vārttika is proposing as something that ought to be done? In response to this objection, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The purpose of the *a* being taught as *vivṛta* is being explained."

How is it known that this [sūtra] teaches the restoration of the closure (*saṃvṛtatā*) of the vowel *a*—which is by nature open (*vivṛta*)—to its state of being closed, as in "a a"? Its intention is as follows: the sūtra "a a" demonstrates that the vowel *a*, which is naturally closed but becomes open during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), regains its state of closure at the time of actual usage (*prayoga*). Furthermore, this sūtra is located at the very end of the treatise.

Therefore, it is understood that the vowel *a* taught in the ten preceding rules prior to that sūtra is *vivṛta* (open). And since the Vārttikakāra declares the purpose [of the sūtra] for the vowel *a* as being taught with such openness (*vivṛtatva*), the sūtra "a a" is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding that specific subject; for there exists another purpose for it.

To explain: in cases such as *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *atimālaḥ*, the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48) prescribes the substitution of the short vowel *a* for the long vowel *ā*. Since the original substitute (*ā*) is *vivṛta* (open), one might expect the resulting *a* to also be *vivṛta* due to phonetic proximity (*sāvarṇya*). Therefore, if it is argued that the rule *a a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68) exists for the purpose of ensuring that this *a* remains *saṃvṛta* (closed), how can that rule serve as a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) [for the existence of the *saṃvṛta* vowel]? [Response: It is not so.

For if the vowel *a* were ever articulated open (*vivṛta*) anywhere in either common usage (*loka*) or the Veda, then—by virtue of positional similarity (*sthāna-āntarya*)—the sounds *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *na* would become open when they replace it. However, the vowel *a* is never open; rather, it is always closed (*saṃvṛta*). Consequently, since the vowel *a* remains closed, the rule "a a" (Pāṇini 6.1.101) does not result in the closure of *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *na* in forms such as *atikhaṭva*.

Furthermore, at the end of the treatise, after the completion of the grammatical derivations (*prakriyā*), the Sūtra which prescribes the closed nature (*saṃvṛtatva*) of the vowel *a* indicates that in the preceding Sūtras, it should be understood that only the open vowel (*vivṛta*) was taught. Consequently, it is established that the Vārttikakāra explains the purpose of that very open vowel which was taught. "Return" (*pratyāpatti*) means the attainment of its own inherent closed nature by that which had naturally become open.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "In the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the vowel *a* is taught as being 'open' (*vivṛta*); in this regard, the statement of restoration (*pratyāpatti*)—namely, *a a*—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The sūtra] *jhrjñāṭa ṛlṛk* || 2 || states: "An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like its original form (*prakṛti*)," because of the mention of *iyaṅ* in rules such as *kṣiyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.59). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the occasion of explaining the purpose for teaching the letter *ḷ* in the sūtra *vi.ṭa ṛlṛk*, one purpose stated is that of imitating what arises from incapacity (*aśakti*).
To illustrate: when a certain Brahmin woman ought to have used the word *ṛtaka*, she used the word *lṛtaka* due to incapacity; regarding that [usage],...

The expression *brāhmaṇylṛtaka* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the speech of one who is unable to pronounce [the sound correctly]; this is called an "imitation arising from incapacity. In that case, when *brāhmaṇī-alṛtaka* is established, because the *ḷ*-sound is a vowel (*ac*), the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies when that [vowel] follows, resulting in the substitution of *yaṇ* for the *ī*-sound, yielding *brāhmaṇylṛtaka*. However, if the *ḷ*-sound were not taught in the *ṛlṛk* sūtra and only *ṛk* were stated, then because the *ḷ*-sound would lack the status of being a vowel (*ac*), the rule *iko yaṇ aci* would not apply.

Therefore, having stated that the instruction of the phoneme *lṛ* must be formulated, its rejection is carried out. For there exists the paribhāṣā: "An imitation (anukaraṇa) is like its original (prakṛti). The meaning of this is that an imitation is like its original—that is, equal to the thing being imitated—and whatever grammatical operation applies to the original also applies to the imitation. In this case, the word *ṛtaka* is the original, and the word *lṛtaka* is the imitation.

The intention is as follows: since the vowel *ṛ* in the word *ṛtaka*—which is an object of imitation (*anukārya*)—is treated as a vowel (*ac*), the rule "a semivowel (*yaṇ*) replaces an *ik* before a vowel (*aci*)" (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies; likewise, that same rule applies to the word *lṛtaka*, which is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). Thus, since the substitution of the semivowel (*yaṇ*) is established, there is no need for the formal teaching (*upadeśa*) of the vowel *lṛ*. As for the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam bhavati*), it is the mention of *iyaṅ* in rules such as "after *kṣi* ending in a long vowel" (Pāṇini 7.2.46).

For instance, the word *kṣi* found in the Sūtra is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *kṣi* as it appears in the Dhātupāṭha. Since an imitative word lacks the capacity to denote an action, it does not possess the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*); consequently, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would be impossible according to the rule *aciśnudhātubhruvām* (Pāṇini 6.4.77). Yet, Pāṇini has prescribed this *iyaṅ*. From this, it is understood that an imitation functions like its original form (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*).

And likewise, since the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs for the verbal root *kṣi*, it ought to occur for the word *kṣi* as well when it is used as an imitation [of that root]; thus, the rule achieves its purpose within its own domain. When someone says "pacantu pacantu" twice, the imitation of that is "dviḥ pacantu."

Since this word *pacantu* does not denote a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), it lacks the status of being a *tiṅ*-ending form; consequently, the *nighāta* accent—which is prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), meaning that a *tiṅ*-ending word following another *tiṅ*-ending word is unaccented—would not apply. However, if one accepts the maxim *anukaraṇaṃ prakṛtivad bhavati* ("an imitation [of a word] is like the original"), then just as the original *tiṅ*-ending form *pacantu* possesses the *nighāta* accent, that same accent will be established for the imitation *pacantu* as well. *jhrjñādṛṭa eoṅ* || 3 ||

From the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of "cow" (*go*), it is understood that a grammatical operation prescribed for a whole does not apply to a part that is not distinct from it. Regarding the rule *vṛdṛṭaṣṭhaeoṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), there arises an inquiry as to whether or not the operations prescribed for the individual phonemes such as *a* apply to those parts which resemble the sounds *ā*, *ai*, *au*, etc., or to the parts of *ṛ* and *ḷ* that resemble *r* and *l*, or to the parts within the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*)—namely *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au*—that resemble *a*, *i*, and *u*. In this context, if one were to include these phonemic parts under the term "phoneme" (*varṇa-grahaṇa*)...

In that case, if the operation regarding phonetic color (*varṇa*) were to be performed, then in examples such as *agne indram*, *vāyo udakam*, and so forth, the long vowel would result according to the rule "a long vowel is substituted for *aka* before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.101). This is because the *ik* portion following the *e* in *agne* is included by the mention of *ik*, and since it is followed by the homogeneous *i* in *indram*; likewise, the *uk* portion within *ok* is followed by the homogeneous *u* in *udakam*. Anticipating this fault, this statement was formulated as a remedy: "The operation does not apply to a constituent part that is not separated [from its context]. (*nāvyapavṛktasyāvayasya tadvidhiḥ*).

The two genitive cases in *avyapavṛktasyāvayavasya* are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa). "Of the undivided" (*avyapavṛktasya*) means: of that collection which is the object of a non-differentiated cognition, which is grasped by a cognition whose object is unity—that is, the object of a cognition in the form "one"—the rule for that [collection] is that it does not become a rule for individual phonemes; such is the meaning of the stated statement.

And thus, when the collection *e* is grasped by the intellect as "the single syllable *e*," then for that constituent *i*-sound—which is not a part of the collection—the rule [applying] to it, such as the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) and so forth, does not take effect. This means that in cases such as *agne indram*, there is no fault of the undesired application of vowel lengthening. He states the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this stated rule: "because of the mention of *go-naus*."

This is the intended meaning: the mention of *go-* in the rule *godvyaco'saṅkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat* (Pāṇini 5.1.39) and the mention of *nau-* in the rule *naudvyacaṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7) serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned statement. Therein, the meaning of the first rule is that the suffix *yat* occurs after the word *go* and after a word consisting of two vowels, in the sense of "its cause," whether that be a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or a portent (*utpāta*). The examples are *gavyam* and *dhanyam*. In that context, regarding the word *go*, there is the vowel *o*, which is a composite of the sounds *a* and *u*; [the indicator applies] to these two components, *a* and *u*.

When there is apprehension through the grasping of distinct forms and through the grasping of the phoneme *u*, the word *go* would already be included by the rule *dhdyac* itself because it consists of two vowels (*dvi-ac*); thus, the explicit mention of the word *go* being otherwise redundant indicates that a whole (*samudāya*) is not apprehended by the grasping of its constituent phonemes (*varṇa*). In this way, according to the second sūtra, the suffix *ṭhan* occurs after the words *nau* and *dhdyaca* in the sense of "one who crosses" (*tarati*); the examples are *nāvikaḥ* and *ghaṭikaḥ*.

In that regard, since the vowel *au* in the word *nau* consists of a collection of two phonemes (*varṇa*), it possesses the quality of being "two-syllabled" (*dvyackatva*); thus, its inclusion would already be established by the rule for "two-syllabled words" (*dvyaca*) alone. Consequently, the specific mention of *nau* would otherwise be redundant, and this redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the following statement: once that [rule] is indicated, because the vowels *o* and *au* are not grasped as consisting of two phonemes, they lack the quality of being "two-syllabled. Therefore, the separate mention of *go* and *nau* is purposeful in its own right (*svāṃśe cāritārthya*).

As for the result of this indication (*jñāpanaphalam*), it is simply what was stated previously: that there is no long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) in cases such as *agne indram*. In the view that "parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*) are not grasped by the term 'phoneme' (*varṇagrahaṇa*)," the fact that the word *tṛpnoti* is listed among the *kṣubhnādi* group indicates that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for a nasal following an *ṛ*-vowel. In the view that "in the rule *ṛlṛk*, those which are parts of diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) such as *ā* and others are not grasped by the separate mention of individual phonemes," the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *mātṝṇām* would not be established.

Since the form *mātṛn* is established, there is no rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* following the vowel *ṛ*. However, in the case of the alternative view that [the *ṛ*] is included, the substitution of *ṇ* would occur by the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.1), because the *n* follows the *r* situated within the *ṛ* vowel. To this objection, it is replied that even in the view that [the *ṛ*] is not included, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* following the *ṛ*-vowel is established on the basis of an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). For instance, the word *nṛnamana* is listed in the *kṣubhnādi* group.

The purpose of that [reading] is the prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel by the rule "kṣubhnādiṣu ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.39). If, however, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel did not occur—since there is no rule providing for it—then the inclusion of words like *kṣubhna* in the *kṣubhnādi* group would be useless, as its purpose would be to prohibit a *ṇ*-substitution that could never have arisen. Nor can it be argued that its inclusion in that group is for the sake of prohibiting the *ṇ*-substitution of the *n* in *nārnamaniḥ* following the letter *r*.

Even so, the inclusion of the word *tṛpnoti* in that group (*gaṇa*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned statement; for since there is no possibility of the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* following the vowel *ṛ* in the word *tṛpnoti*, the prohibition [of *ṇatva*] would be redundant, and thus it indicates that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does indeed occur after the vowel *ṛ*. Furthermore, in the technical abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*) such as *jhr*, *jñā*, *ṭa*, *act*, *dhdyāpya*, and others, the vowels *it* (indicatory letters) are not included, as evidenced by the rule "uṇādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.1) and other such indicators.

(Sūtra 5) *Jharo jhari savarṇe*: In the case of pratyāhāras such as *ac*, *at*, *ap*, *it*, and so forth, there is no inclusion of the letters situated between [the defining sounds]—namely, those bearing the technical name *it* such as *ṇ*, *k*, and others. This is because of the specific formulation *uṇādayaḥ*. If the pratyāhāra *aj-ādi* were to include even the intermediate *it*-sounds, then since the letter *ṇ* would possess the status of *ap* and *act*, the word *uṇ* would have to be formulated as *uṇādayaḥ* (with *yaṇ*-substitution for the vowel *u* before the following *ṇ*), rather than *uṇādayaḥ*. Thus, the fact that it is taught as *uṇādayaḥ* indicates that the intermediate *it*-sounds are not included in these pratyāhāras.

The meaning is that since the term *uṇādayaḥ* is taught without a *yaṇ* [substitution] for *ak*, it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that vowels (*it*) are not included within *pratyāhāra*s; therefore, in cases such as *śrīkāntaḥ*, there is no *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel *ī*. In this context, the inclusion of *it*-vowels even when they fall within *pratyāhāra*s beginning with consonants (*hal*) is not desired. This being the case, we do not understand from where the statement "in *pratyāhāra*s other than those consisting of two vowels" (*actadvayāpyapratyāhāreṣu*) was derived. For this very reason, the *Kaumudī* simply states: "In *pratyāhāra*s, *it*-vowels are not included."

In reality, however, the inclusion of the *its* (the vowels) in the *ac*-pratyāhāra is established solely by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), and the principle of "that which is pervaded" (*tadvyāpya*) does not apply there. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of including the *its* in the *ag*-pratyāhāra and others; for, since the vowel *a* is pronounced in the *hal* [consonant] lists for the sake of pronunciation, it can be maintained that consonants devoid of such phonetic markers are not included in pratyāhāras composed of consonants.

Therefore, the wise should note that in the *Ślokavārttika* on the rule for elision (*pratyāhāra*), regarding the question "How is there no inclusion [of *anubandhas*] in the mentions of vowels (*ajgrahaṇa*)?", it is stated simply as "in the mentions of vowels" (*ajgrahaṇeṣu*). This is also clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Regarding the sūtra *hayavaraṭ* (1.3.3): the prohibition of doubling by the rule *śaro'ci* (8.4.49)—which occurs when the option (*vibhāṣā*) from the preceding rules *halo yamāṃ yami* (8.4.64) and *jharo jhari* (8.4.65) is still in effect—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [that *anubandhas* are not included]. Alternatively, the authoritative explanation (*vyākhyāna*) itself is the refuge.

In the *Hayavaraṭ* sūtra, having asked for what purpose there is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the semivowels (*antaḥsthā*) *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* as *aṇ*s, [the following is explained]: in the case of *saṃyantā*, when it stands as *saṃ yantā*, the *m* undergoes *anusvāra* by the rule *mo 'nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.23), and when its *parasavarṇa* is applied, resulting in *saṃy yantā*, the preceding *y* is included by the term *yagrahaṇa* [in the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā*], and thus by the rule *anaci ca*... [the doubling of the *y* occurs].

Thus, by doubling [the *y*], the form with three *y*-sounds is established. If there were no instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the semivowels (*antaḥsthā*) as *aṇ*, then because the *y* would lack the status of being an *aṇ*, it would not—by the rule *aṇudit-sūtra*—include a homogeneous nasalized *y* (*anunāsika-y*). Consequently, since the preceding nasalized *y* would not be included by the mention of *y* (*y-grahaṇa*), the doubling would not occur. Therefore, the instruction of the *y*-sounds and so forth is for the sake of establishing the doubling. [Objection: But let there be no doubling in this case.

It should not be argued that because there is a difference in form—resulting in a three-*y* form when there is duality and a two-*y* form when there is an absence of duality—duality is necessary. For even when duality exists, if there are three *y*s, the middle *y* is elided by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64), whereby the form with only two *y*s is established. If this is said, it would be so only if the elision in *halo yamāṃ yami* were compulsory; however, it is optional.

And likewise, since there is doubling [of the semivowel], it is necessary for the establishment of the difference in form—resulting in a word with two *y* sounds in the case where the *y* is elided, and three *y* sounds in the case where it is not elided—that doubling occurs only when the semivowels (*antasthā*) are taught as vowels (*aṇ*), as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya according to the reasoning previously mentioned.

Regarding the doubt as to how it is known that the elision [of *y*] by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) is optional, the author of the Vārttika says: "The option (*vibhāṣā*) from [the rule for] *śar* and *ac* follows, since this [present rule] prevents doubling. The meaning of this is as follows: in the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), one must necessarily state that the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over from the preceding rule *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.62).

Otherwise, the prohibition of doubling in the rule *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) would be redundant. For by that rule, *śaro'ci*, the doubling required by the preceding rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (8.4.46) is prohibited. Here, the following objection might be raised: "Let there be doubling here. Once doubling has occurred, we have the form *caturṣu*. Then, by the application of *jharo jhari savarṇe* (8.4.65), the first *ṣ* can be elided, and the desired form is indeed established. Therefore, the rule *śaro'ci* is useless."

In this regard, the following solution must be stated: this sūtra indicates the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the option (*vikalpa*) from the rule *jharo jhari*. Thus, when doubling has occurred, because the elision (*lopa*) is optional, there would result two forms: one with a single *ṣ* in the case of elision, and one with two *ṣ*s in the case of non-elision. However, for us, only the form with a single *ṣ*, as in *caturṣu caturṣu*, is desired. Therefore, the purpose of the sūtra is that it serves as a prohibition of doubling by means of the rule *śaro'ci*.

And thus, by the rule *śaro'ci*, it is established that the term *anyatarasyām* also carries over into the rule *halo yamāṃ yami* (Pāṇini 8.4.64). Consequently, in the case of *saṃyantā*, when the *y* undergoes doubling, there is a distinction between the form with two *y*s (on the view that *halo yamām* applies the elision) and the form with three *y*s (on the view that the elision does not apply); this is the purpose of the section stating that semi-vowels (*antasthā*) are taught as *aṇ*.

Having taken all of this into consideration, he stated that by employing the two rules "halo yamāṃ yami" and "jharo jhari," and then [relying on] the recurrence of the term *vibhāṣā*, [the desired result follows]. Now, in the concluding commentary (*upasaṃhāra-bhāṣya*) on that very point, it was said: "This remains extremely doubtful among the Teachers: whether the recurrence of *vibhāṣā* applies or not. Thus, having raised the doubt as to how this can be so, he says: "Or rather, the explanatory gloss (*vyākhyāna*) is the refuge."

And in every doubtful case, this maxim applies: "The specific determination [of the meaning] arises from the commentary; for there is no rule [to be followed] on account of doubt. Thus, we shall explain that the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) carries over into the two previously mentioned sūtras; therefore, the sense is that there is no fault whatsoever. [Pāṇini 1.1.57: *jhara-jhali ṭu-laṇ*. In the rule *ḍhralopa* (1.1.59), the mention of *aṇ* refers to the former [aṇ of 1.1.56] and not to the latter [aṇ of 1.1.69]. This is because the desired result is already established by the application of the rule *acaśca* (1.2.28); the explicit mention of *aṇ* [in 1.1.59] serves to indicate that the former *aṇ* is intended.

Regarding the *laṇ* sūtra, the following investigation has been undertaken: the letter *ṇ*, in the form of *it*, is repeated twice—in "aiuṇ" and in "laṇ. Consequently, a doubt arises concerning the two pratyāhāras, *aṇ* and *iṇ*: does this [specific] *ṇ* belong to the former pratyāhāra or to the latter? Regarding this doubt, the author of the Vārttikas stated that wherever there occurs the mention of *aṇ* or *iṇ*, a definitive resolution can be made in every such case through the power of an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark).

He summarizes and presents those points with the words "ḍhralopa" and so forth. Regarding the rule "ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.111), there arises a doubt: does the term *aṇ* refer to the pratyāhāra formed by the preceding *ṇ* (in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*), or by the subsequent *ṇ* found in the *laṇ* sūtra? The conclusion is that it refers to the *aṇ* by the preceding [ṇ], not by the subsequent one. To the question "What is the authority for this?", he says: "acaśca" (Pāṇini 1.2.28). This is the underlying intention: if, in the rule concerning the elision of *ḍh* and *r*, the *aṇ* were a pratyāhāra formed by the subsequent [ṇ], then [the rule would apply to cases like] *aṇ*.

By this [statement], these syllables—*a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ, e, o, ai, au, h, y, v, r, l*—are intended to be meant. And therein, the capacity for lengthening (*dīrgha*) belongs only to those ending with *au*. Consequently, when it is said "the long vowel of *aṇ*," the result is effectively "the long vowel of *ac*" (vowels). This being the case, the mention of *aṇ* in the rule concerning the elision of *ḍh* and *r* (*ḍhralopa*) would be redundant.

By the governing rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28), which means that wherever a vowel (*ac*) is prescribed by means of the terms *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, or *pluta*, the word *acaḥ* ending in the genitive case is supplied; thus, through the very presence of the word *acaḥ*, the long vowel of a vowel is obtained. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* being redundant indicates that in this rule, the *pratyāhāra* is formed only by the preceding [vowels]. Consequently, in this rule, the long vowels intended are only these three: *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*.

Furthermore, that [term] would not be obtained when the word *aca* is present; therefore, the mention of *aṇ* serves its purpose within its own scope (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*). The absence of lengthening in forms such as *ātṛḍha* is the intended result. Now, even so, there might be a doubt in the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13) as to whether *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [rule]; regarding this, he says: *jhrjñādṛṭa ata eva*. That is to say, in the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, *aṇ* refers only to the preceding [rule]. *jhrvidṛṭa ata eva*: because it is already established by the presence of the word *aca*; such is the meaning.

The point is this: by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ," a short vowel is prescribed for the *aṇ* [group] when followed by the suffix *kap*. The examples given are *jñakaḥ* and *kumārikā*. In that context, if *aṇ* were a subsequent *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive term), then since only vowels (*ac*) possess the capacity to undergo the operations of lengthening (*ḍhat*), doubling (*ḍhat*), and elision (*sva*), it would follow that a short vowel alone was intended to be prescribed. If that were the case, once the vowel is obtained simply through the presence of the genitive-ending word *acaḥ*, the inclusion of the term *aṇ* would be redundant.

Therefore, this indicates that in this sūtra, the term *aṇ* refers only to the former [definition]. The purpose, however, is the absence of shortening in cases such as *gokā* and *naukā*; everything else remains as before. Now, even if this is so, there might be a doubt as to whether in the sūtra *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), the term *aṇ* refers to the former or the latter definition. To this, he says: In the case of *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*, although one could have simply said *acaḥ* ("of a vowel"), the specific mention of *aṇ* indicates that it refers only to the former [definition]. Thus: *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*.

By the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasya*, an anusvāra is prescribed for an *aṇ* vowel at the end of a word (*avasāna*) that is not a *pragṛhya*. In this context, if *aṇ* were a *pratyāhāra* formed by subsequent vowels, one would simply have said *acaḥ*. Nor can it be argued that the term *aṇ* was used in order to provide for the anusvāra of the letters *ha, ya, va, ra,* and *la* as well.

By the maxim of "negation joined with 'iva' or 'nañ'," the term *apragṛhya* would include both that which is different from a *pragṛhya* and that which resembles a *pragṛhya*. Since the designation *pragṛhya* applies only to vowels (*ac*), that which is different from a *pragṛhya* and resembles it must be a vowel (*ac*) itself; thus, it could have been understood by the word *apragṛhya* alone as being a vowel. Therefore, since it was stated *aṇ* instead of simply saying *ac*, this redundant expression serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, it indicates that here only *a*, *i*, and *u* are intended to be included. Thus, the mention of *aṇ* [in the rule] is understood to refer only to those [three vowels].

If it were stated simply as *aca*, it would not be established; therefore, *aṇ* is stated so that the rule finds its application within its own scope (*svāṃśe*). However, its purpose elsewhere is that in forms such as *kartṛ*, the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the vowel *ṛ* does not occur. Now, even if this is so, there might be a doubt in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51) as to whether *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [vowel]; to address this, he says: *jhrjñāṭa urajraparaḥ*.

Since the sounds *ha*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la* cannot occur in the place of *ṛ*, and since only vowels (*ac*) can occupy the position of *ṛ*, the expression *uraṇ* would be redundant if one were to simply say *uraj*. Nor should it be argued that there is no concern regarding brevity or prolixity because the terms *ac* and *aṇ* possess an equal number of moras (*mātrā*); for when the term *aṇ* is uttered, there occurs the prolixity caused by the presence of more syllables than those presented by the term *aj*, as the latter presents not only the vowels but also the consonants.

Furthermore, while one ought to have said *uraḥ*, the statement *uraṇ* indicates that the term *aṇ* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) formed with the preceding *ṇ*. Consequently, if only *ac* were stated, there would be the inclusion of *ṛ*-vowels and others as well; to exclude those, *aṇ* was stated, thus fulfilling its purpose within its own scope. However, its utility elsewhere is seen in cases such as *mātṝṇām*, where the long vowel (*ṝ*) replacing the *ṛ*-vowel does not become followed by *r* (*rapara*).

But even so, in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), there is doubt as to whether the term *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [ṇ]. To this, he says: [The answer is] that in the rule *aṇudit*, *aṇ* refers only to the following ṇ; this is because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) consisting of the use of the long vowel marker (*taparakaraṇa*) in the rule *urṛt*. Thus, in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, which serves to include homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrāhaka*), *aṇ* is indeed by the following ṇ, not by the preceding one.

In this context, the addition of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) in the rule *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). To explain: in forms such as *acīkṛtat*, derived from the root *kṝ* belonging to the *curādi* class, in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ* (reduplication), after reduplication we have *acīkṝ a at*. Here, by the rule *urṛt* (7.4.7)—which means that when a *ṇi*-affix preceded by *caṅ* follows, an *ṛ* may optionally replace the penultimate *ṛ*-vowel—an *ṛ* is substituted for the *ṝ* of the stem, resulting in the form *acīkṛtat*. The *tapara* marker is employed here so that only an *ṛ* is substituted in place of the *ṝ*, and not an *ṝ*. Without the *tapara* marker, the substitution might result in an *ṝ* instead of an *ṛ*. Thus, the *tapara* marker is used to ensure that the correct short *ṛ* is produced.

If, in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, the term *aṇ* were understood as including the preceding *ṇ* (i.e., the *ṇ* of *aṇ*), then since the vowel *ṛ* would not be an *aṇ* (due to its being distinct in duration from the *ṝ*), it would not include the *ṝ* which differs in length; consequently, only *ṛ* would be the substitute, not *ṝ*. Thus, what would be the purpose of the *tapara* notation (*ṛt*)? Yet, that very notation was made as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the term *aṇ* includes the subsequent *ṇ*.

Furthermore, since the vowel *ṛ* is also included within the *aṇ* group, it would also include the homogenous *ṝ*; thus, at times the *ṝ* might also occur. To prevent this and ensure that only the *ṛ* occurs, the addition of the *t* (in *tapara*) serves its purpose in its own context. However, its utility elsewhere is that the term *ṛ* is the designation for eighteen [sounds].

If it is argued that in the rule *ur ṛt*, even in the absence of the addition of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*), the vowel *ṛ* being prescribed would not include its homogeneous counterparts because it is stated to be "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), making the *ta*-marker redundant; to this, the author of the *Udyota* replies: "In the absence of the *ta*-marker, [the vowel] would not be something to be prescribed (*avidheya*) because it would merely serve to exclude other substitutes, to authorize its own form, and because there would be nothing new to be understood."

But even so, in rules such as *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.39), there arises a doubt as to whether the pratyāhāra *iṇ* includes the preceding *ṇ* or the following *ṇ*; therefore, he says: *jhrjñā.ṭa iṇ pareṇaiva*. Since the term *iṇ* would have been sufficient for the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the explicit mention of *yvōḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *iṇ* here includes only the subsequent [ṇ]. Thus, *jhrvi.ṭa iṇ pareṇaiva*: in the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*, the term *yvōḥ* denotes the inclusion of the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels.

If the *iṇ* pratyāhāra is formed with the preceding *ṇ* (in *ṇau*), then by the term *iṇ*, only the vowels *i* and *u* are included. Consequently, in the word *yvoḥ*, there is one *mātrā* for *yakāra* and *vakāra*, two *mātrās* for *okāra*, and half a *mātrā* for the *visarga*; thus, in total, there are three and a half *mātrās*. However, in the case of *iṇaḥ*, there is one *mātrā* for *ikāra*, half a *mātrā* for *ṇkāra*, one *mātrā* for *akāra*, and half a *mātrā* for the *visarga*; thus, there are exactly three *mātrās*. Therefore, [the former] possesses a deficiency of half a *mātrā*.

Therefore, although one could have simply said *iṇaḥ* for the sake of brevity, the mention of *yvoḥ* indicates that [the term *iṇ*] refers to the letter *ṇ* followed by *i*. Thus, had only *iṇaḥ* been stated, there would have been the inclusion of *ṛ*-sounds and others as well; to prevent this, *yvoḥ* was stated, thereby fulfilling its purpose within its own scope (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*). However, its utility elsewhere lies in rules such as "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.39), where the inclusion of the *o*-vowel also occurs, resulting in the establishment of the substitution of *ṣ* in forms like *goṣūktam*. The inclusion of the term *udātta* (acute) in the rule *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaṅ udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "phonetic qualities (*guṇas*) do not differentiate [the phoneme]. Regarding the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the author of the Vārttika stated that the addition of the *tapara* marker (*ḥ*) after the vowel *ā* must be made for the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). The meaning is this: because qualities do differentiate [the phoneme], when a particular quality is pronounced, there arises the contingency that only a phoneme with that specific quality would be designated by the technical term (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, the *tapara* marker is employed so that the designation may also apply to those phonemes possessing other qualities.

Regarding that, two positions are presented concerning qualities (*guṇas*) such as nasality (*ānunāsikya*), accentuation (*udātta*), and so forth—namely, whether they are differentiators (*bhedaka*) or non-differentiators (*abhedaka*). Having stated both these views regarding the qualities, the author raises the doubt: "Of these two, which is more logical here? and concludes that it is indeed logical that qualities are non-differentiators. Why is this? Because [the author] employs the term "accented" (*udātta*) in the rule: *asthidadhisaktthyakṣṇāmanaṅudāttaḥ*. The author of the Bhāṣya states that if qualities were differentiators, he would have merely pronounced the word "udātta. This is the intended meaning.

Since the accentuation of the *guṇa* vowel as *udātta* alone serves to distinguish it from those [vowels] beginning with the *anudātta*, the exclusion of *anaṅ* vowels that are *anudātta* and so forth will occur. Furthermore, because the word "udātta" is employed as a separate term rather than being read as part of the compound "yata udāttaḥ," it is understood that *guṇas* are non-distinguishing (i.e., they do not inherently differentiate). Consequently, even when the *udātta* accent is applied, since that *udātta*-ness lacks the capacity to distinguish it from others, there would be the inclusion of an *anaṅ* vowel that is *anudātta* as well; therefore, in order to exclude that, the word "udātta" fulfills its purpose within its own scope.

Furthermore, since the vowel *ā* possesses some quality (*guṇa*) that is inseparable from its nature, even when it is pronounced with such a quality, that quality does not differentiate the vowel; thus, the inclusion of *ā* endowed with another quality is established. Consequently, the purpose of the long *ā* (tapara) in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) would be redundant. This is the meaning of the section. [The rule] *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) and the mention of the vowel *ā* in the rule *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) [are explained accordingly].

Furthermore, the statement prohibiting *ni* and *śvi* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) does not apply before the *sic* affix. This [objection] is merely the argument of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*), since the desired result is already established by the fact that [the prohibition] is an exception (*apavāda*). In the rule *viṅati ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the mention of *vṛddhi* is for the purpose of its subsequent application in the rule *viṭa iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3). Otherwise, only the *guṇa* would be prohibited by that rule; consequently, in forms such as *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*, the *vṛddhi* would occur by the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

Having stated that "once the mention of *vṛddhi* is made, there is no fault because even *vṛddhi* is prohibited by the rule *viṅati ca*," he then raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against this: "This purpose [of mentioning *vṛddhi*] does not exist; for since the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs here due to its being *antaraṅga*, the vowel *u* will no longer be present at the end, and thus *vṛddhi* will not occur. Therefore, let the mention of *vṛddhi* in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* be abandoned, as its result—the absence of *vṛddhi*—is already established. To this, he replies: "In the case of the *sic* suffix, an operation is not *antaraṅga*."

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated: "Inasmuch as he [Pāṇini] employs the mention of the vowel *a* in the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.7]. This is the intended meaning: by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ*, an optional *vṛddhi* is prescribed for the short vowel *a* following a consonant (*hal*) at the beginning of a root, when followed by the suffix *sic* that begins with *iṭ* and is accompanied by a *parasmaipada* ending. The examples are *akhādīt* and *akhadīt*.

It must be stated here that if "of the vowel *a*" were not mentioned, then in forms such as *akoṣīt* and *amoṣīt*, where the analysis is *a-kuṣ-īt*, the *vṛddhi* would occur for the *u* of *ukārānta* (the root *kuṣ*) even though it is light and preceded by a consonant. To prevent this, it must be said that the phrase "of the vowel *a*" is stated [in the rule].

If, however, an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) were to occur after the suffix *sic*, then—because it would be internal with respect to the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) which depends on both *sic* and the Parasmaipada endings—the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would apply first; since the vowel *o* would no longer be light, the *vṛddhi* would not occur anyway. Thus, the inclusion of the letter *a* (in the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu*) would be redundant. And that redundancy serves to indicate the maxim: "An internal operation does not take effect when *sic* follows."

Furthermore, because the internal factor (*antaraṅga*) guna would not apply, the *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel *u* would occur due to its higher status [in the order of rules]. To prevent this, the inclusion of the vowel *a* [in the rule] serves its purpose within its own scope. Similarly, the mention of the roots *ṇi* and *śvi* in the rule *hmyantakṣaṇaśvasajāgṛṇiśvyeditām* (Pāṇini 7.2.5) is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned statement. For the meaning of that rule is as follows: there would otherwise be no *vṛddhi* substitution for a root ending in *ha* or *ma*, for roots such as *kṣaṇ* etc., for a root ending in *ṇi*, for the root *śvi*, or for a root having *e* or *o* as its *it*, when followed by *sic* augmented with *iṭ*. Thus, the inclusion of *ṇi* and *śvi* serves as evidence.

The examples are *aunayīt* and *aśvayīt*. If the *sic* suffix were *antaraṅga*, then, because it is *antaraṅga*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply first; once that is done, the desired form would be established, and the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* would be unnecessary. Yet, since that [mention] is actually made, it indicates that *sic* is not *antaraṅga*. Consequently, since the *antaraṅga* *guṇa* does not apply, the *vṛddhi* substitution would occur; the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* is therefore for the purpose of prohibiting that.

And thus, in cases such as *nyanuvīt*, since the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *uvaṅ* does not apply, a *vṛddhi* [substitution] would otherwise result; therefore, in order to establish the prohibition of a *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel via the rule *viṅati ca*, it must be accepted that the *vṛddhi* in the rule *sici vṛddhir iglakṣaṇā* refers to one characterized by an *ik*. For this purpose, the inclusion of the term *vṛddhi* in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* is established.

In reality, however, since the internal *guṇa* is sublated by the *vṛddhi* which serves as its exception (*apavāda*), the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* is for the purpose of prohibiting that *vṛddhi* when it would otherwise apply; thus, it cannot serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned rule. Therefore, he says: "Success [is achieved] because it is an exception."

Regarding the rule *jhrjñādṛṭa ṭhakṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), and the rule *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9): because the *kn* and *san* suffixes have the *kit* designation, this prohibition applies to the *guṇa* substitution even when it is conditioned by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Therefore, the mention of "that which is caused by them" (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) need not be performed. Regarding the sūtra *jhrvidṛṭa ṭhakṅiti ca*, the author of the Vārttikas stated: "In the prohibition [of *guṇa*] before *k* and *ṅit* suffixes, the mention of 'that which is caused by them' is for the sake of the *roravī* [root]."

In the rule *kṅiti ca*, the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). In that context, if the term *kṅiti* were a qualifier of *ikaḥ*, then the meaning of the sūtra would be: "When followed by a *kit* or a *ṅit* [affix], there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for that *ik*. If that were the case, then only in instances such as *ciṃta* (from *cit*) and *stutaṃ* (from *stu*), where an *ik* is followed by a *kit* suffix, would the prohibition of *guṇa* be obtained.

However, in cases such as *bhinna* and *bhinnavān*, in the form *bhid-ta*, the vowel *i* of the penultimate (*upadhā*) would not have a *k*- or *ṅ*-suffixed element immediately following it because of the intervention of the letter *d*; consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* would not be obtained. Therefore, by supplying the word *tannimitta* (having that as its cause), the meaning of the rule must be described as follows: "When *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* would otherwise occur due to a *k*- or *ṅ*-suffixed element, they do not take place. Thus, since the *guṇa* of the penultimate is also caused by a *k*- or *ṅ*-suffixed element, its prohibition is secured, and the desired result is achieved.

Therefore, the mention of that [suffix] as the cause is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* even when there is a *upadhā*. Similarly, in the case of the root *rudh* with *yaṅ*-elision, in the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*), at the stage "roru īti," there occurs *guṇa* of the vowel *u* by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84), which has the *tiP* suffix as its cause, followed by the substitution of *av* for *u*.

The form is *roravīti*. In the absence of the mention of "that cause" (*tannimitta*) [in the rule], since the *yaṅ* suffix is not immediately preceded by that which causes the guna, the guna would not be subject to prohibition; thus, the desired form would be established. Therefore, the intention of the Vārttika is that the mention of "that cause" must be included in the rule *kiṅati ca* both for the purpose of prohibiting guna in cases such as *bhinna*, and for the purpose of avoiding the prohibition of guna in cases such as *roravīti*.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, wishing to establish the prohibition of *guṇa* by means of the indicatory (*jñāpaka*) marker *ikaḥ* in the rule for the *upadhā*, rejected the inclusion of the term *tannimitta* ("having that as its cause"). He states this with the words beginning "trasigṛdhi... etc. By the sūtra "trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.140), the suffix *knu* is prescribed after the roots *tras* and others. In that [sūtra], the letter *k* is an *itsaṃjñaka* (an indicatory marker). Its purpose is to effect the prohibition of *guṇa* in forms such as *gṛdhnuḥ* by means of the rule "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5).

If this [rule] were to prohibit *guṇa* only for that which is followed by a *kṅit* suffix, then because of the intervention of the letter *dh*, the *ṛ*-vowel would not be followed by a *knup* suffix; consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* would not apply. However, the addition of the indicatory letter *k* (*kānubandha*) made for that purpose—though seemingly redundant—serves to indicate that the prohibition by the rule *kṅiti* applies even to *guṇa* characterized as being in the *upadhā* (penultimate) position, even when it occurs across an intervening element.

Similarly, by the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), it is stated that a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a *hal* consonant in proximity to an *ic*-vowel shall be treated as *kit*. In examples such as *jughukṣati*, the purpose [of this rule] is the absence of *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *u*. Since there would otherwise be no prohibition of *guṇa* because the penultimate vowel is not followed by a *kit* suffix, the mention of *kit* would be redundant; therefore, its very presence indicates that there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). This is the meaning.

And thus, in examples such as *bhinnah*, since the prohibition of *guṇa* is already obtained by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the inclusion of the term "having that as its cause" (*tannimitta*) is not necessary; this is the intended meaning. From the indicator consisting of the statement that *yāsuṭ* is marked with the *ṅit* designation, it follows that whatever operation applies to what is marked with *ṅit* does not apply to substitutes for what is marked with *ṅit*.

Regarding the statement “*tena acinavam ityādau na niṣedhaḥ*” (therefore, there is no prohibition in *acinavam* and so forth), this is the opinion of the Vārttika (on Pāṇini 1.1.5). Now, an objection is raised: when the root *ci* is in the *laṅ* tense with the first-person singular ending *mip*, and after the substitution of *am* for *mip*, we have the form *a-ci-nu-am*. Since the substitute *am* for the *laṅ* ending is considered to possess the property of being *ṅit* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) would prohibit *guṇa*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: “*yāsuṭaḥ*. The prescription of the *ṅit*-property for *yāsuṭ* by the rule “*yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca*” (Pāṇini 3.4.103) would otherwise be redundant.

In the form *bhūyāt*, because the substitute *tip* (the ending for the third person singular) is treated as having the property of being *ṅit* by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, and because the augment *yāsuṭ* is established as *ṅit* according to the principle of "that which is added [is like its original]," the prescription of *ṅit*-ness serves to indicate the maxim: "substitutes that are *ṅit* do not become [treated as] *ṅit*. Consequently, since the substitute *tip* for the *ṅit* *liṅ* would not itself be *ṅit*, the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* would otherwise be difficult to establish; thus, the prescription of its *ṅit*-ness is purposeful.

The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is that in forms such as *acinavam*, because the substitute (*ādeśa*) lacks the marker *ṅit*, the prohibition of *guṇa* does not occur. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya, having split the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4) into two parts—namely, *apit* and *ṅit*—and having relied upon the term *ṅit* from the previous rule, has described two possible interpretations of the sentence-meaning: either that what is marked with *ṅ* is not marked with *p*, or that what is marked with *p* is not marked with *ṅ*.

In this view, the prescription that *yāsuṭ* is *ṅit* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), but rather it is a rule prescribing *ṅittva* where it was otherwise unobtained, as in forms such as *mṛjyāt*. Having kept this in mind, he says: "This is the opinion of the Vārttika. The protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*) by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rules *jñādṛṭa ṭhaīdūdeddvivacanam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11) and *plutapragṛhyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.125). Alternatively, the status of being established (*siddhatva*) for the *pluta* is already secured by virtue of its dependence [on the preceding rule], just as in the case of the substitution of *u* for *ru*.

An objection is raised that because the term *tapara* (indicating a long vowel) in the rule *jhrvidṛṭa īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* excludes vowels of a different duration, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply to those [pluta vowels] which have a different duration. To resolve this, it is argued that since the *pluta* vowel is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the *pragṛhya* designation is to be applied, the *ī*-sounds and others will indeed possess a duration of two morae (*dvimātra*) and thus the *pragṛhya* designation will apply. Subsequently, the author of the Bhāṣya states by way of an objection: "The *pluta* is established in the context of vowel sandhis (*svarasandhi*)."

When this [sūtra] teaches the original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) by stating, "The protracted vowel remains in its original form," how is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For it is a principle that an effect can only occur when there is an existing subject to which that effect applies. By the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam*, the original state of the protracted vowel is prescribed. If the protracted vowel were non-existent (*asiddha*) within the context of vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*), then, because the protracted vowel itself would not exist, it would be illogical to prescribe its original state by taking the protracted vowel as the subject of the operation.

By this it is inferred that his intention is that the *asiddhatva* (non-validity) of a *pluta* vowel does not apply in the context of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*). Thus he says: "pluta... [etc.]. It is not intended to indicate validity generally for the subject matter of the section on vowel-sandhi; rather, with the intention that it applies only to the present case of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), he says: "or else" (*yadvā*), referring to the present context.

The reading *eva* is correct. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the status of being established (*siddhatva*) by virtue of its being a *pluta* vowel is [applicable] precisely to what is under discussion (*prakṛta*). By the rule *niāta ekāc* (Pāṇini 1.1.14), this very mention of the word *eka-* indicates that when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the entire class (*jāti*) is understood. Its meaning is that there is no mention of multiple instances based on properties such as *altva* (the property of being a vowel). Thus, the mention of the word *eka-* in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14) may be omitted.

Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that [term], because the vowel (*ac*) is a qualifier of the particle (*nipāta*), the meaning of the rule would be "a particle ending in a vowel receives the designation *pragṛhya*"; consequently, in examples such as *predaṃ brahma*, at the stage *pra-aidam*, since the particle *pra* ending in a vowel would be *pragṛhya*, the sandhi operation would not take place.

If one were to accept the meaning of the sūtra as being that "the designation *pragṛhya* applies to that vowel (*ac*) which is of the nature of a particle (*nipāta*), by relying on the fact that the particle qualifies the vowel," then since the particle *pra* lacks the form of a vowel (*aj-rūpatva*), it would not be subject to the *pragṛhya* designation. Consequently, raising the objection that the mention of *eka* (in the sūtra *eko 'ci*) would thus be redundant, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "In that case, since [the result] is already established, the fact that the Teacher makes the mention of *eka* while the mention of *ac* is being made indicates that 'in other instances where there is a mention of a phoneme (*varṇa*), there is a mention of the class (*jāti*')."

If there were the mention of "varṇa" (phoneme), then by the term *ac*, there would be the inclusion of a collection of multiple phonemes based on their status as vowels (*actva*). Consequently, in cases such as *au akarot*—where the word *titau* has its final portion [the vowel *au*] treated as a particle (*nipāta*) and thus designated as *pragṛhya*—the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the entire collection *au*. Therefore, the mention of "eka" (single) is made to prevent that [undesired result].

And once that [rule] has been established, by virtue of its capacity, there is no fault because the *pragṛhya* status belongs only to that single vowel *a* which is a particle (*nipāta*) having that form. Furthermore, the purpose elsewhere is stated in the Bhāṣya: "That which was said—that [the rule] is established because the mention of *hal* in *dambheḥ* denotes the class (*jāti*)—is thereby justified."

This is its meaning: from the root *dambh*, with the suffix *san*, by the rule "dambha icca" (Pāṇini 7.4.56), the vowel *a* of the root is changed to *i*, resulting in *dimbh-sa*. Then, because the suffix *san* is *kit* according to the rule "halantācca" (Pāṇini 1.2.10), the *n* of the penultimate vowel of the root is elided by the rule "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Following this, through the substitution of *bhaṣ* for *dh*, the form *dhīpsati* is obtained.

In this context, the meaning of the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10) is that a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a consonant (*hal*) in proximity to an *ic*-vowel shall be *kit*. In the state *dinbh-sa*, the suffix *san* does not follow a consonant (*hal*)—namely the letter *n*—in proximity to an *ic*-vowel; nor does it follow the letter *bh*, for that *bh* is not in proximity to an *ic*-vowel due to the intervention of the letter *n*. Consequently, in the absence of *kit*-status, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would be impossible.

If one accepts that the mention of a *varṇa* (phoneme) implies the inclusion of its *jāti* (universal class), then the purpose [of this rule] is established as follows: because the universal class *haltva* (being a consonant) resides in multiple instances, there is proximity (*ekasamīpatva*) to one [consonant], and from that [proximity], there is the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) to the suffix *san*. Consequently, when that [suffix] is *kit*, and when the *nakāra* of the verbal root is elided before that [suffix], the form *dhīpsati* is successfully derived. Regarding the sūtra *bahu-gaṇa-* (Pāṇini 1.1.23): in the rule *nadī-paurṇamāsī-āgrahāyaṇī-* (Pāṇini 5.4.110), the term *nadī* does not refer to words designated by the technical name *nadī*; this is because of the force of including the specific terms *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*.

In the sūtra *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṅkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), the inclusion of the term *saṅkhyā* (number) must be made. It must be stated that *bahū*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* receive the designation *saṅkhyā*, and that *saṅkhyā* itself receives the designation *saṅkhyā*.

Otherwise, according to the *paribhāṣā*—"between a technical (*kṛtrima*) and a non-technical (*akṛtrima*) term, the understanding applies to the technical one"—in the prescriptive rules (*vidhisūtra*) containing the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*), the term "number" would refer only to the technical numbers such as *bahūn*, *gaṇaḥ*, and so on, and not to numbers such as "one" (*ekādi*). This was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*. In response to this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "If, then, between a technical and a non-technical term, the understanding applies to the technical one, then [the rule] *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ* would also apply [undesirably] here."

An objection has been raised: if the principle of "artificial versus non-artificial" (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*) is accepted, then in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī*, the term *nadī* would refer only to those vowels ending in *ī* or *ū* that are designated by the technical term *nadī* as taught in the rule *yū stryākhyau nadī* (Pāṇini 1.4.3), and not to the word *nadī* itself; such is the meaning of the objection. To this objection, the *bhāṣya* provides the following resolution: "It will not [apply] because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the inclusion of the words *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*."

If the word *nadī* as taught by the technical definition (*saṃjñā*) in the grammatical treatise were to be included by the term *nadī* [in the rule], then since both *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* also possess the designation *nadī*—being always feminine and ending in long *ī*—their inclusion would already be established by that very term *nadī*. Consequently, their separate mention in the sūtra would be purposeless. Yet, that mention was indeed made in the sūtra *nadīpaurṇamāsī*. This indicates that the word *nadī* in this rule does not denote the technical designation *nadī*, but rather refers to the actual word *nadī* itself. Thus, there is no fault; such is the intended meaning.

This is what he says with the words beginning with *nadī*. Immediately following that, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *nadīpaurṇamāsī*, the following is stated: "If the word *nadī* in this sūtra were intended to refer to rivers as they are commonly known in the world, then words denoting specific rivers such as *gaṅgā* and *yamunā* would also be included by the term *nadī* in that sūtra. Anticipating this objection, it is said: 'The activity of the Teacher indicates that [the rule] does not apply to those specific [rivers]; for this reason, he includes the word *vipāṭ* among the *śarad-* group.'"

The suffix *ṭac*, which is prescribed by the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī* (Pāṇini 5.4.155), does not apply to words such as *gaṅgā* that denote specific rivers. If it were to apply, then the inclusion of the word *vipāṭ* in the list beginning with *śarat* would be redundant. For its purpose is to ensure the formation of *ṭac* in examples such as *prativipāśam* by means of the rule *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.107).

In this regard, the intention is as follows: because the word *nadī* in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī* includes even the word *vipāṭ*, which denotes a specific river, the suffix *ṭac* is established by that very rule; thus, the inclusion of the word *vipāṭ* in the *śarat*-group (the list beginning with *śarat*) is redundant. This redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in that rule, the word *nadī* does not refer to a specific river. This is what he states: "Because of the reading of the word *vipāṭ* in the *śarat*-group, by virtue of that indicator, there is no reference to a specific [river]. Furthermore, in the rules concerning numbers and substitutes, there is a reference to numbers such as *eka* and so forth.

In the rule for the formation of ordinal numbers (*kan*), because of the prohibition [of *kan*] by the sūtra "atiśadantāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.22), there is an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*). In order to refute the Vārttika which states that the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) must be explicitly mentioned in the sūtra "bahuguṇavatuḍati" (Pāṇini 1.1.23) so that numbers beginning with one (*ekādi*) may also be established as having the technical designation "number," it is argued—by means of that same indicatory mark—that numbers beginning with one are included in all instances where "number" is referred to. He says this: "in the instances of 'number' (*saṃkhyādeśeṣu*)."

In the prescriptive rules (*vidhisūtra*) containing the word *saṃkhyā* (number), such as those concerning the suffixes [beginning with *kan*], the term *saṃkhyā* includes numbers starting from one as well. He states the authority for this: "in the rule regarding *kan*" (*kanvidhau*). This is the meaning: the rule "from a number ending in *ati* or *śat*, the suffix *kan* [is applied] in the sense of 'worth'" (*saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*, Pāṇini 5.1.22), while prescribing *kan* for a number in the sense of "worth" (*ārhīya*), excludes it for numbers ending in *ti* or *śat*; for example, *sāptatikaḥ* (worth seventy) and *cātvāriṃśatkaḥ* (worth forty).

In both cases, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *tena krītam* (Pāṇini 5.1.37). If, in the rules prescribing [suffixes], the term *saṃkhyā* were not intended to include non-artificial numbers such as one (*eka*) and so forth, then since terms like *viṃśati* and *catvāriṃśat* would not be included under the designation *saṃkhyā*, the suffix *kan* would not apply to them; consequently, the prohibition *atiśadantāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.22) would find no scope. Therefore, that prohibition serves to indicate that even artificial numbers such as *eka* and the rest are to be understood in all instances where the term *saṃkhyā* occurs.

Pāṇini 1.1.24 states: *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* ("Those ending in ṣ or n are called ṣaṭ [six]"). The mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the word *aṣṭan-* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the term *ṣaṭ* applies to the number eight as well. The mention of the long vowel *ā* in *aṣṭan-* is for the sake of the augment *maṭ* (which becomes *nuṭ*). In the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*, the term *upadeśa* ("original enunciation") must be supplied. It should be stated: "A numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n* in its original enunciation (*upadeśe*) receives the designation *ṣaṭ*. Otherwise, in forms such as *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*, once the augment *num* is applied, they would end in *n*. Consequently, they would receive the designation *ṣaṭ*, leading to the undesirable result of the elision (*luk*) of the case-endings *jas* and *śas* by Pāṇini 7.1.22 (*ṣaḍbhyo luk*).

Regarding the form *aṣṭānām*: when *aṣṭan* and *ām* stand together, since the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84) applies both because it is subsequent and because it is obligatory, the *n* is replaced by *ā*. Consequently, because the word no longer ends in *n*, the designation *ṣaṭ* (the name for numerals six and those ending in *ṣ* or *n*) does not apply; and since the designation *ṣaṭ* is absent, the insertion of *nuṭ* by the rule *ṣaṭ-catur-bhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55) would be impossible. Having raised this objection, [the author] refutes it by showing that in cases such as *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*, the designation *ṣaṭ* is precluded by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), whereas in the case of *aṣṭānām*, even though the *ā*-substitution has occurred, the designation *ṣaṭ* is established by the force of a *jñāpaka* (an indicative mark).

In the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, it is said: "The mention of the long vowel [in the rule] regarding *aṣṭan*. By the rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.182), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is prescribed for case endings beginning with *śas* that follow the word *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel. In that context, the mention of the long vowel is made in order to prevent the acute accent of the case ending in the form *aṣṭasu*.

Furthermore, if the designation *ṣaṭ* were not applied to that which has undergone the substitution of *ātva*, then in the case of *aṣṭasu*, the rule "the penultimate syllable is acute" (*jhalyupottamam*, Pāṇini 6.1.180)—which, by virtue of its position as a subsequent rule relative to "aṣṭanaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.182), means that when a case-ending beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows the words *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate syllable of that word becomes acute—would result in the vowel following the *ṭ* being acute. Since the desired accent would thus be established, what is the purpose of including the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*)?

It should be stated that because [the rule] is an exception (*apavāda*), in the case of *aṣṭasu*, the accent prescribed by the rule "aṣṭanaḥ" would indeed prevail, overriding the accent prescribed by "jhalyupottamam. This is so even in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* occurs, as in *aṣṭāsu*, according to your own reasoning regarding that which has undergone the *ātva* substitution.

Since the designation *ṣaṭ* (six) does not apply [to *aṣṭan*], the penultimate accent (*upottama-svara*) does not occur; consequently, the rule "aṣṭana" (Pāṇini 6.1.172) retains its scope there, and thus it cannot be considered an exception (*apavāda*) to that [penultimate accent]. Therefore, in the form *aṣṭasu*, the penultimate accent alone will prevail due to its higher status (*paratva*), and since the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) would not otherwise apply, the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*)—which is made for the purpose of excluding that [case-ending accent]—would be entirely redundant. Yet, because it has been included, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the word *aṣṭan* retains the designation *ṣaṭ* even when it undergoes the substitution of *ātva* (the change to *aṣṭā-*).

Furthermore, even in a case where the *ātvam* (substitution of *ā*) has been applied, when the rule *jhalyupottamam* would otherwise have provided for the acute accent (*ṣaṭsvara*) on the penultimate syllable, the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt* is initiated; by the principle of *yena nāprāpte*, this very rule *aṣṭan* operates as an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, in the form *aṣṭasu*, even in the alternative where the vowel is not long (*adīrgha-pakṣa*), the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) would apply because [the rule *jhalyupottamam*] is an exception; therefore, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha-grahaṇa*) must be made to prevent that. In this way, the rule achieves its purpose within its own scope (*svāṃśe caritārthatā*).

The intended meaning is that, in the rule *anyatra prayojanam aṣṭānām* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the designation *ṣaṭ* applies even to that form where the vowel substitution (*ātva*) has occurred; thus, the addition of the augment *nuṭ* by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55) is established. Regarding the rule *sarvādīni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27): in the context of the designation *sarvanāman*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur because it is an indeclinable (*nipāta*). The forms *purāṇa* and *purātana* are established as referring to what is ancient and what is continuous respectively, being derived from the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

In the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhasarvādīni sarvanāmāni*, one might raise the objection that in the word *sarvanāma* (the technical term for "pronoun"), the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would apply by the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyāmagaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3). Having resolved this by stating that the absence of *ṇ*-substitution is due to *nipātana* (irregularity), one might further object: "Let there be the absence of *ṇ* by *nipātana*, but let the *ṇ*-substitution that is otherwise applicable also remain; for the purpose of *nipātana* is to establish the correctness of that specific form, not to exclude other forms. To this, it is replied: the *nipātana* is introduced precisely because the *ṇ*-substitution has not [otherwise] already occurred.

"It will be an exception (*bādhaka*) to that," is stated in the Bhāṣya. He says this with the words: "In the case of the technical name *sarvanāman*. Now, when the form *saṃ-tata-* remains, it is desired that the word *satata-* be established as correct by means of the elision (*lopa*) of the *m*, based on the rule "The forms *aparaspara-* etc. are established by nipātana when there is continuity of action" (Pāṇini 6.1.144). Since this nipātana for elision is commenced while the elision [of the nasal] prescribed by the rule "before a suffix beginning with a vowel" (6.1.68) has not yet taken effect, it would act as an exception to that elision. Consequently, the form *saṃtatam* would not be established.

Likewise, regarding the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105), there arises the concern that the word *purātana* would be sublated by the word *purāṇa* as prescribed therein; consequently, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word *purātana* would not be established. Anticipating this objection, he says: *purāṇapurātanau*. Thus, the correctness of both *saṃtata* and *satata*, as well as *purāṇa* and *purātana*, is established solely by their inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, and not by means of a specific nipātana (irregular derivation). Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the intended meaning.

In the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, the maxim (*paribhāṣā*) is recited: "The irregular forms (*nipātana*s) are indeed sublaters [of general rules]. Regarding the rule *pūrvaparā* (Pāṇini 1.1.34): the list of words beginning with *pūrva* occurs first, while the list of technical suffixes (*pratyāhāra*) occurs later. This is known from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *pūrvādibhyo vā* (Pāṇini 8.1.16), where the mention of the word "nine" (*nava*) serves as the evidence; for in the list of suffixes, there are exactly nine items beginning with *pūrva*.

Regarding the rule *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām*: for what purpose are the words beginning with *pūrva* listed individually in the *jas* case ending for the sake of the optional (*vibhāṣā*) designation? For indeed, they are listed in the *gaṇa* (list) with specific meanings for the sake of the compulsory (*nitya*) designation as pronominals (*sarvanāman*). In that case, the rule should have been stated simply as "the nine beginning with *pūrva*."

Anticipating the objection that this [usage] might be considered a later innovation (*prāptābhiyāṣā*), he provides the following resolution: "This would indeed be the case if the *gaṇapāṭha* were prior and the *Pāṇinisūtrapāṭha* were subsequent; however, this is not so, as there is no evidence for such a sequence. Having thus established the point, the *Bhāṣya* supports the priority of the *gaṇapāṭha* over the *Pāṇinisūtras* by means of an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*): "In that case, the activity of the Teacher indicates that 'this is the earlier recension' and 'this, moreover, is the later recension.'"

Regarding the fact that [Pāṇini] employs the mention of "nine" in the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*, it is because there are exactly nine items beginning with *pūrva*. Thus he says: "The list of the *gaṇa* is prior. In the sūtra *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*, the mention of "nine" is made for the purpose of excluding *tyad* and the other pronouns. If the *gaṇa*-reading were a fixed arrangement, then by the expression *pūrvādibhyaḥ* the *tyad* and others would also be included; therefore, the mention of "nine" must be made in order to exclude them.

The point is this: if the *Pāṇini-sūtra* existed prior to the *Gaṇapāṭha*, then since the nine [words] beginning with *pūrva* would have been specifically designated in the *Pāṇini-sūtra* by the three rules beginning with *pūrvaparābhyām* (P. 1.1.34), there would be no possibility of including the nine [words] beginning with *tyad* under the rule *pūrvādibhyaḥ* (P. 7.1.16). Consequently, the inclusion of the word *nañ* [in that rule] would be redundant; thus, it is inferred that the *Gaṇapāṭha* is older. The phrase "sūtrapāṭhe" means "in the recitation of the *Pāṇini-sūtras*."

Due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1), etc., there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words such as *pūrva* by means of the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth. [End of commentary on] *vi*.ṭa.

Regarding the doubt as to why, when it would have been more concise to simply read "nine beginning with *pūrva*" in that very same sūtra, the three sūtras beginning with "*pūrvapara*" are instead recited specifically, the resolution is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In that case, this is the purpose: so that there may not be an exclusion [of these words] by the exclusion of 'two and so forth' (*dvyādi-paryudāsena*). Kaiyaṭa explains the intention behind this as follows: "After listing the *tyad*-class words, some have included the words beginning with *pūrva* in that list."

In that regard, by the rule *kiṃsarvanāmabahubhyo 'dvyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.2), there arises the contingency of a prohibition of the suffixes beginning with *tasil* after words such as *pūrva*. However, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) applies to those words, the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are prescribed for them. Consequently, the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth (*dvyādiparyudāsa*) would be sublated. Immediately following this, the author of the Bhāṣya, refuting this solution, says: "Even this is not a purpose [for the rule]. The activity of the Teacher indicates that there is no sublation of these [words] by the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth."

"Because he provides this specific grammatical formulation (*nipātana*) stating *pūrvatrāsiddham*. If, by means of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words such as *dvi* and so on, there were a prohibition of suffixes like *tasil* after words beginning with *pūrva*, then the reference to the word *pūrva* in the form of the suffix *-tral* (as in *pūrvatrasiddham*) would be without authority. The meaning is that, by the force of this very reference, it is indicated that there is no exclusion of *pūrva* and the others through the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth. Keeping all of this in mind, he says: "On account of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, etc."

And by the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), the term *uttaratra* from the Vārttika—"If it is argued [that the substitution of *ś* for *s*] is due to the presence of *j*, then because of the absence of *ḍh* in what follows, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an exception"—is referred to. According to the view that "a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *m* is indeclinable" (Pāṇini 1.1.39), the word *praśān* is read among the *svarādi* (indeclinables); therefore, by this *jñāpaka*, it does not receive the designation of *avyaya* through the application of the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

A twofold interpretation has been given for the sūtra *kṛnmejanta* (Pāṇini 1.1.39): one interpretation is that a word ending in a kṛt-affix which ends in either a long *m* or an *e*-vowel is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); the second interpretation is that a word ending in a kṛt-affix which ends in a long *m* is designated as an indeclinable.

Regarding this, in the second explanation, one might raise the objection that when the suffix *kvip* is elided after the root *mā* preceded by the prefix *pra*, even though the suffix is lost, the form *pratām* retains its status as a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix) and its status as ending in the letter *m* by virtue of the rule on the "characteristics of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, it would be subject to the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Anticipating this, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "The activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation of an indeclinable does not occur by virtue of the characteristics of a suffix; for he recites the word *praśān* among the *svarādi* (indeclinables)."

If the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) were to occur by relying on the status of being a *kṛt*-derived form through the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), then even in the word *praśān*, since the substitution of *n* for *t* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it would possess the quality of ending in *m*. Furthermore, because it would have the status of a *kṛt*-derived form via the characteristic of a suffix, its status as an indeclinable would be established by the rule "kṛnmejanta" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) alone; consequently, the inclusion of the word *praśān* in the *svarādi* list for the purpose of designating it as an indeclinable would not be necessary. Yet, it has been included there. Therefore, the meaning is that this [inclusion] indicates that the designation of an indeclinable does not occur by means of the characteristic of a suffix.

This is what he states with the words beginning "kṛdantam" and so forth. Regarding the rule *tisṛcatasrorṅīṃbabhāve* ("In the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, [the forms] *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* [are used]"), the prohibition of lengthening in the *nām* context by the rule *na tisṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ṭhakṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), after citing the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the technical rule concerning the destruction of a cause), many purposes (*prayojana*) for it are enumerated. Among those, "for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* to *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*" is also one such purpose.
