When the suffixes *jaś* and *śas* follow the words *tri* and *catur*, the substitutes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are applied in the feminine; because these forms then end in *ṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* would be required by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5). However, that [application of *ṅīp*] does not occur due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*. Having made the presence of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) the cause for the production of the substitutes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, those two substitutes do not become the cause for the *ṅīp* which destroys that very [condition]. The intention is this: if *ṅīp* were present, it would create an intervention, resulting in the loss of the presence of the case-ending.

And the author of the Bhāṣya refuted this purpose—establishing it instead by means of the power of an *jñāpaka* (an indicator)—prior to the absence of the suffix *ṅīp*: "This too is not a purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur when the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* have been applied; for he teaches the prohibition of lengthening in the *nām* [vowel] in the rule 'na tisṛcatasṛ'."

Regarding the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*: since these are separated from the suffix *nām* by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, they lack the condition of being followed by *nām*; consequently, the rule *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3), which prescribes lengthening, would not apply. Therefore, what is the purpose of explicitly prohibiting that lengthening? The prohibition of lengthening indicates that the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after these two stems. Consequently, since the absence of *ṅīp* in the forms *tistraḥ* and *catastraḥ*—even for the case-endings *jaś* and *śas*—is established by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the point is that the absence of *ṅīp* here does not serve as an illustration of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*.

This is what he says: "In *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, there is the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, etc. Now, if the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the destruction of a cause) is accepted, then in forms such as *yā* and *sā*, the suffix *ṭāp* would not occur; for when the case-ending *su* follows the words *yat* and *tat*, the *da* is changed to *a* by the rule "*tyadādīnām aḥ*" and, after the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the stem ends in *a*.

One might raise the objection: "The suffix *ṭāp* must be prescribed by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*; however, that is not possible. For the property of having a vowel (*atva*), which is caused by the presence of a case-ending (*vibhakti-saṃnipāta-nimittaka*), cannot serve as the cause for a *ṭāp* that destroys that very [condition]. Anticipating this, he says: "By such indications (*jñāpaka*) as the rule *ṭhana-yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45), it is known that the *paribhāṣā* concerning the destruction of a grammatical configuration (*saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*) is not universally valid (*anityā*)."

According to the previously stated method, if the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were not applied to the pronouns *yad* and *tad* due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*, then the sūtra-author’s own usage of the forms *yā* and *sā*—which end in *ṭāp*—would be inconsistent. Therefore, the meaning is that the authority of this specific usage (*nirdeśaprāmāṇyena*) necessitates the assumption that the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*). Consequently, in forms such as *rāmāya*, the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) is successfully established.

Otherwise, it should be understood that since the substitution of *y* caused by the conjunction of vowels (*adanta-saṃnipāta*) would not be a cause for the long vowel that destroys that very conjunction, such a long vowel would be impossible. [Pāṇini 1.1.43: *jhrjñā.ṭa suḍaḍḍatdh;na*. By stating this as an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound where the members are not semantically connected), it is indicated that the particle *a*—meaning "prohibition"—is non-animate (*aprāṇāṇika*).

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *jhra vi.ṭa suḍaḍḍatdh; napuṃsakasya*, it is stated: "This should be regarded as an *asamartha-samāsa* [an irregular compound] with respect to the word *anapuṃsakasya*. For there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the negative particle *nañ* and the neuter gender. With what, then? With the verb *bhavati*. It means 'it does not belong to the neuter'. By this, having accepted the *asamartha-samāsa*, the sūtra is explained as being intended to express a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).

In this context, if the indeclinable *a* were something having the sense of negation, then by accepting *a napuṃsakasya* as separate words, one would obtain a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—namely, "it does not apply to the neuter"—even without resorting to an *asamarthasamāsa*. Therefore, the assumption of an *asamarthasamāsa* would be unnecessarily cumbersome and should not have been resorted to. Yet, that very assumption indicates that there is no such indeclinable *a* with the sense of negation.

Furthermore, the phrase *anapuṃsakasya* is a compound word (*samasta-pada*). The intention is that the authors of the Bhāṣya stated it in this way because they considered that, without its being an *asamartha-samāsa*, its function as a prohibitive term could not be obtained. By this, those who interpret the Vedic scripture *asad brahmeti veda cet* by treating *a* as a separate word and explaining it as "if one does not know that Brahman is existent" (*brahma sat*) are to be understood as refuted. [Jñā.ṭ. *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Sūtra 1.1.51).

The mention of *bhrātuṣputra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule for the substitution of *ṣ*—namely, *idudupadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.41)—does not apply to what follows an *ekādeśa*. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, which prescribes that the substitute *aṇ* for the vowel *ṛ* is followed by the augment *r*, one would admit the application of the *rapara* augment even to an *aṇ* that occurs in place of both *ṛ* and another vowel; for that *ekādeśa* does not lose its status as being in the place of *ṛ*.

Furthermore, in the case of *mātṛ-ṅas*, when the *ṛ* and *a* are replaced by *u* followed by *r* according to the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111), the form *mātuḥ s* is obtained. Then, by the rule *rāt sasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), the *s* is elided and the *r* is replaced by a visarga, resulting in *mātuḥ*. Subsequently, upon conjunction with the word *karoti*, since the visarga is not part of an affix (*apratyaya*), the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) requires the substitution of *ṣ* for the visarga.

Nor does the phrase "not of a suffix" (apratyayasya) mean "different from a part of a suffix. One should not argue that since the vowel *a* is a part of a suffix, its substitute, the visarga (*viśarga*), must also be a part of a suffix, and thus how could there be the application of the rule for *ṣatva*? For even if one somehow concedes that the substitute *ur* (which stands in place of *a*) is a part of a suffix, it remains difficult to establish that the visarga—which occupies the position of the *r* within that *ur*—is itself a part of a suffix.

Then, suspecting that the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) would be unavoidable, he says: "the mention of *bhrātuṣputra*. According to the previously stated method, since the substitution of *ṣ* in the word *bhrātuṣputra* is already established by the rule *idudupadhasya* itself, the inclusion of this word in the *kaskādi* group—which serves the purpose of establishing *ṣatva*—is redundant. Being thus redundant, it indicates that there is no *ṣatva* for a visarga following what has as its cause a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation. The meaning is: there is no *ṣatva* for a visarga that follows that which has a rule of single-substitution as its cause.

The meaning is that because the rule *ṛto ṅsi ṅsoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.110) is the cause for the letter *u*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for the visarga following it; thus, in the case of *mātuḥ karoti*, there is no occurrence of *ṣ*. However, in the word *bhrātuṣputra*, the substitution of *ṣ* is established due to its inclusion in the *kaskādi* group. In the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, however, it is stated that the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for a visarga caused by a rule regarding a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

In that context, it should be understood that because the *repha* (the letter *r*) in the constituent part of *ur* is the substitute for the *visarga*, the [substitution] is caused by the rule of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). Regarding the doubt as to why this, which is not recorded in the *Bhāṣya*, is recited in the *Kaumudī*, it is stated thus in the *Manoramā*: "In the original source (*ākara*), however, the prevalent reading is 'caused by the rule of a single-substitute' (*ekādeśa-śāstra-nimittāt*). In that [reading], the rule of a single-substitute is the cause of the *ukāra*."

"Therefore, this is the meaning. However, in the *Śabdaratna*, it is stated: "The result [of the rule] is said to be the prevention of the *ṣatva* substitution in cases such as *oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi*; and since that [result] is Vedic (*chāndasa*), the form with the genitive ending (*oṣadhīnām*) alone has been read [in the commentary]. Bhairavamiśra and others have maintained that the reading with the ablative ending (*oṣadhībhyaḥ*) alone is correct; enough of this elaboration here. Regarding the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53): although the substitution of *tāt* for the suffixes *tu* and *hi* in the imperative (*loṭ*) when expressing a benediction (*āśis*) would be established by the rule *loṭa eruprakaraṇe tuhyostā dāśiṣī* (6.4.62), the fact that the marker *ṅ* is attached to *tāt* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *tāt* is a complete substitute (*sarvādeśa*).

Objection: By the rule *ṅicca*, it is stated that a substitute containing the marker *ṅ* (an *itsaṃjñaka*) occurs in place of the final [element]. Consequently, since the substitute *tātaṅ* also possesses the quality of being *ṅit*, one might suspect that when *tātaṅ* replaces *tu* or *hi*, it would apply to the final *u* or *i*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the section concerning *er* for the imperative (*loṭ*). Even without the quality of being *ṅit*, by the rule *eruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86)...

In the section concerning final substitution (*antyādeśa*) under Pāṇini 3.4.86, when *tāt* is prescribed, the status of being a final substitute is already established; thus, the indicatory letter *ṅ* in *tātaṅ* would otherwise be redundant. This redundancy serves as an indicator that *tātaṅ* is not a final substitute. By means of this, it suggests that the property of being *ṅit* has the result of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Consequently, the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53)—which finds its application in cases like *anaṅ* where the *ṅ* serves no other purpose—does not apply to *tātaṅ*, because its *ṅ* possesses a valid purpose in the sense of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

And thus, the intention is that *tāt* is a substitute for the whole [of the original element] because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). [Pāṇini 1.1.55: "That which consists of more than one phoneme [is a substitute for the whole]. Here, the statement "that which has *ś* as an indicatory letter (*śit*) is for the whole" indicates that the status of having more than one phoneme is not caused by an *anubandha*. [Objection: But surely, since forms such as *auś*, *iś*, and *śī* are already established as substitutes for the whole simply because they consist of more than one phoneme, the inclusion of the term *śit* in the rule "anekāl śitsarvasya" is redundant. To this, he says: "here... [referring to the following explanation].

Therefore, having attached the *anubandha* as a formal marker (*alaṃ*), one does not rely on its being "consisting of more than one phoneme" (*anekāltva*). Only if it were "consisting of more than one phoneme" after discarding the *anubandha* would it be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). However, in the case of forms such as *auś*, since they lack the status of "consisting of more than one phoneme" once the *anubandha* is removed, they would not obtain the status of a whole-replacement; thus, the inclusion of the term *śit* (to indicate that which has a *ś* as an *anubandha*) is for the purpose of ensuring their status as whole-replacements—this is the underlying intention. Consequently, the result to be understood is that [by this implication] forms such as *arvaṇas tṛ* do not become whole-replacements.

In this treatise, certain technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) of this kind have also been incorporated. We do not know the purpose for that. [Regarding the rule *sthānivad ādeśo* (Pāṇini 1.1.56): It is known from the fact that the augment *ś* is applied to *śyan* and others in an exception (*apavāda*), which indicates that what was done by the general rule (*utsarga*) applies here. Alternatively, it is established by continuing the word "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [from the preceding sūtra], such that the substitute (*ādeśa*) of that which is designated by the sixth case is like the original (*sthānivat*).

In the sūtra *sthānivadādeśo’nalvidhau* ("a substitute is like the original in respect of that which is not an operation concerning an *al*"), if the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* were merely a transformation of cognition—meaning that when the cognition of the substitute arises, the cognition of the original must be performed—then one might raise the following objection: even in the case of the suffix *ka*, which is prescribed as an exception by the sūtra *āto’nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), since it would be a *sthānivadbhāva* for *aṇ*, whatever grammatical operation applies to *aṇ* would consequently apply here as well. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: "An operation prompted by the general rule (*utsarga*) does not take effect when an exception (*apavāda*) is present."

And thus, when the suffix *ka* is an exception (*apavāda*), the operation conditioned by the general rule (*utsarga*) suffix *aṇ* does not take place; therefore, there is no fault. In this regard, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the addition of the marker *ś* in *śyan* and other suffixes which are exceptions to *śap*. For if, in the case of an exception, the operation performed by the general rule were to occur through the principle of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), then since *yan* would also—by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*—be treated as having the marker *ś* like *śap*, the operation dependent on the presence of the marker *ś* would already occur [for *yan*] as well. Consequently, the addition of the marker *ś* in *śyan* and others would be purposeless.

This indicates that once an exception (*apavāda*) has been applied, the operation prescribed by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not take effect. Alternatively, one may explain the rule *sthānivadādeśaḥ* as follows: by carrying over the word *ṣaṣṭhī* from the preceding rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (Pāṇini 1.1.49), changing it into the instrumental case, and supplying the word *nirdiṣṭasya*, the rule should be interpreted as: "An substitute (*ādeśa*) in the place of that which is indicated by the genitive is like the original (*sthānin*). Furthermore, the suffix *kap* is not prescribed in the place of the *aṇ* that is indicated by the genitive.

Therefore, there is no fault because [the substitute] does not behave like the original (sthānivat); thus, two-fold solutions have been provided in the source treatises. He states this with the words "it is not an exception" (*nāpavāda*), and so forth. Regarding the word "established" (*siddha*): the remainder of the sense is that it follows the maxim that "in the case of an exception, the operation of the general rule [does not apply]. In the case where the substitution of *ātha* is to be performed, by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule "āhasthaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.35), the augment *iṭ* does not occur after *ah*.

In the *sthānivadādeśa* rule itself, [the author] raises an objection: if a substitute (*ādeśa*) is treated like its original (*sthānin*), then in the second person singular present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *brū*, since *āha* is the substitute for *brū*, the augment *īṭ* would apply to the suffix *thal* following it by the rule "bruva īṭ" (Pāṇini 7.3.93). Consequently, the author of the Vārttika stated that a prohibition of this *īṭ* must be formulated. Refuting that, the author of the Bhāṣya said that a prohibition of *īṭ* after *āha* need not be stated, because it is established by a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) that *īṭ* does not occur after *āha*. If one asks what the *jñāpaka* is, it is the prescription of the substitution of *tha* in the rule "āhasthaḥ."

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). To explain: the rule *āhasthaḥ* prescribes the substitution of *tha* for *āha* when followed by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant. *Āttha* is the illustrative example. If, in this case, one were to assume that *āha* possesses the status of *brū* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, and consequently the *thala* affix following it were to take the augment *īṭ*, then—since the *thala* affix beginning with the vowel *ī* would no longer begin with a *jhal* consonant—the substitution of *tha* could not occur when that [affix] follows. Therefore, this indicates that the substitution of *tha*, which is prescribed when a *jhal* follows, does not occur for *āha* when *īṭ* is present.

If it is argued: "But surely, by the rule *āhasthaḥ*, the substitution of *tha* is prescribed when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound follows [the root]. Even though the augment *iṭ* has now been added to *thala*, so that it no longer begins with a *jhal*, the status of beginning with a *jhal* existed previously; therefore, by taking that into account, the substitution of *tha* will occur. Thus, since there is no lack of purpose [for the rule], how can this [rule] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?"—[The answer is: if one were to rely on the consideration of what existed previously, then even for the [suffixes] *ṇal* and the others, the status of beginning with a *jhal* would exist by taking their original state (*sthānyavasthā*) into account; thus, [the rule would apply] to all five [perfect endings].

It would follow that the form *āha* is obtained from [the root] *brū* when followed by *thal*. If this were the case, then instead of stating the substitution of *āha*, one would simply have prescribed the substitution of *ātha* in the rule "After *brū*, there is *ātha* for the first five [roots], and *bruvaḥ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.84), and one would not have composed a separate rule such as "āhastha. Since a separate rule has been made, it is understood that here the status of having previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*) is not accepted. Consequently, among the five [roots], *thal* alone is the one beginning with a *jhal* sound.

If *īṭ* were to occur for that [root], its status as beginning with a *jhal* consonant would be destroyed; consequently, the substitution of *th* prescribed after a *jhal*-beginning suffix would become devoid of scope (*anavakāśa*). Therefore, it indicates that *īṭ* does not follow *ah*. Having taken all this into consideration, he says: "when the substitution of *ā* is to be performed. By the force of the *tapara* notation in the rules *jñā.ṭa* "ṭhagotaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.90) and "otaḥ" (6.1.93), there is no substitution of *ṇi* or *v* in cases such as *citraguḥ* and *citrakum*.

In the section enumerating objections regarding the *sthānivat* sūtra (*jhrviṭa`), a doubt is raised that the properties of being *ṇit* and the substitution of *ā* would apply to the word *go*. In response, it is stated in the original treatise (*ākara*) that because of the functional significance of the *tapara* marker, these two properties do not apply. This is what [the author] expresses by saying "gotaḥ."

The intention is as follows: if an ādeśa were to be treated like its original (sthānivadbhāva), then in the case of *citraguḥ*—where, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose cows are brindled," the vowel *o* is replaced by the short *u* according to the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48)—that *u* would, by virtue of being like its original, still be an *o*-vowel. Consequently, it would follow that the suffix *su*, which is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, occurs after the word *go*. This would trigger the application of the rule *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90), whereby the suffix is treated as having a *ṇit* marker; and because of that *ṇit* status, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.1.15) would require the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel *u*.

[The objection: One would thus obtain [the form] *trigum* in the case of *triguṇam*. Because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the vowel *u*, it would be treated as *o*; consequently, when *am* follows a word ending in *o* and an *ac* vowel follows, the rule "auto'mśasoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.93) would require the substitution of *ā* for both the preceding and following sounds. [The resolution: However, the solution is that in both rules [concerned], the term *otaḥ* contains the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*). Since this makes it a rule concerning a specific phonetic element (*alvidhi*), the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning a phonetic element" (*analvidhau*) applies, and thus there is no status of the substitute. Indeed, the purpose of the marker *t* is to exclude the *u* in the word *gu* (as in *triguṇam*).

If the rule were to apply there as well by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, then the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) would be purposeless. [This concerns] Pāṇini 1.1.59: *dvirvacane’ci*. However, the mention of the vowel (*ajgrahaṇa*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the existence of *rūpasthānivadbhāva* (the status of being a substitute based on form). For *jeghrīyate* is indeed its counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). [Objection: But surely the meaning of the rule *dvirvacane’ci* is that when a vowel (*ac*) which is the cause of reduplication follows, a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśaḥ*) is like the original (*sthānivat*).

Furthermore, in the view that this is an "extension of the operation" (*kāryātideśa*), forms such as *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ* would not be established. In the case of *kṛ-atuḥ*, when the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution to become *r*, resulting in *k-r-atuḥ*, the doubling prescribed for a monosyllable (*ekāc*) cannot apply because the syllable is now vowelless (*anack*). Even if it were to apply by means of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), due to the extension of the operation, it would apply only to what was already stated regarding the *yaṇ*-substitution. Consequently, in the state *k-r-k-r-atuḥ*, after the application of *halādiśeṣa* and other rules, the form would result only in *ccakratuḥ*.

Fearing that the form *cakratuḥ* would not be established because it is distinguished by the practice [of reduplication] joined with a non-vowel (*akāra*), he says: "But the mention of *ac*. The intention is this: one should not think that the extension (*atideśa*) in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*—namely, "a substitute is like the original"—is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), in the sense that whatever effect occurs when there is an original element (*sthānin*) also occurs when there is its substitute (*ādeśa*). Rather, it is an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*), in the sense that whatever form belongs to the original element also belongs to its substitute.

Likewise, in the case of *kṛ-atuḥ*, once the substitution (*yaṇādeśa*) has been applied, the form *cakratuḥ* is established through the doubling of the element *kṛ*—which is characterized by the vowel *ṛ*—by virtue of the extension of the original form (*sthānirūpātideśa*). Thus, there is no fault. As for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the extension of the form itself, it is the mention of the vowel *ac* in the rule *aci*. For its purpose is to ensure that in forms such as *jeghrīyate*, there is no application of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*).

From the root *ghrā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, by the rule "ī ghrā-dhmoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.31), the vowel *ā* of the root becomes *ī*, resulting in *ghrī*. Following this, after reduplication (*dvitva*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, *cutva*, and *jaśtva*, and finally the strengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule "guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.82), the form *jeghrīyate* is obtained.

In this context, because the *yaṅ* suffix is the cause for doubling (*dvitva*), when that suffix follows, there would be a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*) for the substitute *īkāra* (the result of the *ākāra* replacement) by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*; consequently, upon doubling the element *ghrā*, the resulting form would be *jaghrāyata*. To prevent this, the mention of *ac* (*ajgrahaṇam*) was made. Once that is established, the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* for a substitute of an *ac* vowel occurs only when another *ac* vowel follows as the cause for doubling.

Furthermore, since even that which is the cause of doubling (*dvitvanimitta*) does not possess the status of being a vowel (*actva*), there can be no transfer (*atideśa*) of the form *ākāra* to the *īkāra* by virtue of its being a *sthānivadbhāva* when that [vowel] follows; thus, when *ghrī* undergoes doubling, the desired form *jeghrīyate* is established. In that case, if one adopts the view that there is a transfer of the operation (*kāryātideśapakṣa*), then only the operation of doubling itself would be transferred to *ghrī*, and since there is no transfer of the form *ākāra*, there is no fault even if *sthānivadbhāva* applies—so what is the purpose of including the mention of *ac* (*ajgrahaṇa*)?

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *aj* (vowel) in the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which effects the extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being an original element (*sthānivattva*), indicates that this extension refers to the *rūpa* (form). This is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the status of being an original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇi*). [Objection: But in forms such as *avannāvayiṣati* and *avacukṣāvayiṣati*, the augment *suṭ* occurs after the causative forms of the roots *ava-nu* and *ava-ksu*.

In that context, when the suffix *ṇic* follows—as in the case of the root *nau*—the vowel *u* undergoes *vṛddhi* by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), and the *ā* substitution (*āvādeśa*) takes place. Thus, the form *nāv-i-sa* is established. At this point, if one were to apply the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* to the *āvādeśa*, thereby extending the form of the diphthong *au* [to the substitute], then upon the doubling of the word *nau* in the sequence *nau nau isa*, the *ābhya-sthasvara* would apply, followed by the *āvādeśa*, resulting in the form *nunāvayiṣati*. However, in that situation, the application of *sthānivadbhāva* is difficult to establish.

By the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for an *aj*-substitute is stated only when an *ac* vowel follows that serves as the cause for reduplication (*dvitva*). Since the affix *ṇic* is not here the cause for reduplication, one might ask how an *aj*-substitute applied after it could obtain the status of being like the original. To this, he says: *oḥ puyaṇji*. Thus, the status of being like the original (*sthānivattva*) indeed exists for an *aj*-substitute applied after *ṇic*; in this regard, the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini 7.4.80) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The meaning of that sūtra is as follows: when there is a suffix beginning with *sa* (san), the *it* (short *i*) substitution shall occur for the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of that base (*aṅga*), provided that the following sounds are *pa*, *ya*, *ṇ*, *ja*, or *ka*, and they are preceded by an *ava*-vowel. An example is *yiyaviṣati*. If the expression *pu-yaṇ-ji* were not stated therein, the *it* substitution would also occur for the *u* of the reduplicated syllable in forms such as *avanunāvayiṣati*; therefore, *pu-yaṇ-ji* is stated in order to prevent that.

If, moreover, there were no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) for what is produced by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then the form of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) containing the vowel *u* would be impossible here; because the vowel *u* would not exist in the reduplication, the substitution of the vowel *i* would not take place, so what would be the use of including the term "pu-yaṇ-jis"? The point is that since that [term] has been included, it indicates that *sthānivadbhāva* does indeed apply to what is produced by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). [Note: *ṭha-pratyayasya luk* (Sūtra 1.1.61)].

By the force of the word *pratyayasya* ("of the suffix") in this context, and by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *lugvā duha* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), *luk* and the other elisions are replacements of the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Regarding the rule *jhrviṭaṭhapratyayasya lukślulupaḥ*, the author of the Vārttika stated that the mention of the word *pratyaya* ("suffix") is for the purpose of establishing that *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are replacements of the whole. However, the author of the Bhāṣya, refuting that [view], said: "Even this is not a purpose."

The activity of the Teacher indicates that *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are replacements for the whole [stem]. This is because, in the rule "optionally *luk* after *duh*, *dihi*, *lih*, and *guh* when the *taṅ* [suffixes] beginning with a dental follow" (*lugvā duhadihalihaguhāmātmanepade dantye*), he prescribes *luk* even though elision (*lopa*) was already applicable. By the rule "optionally *luk* after *duh*" (*lugvā duha*, Pāṇini 7.3.73), the optional elision of the *kṣa* suffix of the roots *duh* and others is prescribed when a *taṅ* suffix beginning with a dental follows; examples include *aduggha* and *adhukṣata*.

In that context, regarding the sūtra *ghorlopo leṭi vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.70), although the desired result could have been established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *lopa* from the preceding rule, the explicit mention of *lug* serves to indicate that the disappearance (*adarśana*) prescribed by the mention of *lug* is a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). As for *lopa*, however, it applies only to the final phoneme. If *lug* were also to apply only to the final phoneme, then the desired result could have been achieved simply by the continued application of the term *lopa*; what, then, would be the purpose of mentioning *lug*? The point is that the inclusion of the term *lug* is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its status as a total replacement.

He states this very point with the words "by the force of the word *pratyayasya*," and so forth. This is according to the view of the Vārttika. According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, he says: "and because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *lugvā duhaḥ*. Regarding the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62): since there is a prohibition by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), it is known from that indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even operations such as elision (*luk*) and others are indeed cases of "elision" (*lopa*). Now, regarding the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*: even when there is an elision of a suffix, an operation caused by that suffix [should still take place].

It is said [in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*]: "In that case, when there is the elision (*luk*) of an affix, an operation conditioned by that affix does not take effect, because *luk* is a form of deletion (*lopa*). Consequently, in examples such as *pañca* and *sapta*, when *jaś* and *śas* are elided by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), the status of being a *pada* would not belong to *pañcan*, *saptan*, and so on; and due to the absence of *pada*-status, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would not occur. For the status of being a *pada* must be asserted by relying on the fact of ending in a *sup* [case-ending], which is established through the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of an affix despite its elision)."

Anticipating the objection that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) applies only when there is a *lopa* (elision) of the suffix and not when there is a *luk* elision, he says: "Because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.63], *na lumatāṅgasya*. This prohibition—that when a suffix is elided by the word *luk* or similar terms, the operations of the stem (*aṅgakārya*) conditioned by the suffix do not apply—is only appropriate when there was a prior possibility for the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* to apply. A prohibition is illogical where there has been no prior application. Furthermore, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* applies to what is elided by the term *luk* only when *luk* itself is designated as a *lopa* (elision), because of the statement [in Pāṇini 1.1.62]: "*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*" ("When a suffix is elided, the operation conditioned by the suffix takes place").

Therefore, the underlying intention is that by the fact that negation would otherwise be inexplicable (*niṣedhānyathānupapatti*), it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that elision (*lop*) applies to *luk* and the others as well. [Regarding the rule] *tasminniti* (Pāṇini 1.1.66): under the view that these two rules (*tasmin* and *tasmāt*) are generators of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-prakalpaka*), the seventh and fifth cases do not simultaneously generate [the genitive]. This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84).

If it is accepted that the *paribhāṣā* "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (P. 1.1.66) provides a genitive for the preceding element, and the *paribhāṣā* "tasmādityuttarasya" (P. 1.1.67) provides a genitive for the subsequent element, then in a rule where both the locative and the ablative are heard, there would be the provision of a genitive for both the preceding and the subsequent elements. Consequently, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) would apply to both.

Just as in the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātuke'nudāttam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *tāsya-ādibhyaḥ* should effect a change into the genitive case for the locative case (*saptamī*) in *lasārvadhātuke*; likewise, this locative case in *lasārvadhātuke* should effect a change into the genitive case for the ablative case in *tāsya-ādibhyaḥ*. Thus, this locative case in *lasārvadhātuke* should effect a change into the genitive case for the ablative case in *tāsya-ādibhyaḥ*.

In this regard, having raised the objection that the property of being *anudātta* (unaccented) would result for both [the preceding and following elements], he says: "of these two rules. If, due to the mention of both, there were a mutual application such that the meaning of the sentence were: "when a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix follows *tāsi* and so on, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix becomes *anudātta* after *tāsi* and so on," then even in cases such as "āṭguṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87), because of the continued application of the word "in a vowel" (*aci*), one would have to rely on a mutual application and explain it as: "there is *guṇa* substitution of a vowel for a vowel, and of a vowel following a vowel."

If the *guṇa* substitution were established for both the preceding and the following sounds, the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.84) would be redundant. Since that rule has indeed been composed, it follows that the simultaneous application of both the ablative (*pañcamī*) and the locative (*saptamī*) cases is not accepted here. For if both were relied upon, the ablative designation would be stronger; consequently, because the ablative alone would be the basis for the application of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the *guṇa* would belong to the subsequent sound. Therefore, the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" is established so that the *guṇa* may be achieved for both the preceding and the following sounds.

Furthermore, in rules such as *tāsy-anudātta-it* (Pāṇini 6.4.71), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) effects the substitution of a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the locative (*saptamī*). Thus, the intention is that the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) applies only to the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following *tāsī* and so on, and not to both the preceding and following elements; therefore, there is no fault. Regarding the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72): by the statement *nedamadasorakoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.11), it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that when the word *akoh* is used, the term *tad* included therein is understood to include its constituent parts (*tadekadeśabhūtam*).

Indeed, even if one explains the rule *jhrvidṛṭ* as a qualifier such that the technical designation applies to that [element] and to what ends with it, the substitution of *śī* for the nominative plural *jas* would still not apply after *sarvaka*, because of the presence of the suffix *akac*.

For instance, when *sarva* is followed by *jas*, as in *sarva + akac + jas* resulting in *sarvaka + jas*, the form *sarvaka* lacks the status of being the word *sarva* itself and also lacks the property of having *sarva* as its final member. Consequently, because it is not captured either by the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ prātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 1.1.42) or by the rule *sarvanāmāntāt prātipadikāt* (which would require an interpretation that includes the suffix), the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17) does not apply.

In this regard, one might raise the objection that since *bhid* alone is the verbal root (*dhātu*), whereas *bhinad*—which possesses the *śnam* suffix—is a different word and not a verbal root, the rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.162) would not apply, and thus the prescribed udātta accent on the final syllable would not occur. Anticipating this, he says: "Not for *idam* and *adas*, except when followed by *akac*" (*nedamadasorakor*, etc.). The sūtra "not for *idam* and *adas*, except when followed by *akac*" (*nedamadasorakor*, Pāṇini 7.1.11) establishes that the substitution of *es* for the case-ending *bhis* does not occur after *idam* and *adas* when they are devoid of the letter *k*. By the phrase "when devoid of the letter *k*," he refers to forms such as *imaka* and *amuka*, which are characterized by the addition of the *akac* suffix.

The exclusion of *idam* and *adas* is intended [by the rule]. In that case, how could a prohibition stated regarding the domain of *idam* and *adas* apply to those two when they are distinct from them and characterized by the suffix *akac*? Therefore, even though the words "of *a* and *ku*" (*akor*) are not explicitly mentioned, since the exclusion is established through the very difference of the words themselves, the fact that the term "of *a* and *ku*" (*akor*) is redundant indicates that it is understood as including its constituent parts by means of the mention of the whole.

And likewise, since the suffix *akac* occurs within the words *idam* and *adas*, it would be included by the mention of *idam* and *adas* because it is a part of them; therefore, the term *akoḥ* is meaningful for the purpose of excluding that [suffix]. In this way, since the word *sarvaka* is also included by the word *sarva*, it possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); consequently, when the replacement *śī* is applied to the case-ending *jas* following it, the form *sarvake* is established.

The meaning is as follows: in the case of *bhinad*, the augment *śnam*—which occurs as a constituent part of *bhid*—is included by the mention of *bhidr*. Consequently, because *bhinad* is also a verbal root (*dhātu*), the final acute accent prescribed by the rule "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is also established. This very principle is also stated as: "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing. Regarding the phrase "of those whose measure is not fixed," the meaning is "of those whose measure is delimited. Regarding the term "thatness" (*tattvam*), the meaning is "the state of being a verbal root and so forth."

The *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) in Pāṇini’s sūtras 5.2.86 (*jhrjña.ṭa ṭhapūrvādiniḥ*) and 5.2.87 (*sapūrvācca*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "the designation [of a grammatical element] applies as if it possessed that designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*), provided that the element is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikena*). Now, an objection: If the sūtra 1.1.72 (*yena vidhistadantasya*), which states that "that by means of which a rule is prescribed applies to the whole ending in that," were stated merely as "the designation applies to what ends in that," then the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the sūtra 4.2.78 (*roṇī*) would apply only to a word like *ajakaroṇī* (which ends in the word *roṇī*), and not to the word *roṇī* alone.

Furthermore, considering that [otherwise] *rauma* would not be established, the author of the *Ākara* explains that the qualification "ending in that" (*tadanta*) applies, and that this [term] should be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). In that context, the portion "and of that" (*tasya ca*) is not to be accepted. Anticipating the objection that even in its absence, the suffix *aṇ* would be established by taking the word *roṇī* as ending in the word *roṇī* through the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), he says: "By the rule *pūrvādiniḥ*, etc."

The point is that, since the designation "as if possessing a distinct name" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the word *roṇī* lacks the property of ending in the word *roṇī*; therefore, it must necessarily be stated that a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply to it. As for the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for this maxim (*paribhāṣā*)—"the designation 'as if possessing a distinct name' does not apply to what is not a nominal stem"—it is the split of the rule into two separate yoga-sutras in the form *pūrvādiniḥ*.

The intention is as follows: by treating *pūrvāt sapūrvād iniḥ* as a single sūtra, one could justify the suffix *-in* in both instances—namely *pūrvī* and *kṛtapūrvī*—because in the former case the word *pūrva* is preceded by nothing, while in the latter case the word *pūrva* is preceded by the word *kṛta*, and thus, by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the word *pūrva* alone can be considered as having something preceding it. However, by the power of making a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule into two parts—"*pūrvād iniḥ*" and "*sapūrvāc ca*"—it is indicated that the principle of "designation as if possessing" does not apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*). This is the underlying sense.

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter. Regarding the rule *tasyāditaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.32), the statement that [the word] *deva* and *brahman* are *anudātta* when following a *svarita* vowel is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this section (*kāṇḍa*) follows the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66). This [section] is this [section]. This [section] is this [section].

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *tasyādita udāttamardhahrasvam* (Pāṇini 1.2.32), having established the meaning of that sūtra as being that the first constituent part of a svarita vowel, consisting of half a mātrā, is designated as udātta, [the author] states that the group of nine sūtras beginning with *tasyādita udāttam* (1.2.32) and ending with *udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ* (1.2.40) should be recited after the sūtra *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (8.4.66).

Having stated this, the purpose is explained: "So that there may be success [based] on the *svarita*," according to the rule "In *saṃhitā*, for *anudātta* vowels following a *svarita*" (Pāṇini 1.2.39). This is its meaning: in the phrase "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri," because the words *gaṅge* and so forth—which follow the *svarita* word *me*—are vocatives (*āmantrita*) and thus *anudātta*, they become *ekaśruti* (monotone) by the rule "In *saṃhitā*, for *anudātta* vowels following a *svarita*."

Regarding the *svarita* accent of the word *me*: according to the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.39), when the single tone (*ekaśruti*) is to be applied, the *svarita* of the word *me*—which is prescribed by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66)—is considered unestablished (*asiddha*). Consequently, since the words *gaṅge* and so forth do not follow after a *svarita*, the single tone would not be established, according to the literal reading of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

Regarding the previously mentioned nine sūtras, if the reading were immediately after "udāttādanudāttasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.66), then because the sūtra "svaritātsaṃhitāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.39)—which prescribes *ekaśruti*—is also included within those nine sūtras and would thus be immediate [to the preceding rule], [the result] prior to that would be as follows:

The rule *udāttādanudāttasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66) is not considered *asiddha*; thus, by establishing the *svarita* nature of the word *me*, the *ekaśruti* (monotone) for the subsequent *anudātta* words such as *gaṅge* and so forth is established without obstruction. It should not be argued that this effort is futile on the grounds that, since the prescription of *ekaśruti* for *anudātta* syllables depends upon the preceding *svarita* (via the rule *svaritātsaṃhitāyāmanudāttānām*), the *svarita* must be regarded as *siddha* (established), because if it were *asiddha*, the dependence on the *svarita* would be impossible. [This is not so.]

Where there is no possibility of the svarita being considered asiddha, the rule is meaningful by prescribing a single accent (*ekaśruti*) for the subsequent unaccented (*anudātta*) syllables, based on the condition *svaritāt*. For example, in the phrase "kāryaṃ devadattayajñadattau," the word *kārya* ends in the suffix *ṇyat*; by the rule "titsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185), it has a svarita at its end. Consequently, the two subsequent unaccented syllables, *devadatta* and *yajñadatta*, undergo *ekaśruti*.

In this context, since the rule *titsvaritam* does not belong to the final three chapters (*tripādī*), there is no possibility of its being considered *asiddha*. Therefore, by relying on the circumflex (*svarita*) here, the sūtra achieves its purpose by prescribing a single accent (*ekaśruti*) for the following unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel. Consequently, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that, in order to avoid the aforementioned inconsistency in the case of *imaṃ me gaṅge*, the previously mentioned new sūtra should be inserted immediately after *udāttādanudāttasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66).

Having thus stated the reading of the nine *sūtra*s in the eighth chapter, the *bhāṣya* on that very point provides the evidence as well, stating in the passage: "The mention of the anudātta for 'deva' and 'brahman' is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this section of *sūtra*s follows after that. By the rule "anudāttaḥ devabrahmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.38), an anudātta is prescribed for the words *deva* and *brahman* when they occur within the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*; for example: "devā brahmāṇa āgacchata" ("O gods and Brahmins, come!").

In the case of these two words, *devāḥ* and *brahmāṇaḥ*, by the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.198), the first syllable becomes udātta. Subsequently, when the remaining syllables are subjected to the rule of nighāta (suppression of accent), an anudātta is prescribed for that [following] syllable by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.38).

In that context, regarding the rule *devabrahmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.38), although an *anudātta* accent ought to be applied, because the *svarita* prescribed by *udāttādanudāttasya* (8.4.66) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), only the *anudātta* remains; thus, the further prescription of an *anudātta* for that [vowel] would otherwise be purposeless. This purposelessness serves to indicate that the group of nine sūtras beginning with *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* follows after this point.

And according to that principle, by means of the subsequent sūtra "devabrahmaṇoḥ" within the section consisting of nine sūtras, the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the circumflex (*svarita*) resulting from the preceding rule "udāttādanudāttasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.66) does not occur; thus, the statement of its being unaccented (*anudātta*) is purposeful. This is the intent of the explanatory commentary (*bhāṣya*) which provides this indication (*jñāpaka*). Having kept all of this in mind, he says: "of the circumflex," and so forth.

The meaning is that, while the word *svaritasya* is being carried over [from a previous rule], the sūtra *“devabrahmaṇoranudāttaḥ”* (P. 6.2.199), which prescribes an *anudātta* accent for *deva* and *brahman*, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned point. Regarding the sūtra *“apṛkta ekāl”* (P. 1.2.41): this inclusion of the term *eka-* also indicates that when a single phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the entire class (*jāti*) is understood. Regarding the phrase *“this too”*: by the word *api*, the inclusion of the *eka-* from the sūtra *“nipāta ekāc”* (P. 1.1.14) is also combined.

And since this has already been explained previously, it is not elaborated upon here. [From the *Mahābhāṣya* on *Pāṇini-sūtra* 1.2.45]: *arthavad adhātuḥ* ("That which is meaningful and is not a verbal root"). Regarding the rule *apratyayaḥ* ("not a suffix"), because it is a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), the fact that bases ending in *ūṅ* and so forth possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is known from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *noṅdhātvoḥ* (P. 6.1.175), which prohibits the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*).

In the rule *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*, regarding the phrase *apratyayaḥ*, if one adopts the position that it expresses a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—meaning "that which is not a suffix"—then the meaning of the sūtra would be: "that which ends in a suffix and a suffix itself do not receive the designation of *prātipadika*."

Furthermore, from the word *brahmabandhu*, when the feminine suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *ūṅutaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.66), we have *brahmabandhū*. When the long vowel substitution for homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the form *brahmabandhū* is established. At this point, one might raise the objection that since the single-substitute *ū* is treated as if it were the subsequent element (*paranipāta*), it is a suffix; thus, because *brahmabandhū* would end in a suffix, its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would be prohibited, and consequently, the case-endings (*svādi*) could not arise. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] establishes that a word ending in *ūṅ* is indeed a nominal stem.

He establishes this by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words "of the word *apratyaya*" and so forth. This is the underlying intention: although a stem ending in *ūṅ* is technically not a suffix (*pratyaya*), it still receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In this regard, the indicator is the prohibition of accentuation for the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) in the rule "noṅdātvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.175). For by that very rule, [the accent of] *ūṅ*...

It is established that the case endings beginning with *śas* following the substitute *aṇ* for a root (*dhātu*) would not be acute; thus, *brahmabandhvāḥ* is given as an example. Since a stem ending in *ūṅ* would lack the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case endings beginning with *śas* following it would be impossible to obtain. Therefore, the prohibition of the acute accent for *śas* and the others serves to indicate, by way of making known that the stem ending in *ūṅ* is indeed a nominal stem, that case endings are produced after it. In the Bhāṣya, however, the actual wording of the rule is seen as: "The case endings beginning with *su* are produced after a stem ending in *ūṅ*."

The intended meaning of that [rule] is precisely what has been stated. Because of the prohibition in the rule *jhrjñā.ṭa ṭhana ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), by means of that indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the prohibition [of the final *n*] by the rule *apratyaya* (8.2.16)—which applies by virtue of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—does not apply. In that very same rule (*jhrvi.ṭa*), according to the view that it is a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), when the form *rājan s* is established, after lengthening [the vowel] and the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule *halṅyādinā*, we have *rājān*. At this point, one expects the form *rājā* to result from the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7). However, that would not occur [under the view that the prohibition in 8.2.8 is a simple negation].

Raising the objection that even if the *su* suffix is elided, because the resulting form ends in a suffix by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, it would not be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) since "that which ends in a suffix" is excluded from the definition of a nominal stem—and thus the elision of the *nal* (the *n* of *su*) conditioned by that designation would be impossible—he resolves this by stating: "There is no fault, because of the indicatory power (*jñāpaka*) of the prohibition 'not in the case of *ṅi* or the vocative' (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*)," which makes known that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule does not apply within the scope of the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*).

For by the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*, it is stated that the elision of *n* should not occur in the locative singular (*ṅi*) or in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). The example for the locative in Vedic usage is *parame vyoman*. Here, after the elision of the case-ending (*ṅe*), one might argue that because the suffix is still present by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle, the prohibition *apratyayaḥ* (it is not a suffix) prevents it from being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, since the condition for the elision of *n*—namely, being a nominal stem—is not met, the elision of *n* would not take place anyway; thus, the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*, which prohibits the elision of *n*, would be redundant.

And that has been done: by relying on the definition of a suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), it indicates that the prohibition "it is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) does not apply. Therefore, the sense is that there is no fault. In the rule *ṭhatiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.63), because of the inclusion of the plural number (*bahuvacana-grahaṇa*), it is indicated as a *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) that every *dvandva* compound optionally takes the singular form (*sarva-dvandvo vibhāṣayaikavat*). Thus, *tiṣyapunarvasu* is the counter-example (*tad-vyāvartyam*) to this. Alternatively, the singular form is due to the rule *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6), which prescribes the singular for non-sentient beings when they constitute a genus.

"Venerable sirs, these are not living beings; rather, venerable sirs, these are merely the vital breaths. [Viz. Now, regarding the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvornakṣatradvandve bahuvacanasya dvivacanaṃ nityam* (Pāṇini 1.2.63), for what purpose is the mention of "bahuvacanasya" (of the plural)? It should not be argued that in its absence, even the singular would undergo the dual, and consequently, the form ending in the singular, *tiṣyapunarvasu*, would not be established.

In the case of the *dvandva* compound *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ*, the use of the singular number is difficult to justify because there is no possibility of its occurrence in place of the dual; for [if one were to argue that] it is a collective *dvandva*—meaning "Tiṣya and the two Punarvasus"—whereby the singular would be easily obtained due to the rule of singularization (*ekavadbhāva*), this cannot be maintained. This is because the formation of a *dvandva* for a collective is prescribed only for things such as parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*). Nor can it be argued that the singularization here occurs through the rule "A genus-term for non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*), because that very rule contains the restriction "for non-living things" (*aprāṇinām*), which excludes this case.

And thus, since the word *tiṣyapunarvasu* does not exist in the singular number, there is no possibility for the singular to become dual; therefore, one might suspect that the mention of the plural in the rule "tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ" is redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "For this very reason, it indicates that every dvandva compound is optionally singular."

And likewise, in the case of *tiṣyaśca punarvasū ca* (Tiṣya and Punarvasu), where the *dvandva* compound denotes mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there is an option for it to be treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). To ensure that the singular number in the form *tiṣyapunarvasu* does not result in a dual number, the word "plural" (*bahuvacanasya*) was stated [in the rule]. However, the purpose of this indication (*jñāpanaphala*) is that in the *itaretarayoga-dvandva* *bābhravāśca śālaṅkāyanāśca* (the Bābhravas and the Śālaṅkāyanas), the form *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanam* ending in the singular is grammatically correct; this is stated in the Bhāṣya. This very point he expresses: "here, by virtue of the mention of the plural, which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)."

"Tadvyāvartyam" (that which is to be excluded by it) means that which is to be excluded by the plural number (*bahuvacanasya*). In reality, however, because the pair Tiṣya-Punarvasu is not conventionally treated as "living beings" (*prāṇin*) in common usage, and because a genus (*jāti*) based on Tiṣya-Punarvasu could exist across different *manvantaras* through the variation of constellations, there is the possibility of their being designated as a genus of non-living things. Consequently, since the rule "the singular form is used for non-living genera" (*jātiraprāṇinām*) would apply, the singular number would result. To prevent the dual number from occurring in place of this singular, [the word "dvandva" is included].

He says "or rather" (*yathā vā*) because it is more appropriate to take [the word] as plural. The sense is that since living beings depend for their existence upon Tiṣya and Punarvasu, one can somehow speak of Tiṣya and Punarvasu as *prāṇa* (breaths/lives), but not as *prāṇin* (living beings). Consequently, the prohibition "not of non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*) does not apply; this is the intended meaning. [In the case of] *bhrātṛ-putrau* (brother and son) and *svasṛ-*...

(On *Pumān striyā*, Pāṇini 1.2.67) || Since this would have been established by the rule "The masculine [remains] when with the feminine" (1.2.67), this present rule (*Bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām*, 1.2.68) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the following meaning: "Where there is a distinction characterized by the [respective] gender beyond the common base (*prakṛti*), there the *ekaśeṣa* applies according to the rule 'the elder [remains] when with the younger,' and so forth. [Objection: But then, in the section on *ekaśeṣa*, the rule "Brother and son [remain] when with sister and daughter" (1.2.68)—which has the sense that when a brother is mentioned together with a sister, or a son together with a daughter, both "brother and son" remain as the residue—is rendered useless.

Anticipating the objection that the purpose is already served by the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), he states its meaningfulness as being intended to provide a specific technical indication (*jñāpana*): "pumān striyā" and so forth. This rule *pumān striyā* applies only where there is a distinction characterized by gender after the base form (*prakṛti*), but not within the base form itself; for example, in the case of *haṃsaśca haṃsī ca*, the base form *haṃsa* is the same in both instances.

Since the distinction exists only after that [application of the rule], in the case of *pumān striyā* (a male and a female), when the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies, the form becomes *haṃsau* (two swans). Therefore, in the case of *haṃsaś ca varaṭā ca* (the male swan and the female swan), there is no *ekaśeṣa*, because even in the original state (*prakṛti*) there is a distinction. In the case of *bhrātā ca svasā ca* (a brother and a sister) as well, since the distinction exists in the original state itself, the rule *pumān striyā* does not apply; thus, the rule *bhrātṛputrau* is meaningful as it prescribes *ekaśeṣa* in those instances. This concludes the second quarter of the first chapter.

Pāṇini 1.3.1: *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. The inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning with) indicates that there is indeed a recitation [of roots], and that this recitation is external to the sūtra itself. Objection: In the sūtra *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, the inclusion of the word "ādi" is redundant. To explain: if the author of the sūtras, after having recited the roots beginning with *bhū*, were to refer to them by the term *bhūvādi*, then the sūtra should simply have been read as *te dhātavaḥ* ("those are verbal roots").

Furthermore, one might raise the objection that if the author of the Sūtras had not recited "bhūvādayaḥ" (beginning with *bhū*), then even by using the phrase "bhūvādayaḥ," those [roots] could not be referred to; anticipating this, he says: "the inclusion of the word 'ādi'. The sense is that the author of the Sūtras employed the word "ādi" in order to indicate that the Dhātupāṭha exists outside the Sūtras, where the reference to the roots situated therein by means of the word "ādi" is easily accomplished.

Furthermore, since the author of the Sūtras stated "those are roots" (*te dhātavaḥ*) after completing the list of *mṛḍ*, *ḍīḍ*, *mṛd*, and so forth as they are recited in the Sūtras, then even for forms such as *āṇavayati* which are not recited therein, the designation "root" would still apply. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "bhūvādayaḥ" was stated specifically to ensure that the designation "root" applies only to those forms seen in the Sūtras, Vārttikas, Bhāṣya, and the Gaṇapāṭha. 1.3.43.]

It was stated that it should be specified as "not in a *taddhita* [suffix]. This was rejected on the grounds that the letter *u*, used as an *it*-marker (*anubandha*), serves to protect the *ma* of *tham* from being designated as an *it* when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), thereby making it known that the prohibition does not apply to *taddhita* suffixes. Now, however, the suffix will be made to end in *y*; the *y* is indicated as having been elided. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "na vibhaktau tusmāḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.4), the designation of *it* is prohibited for the dental stops (*tavarga*), *s*, and *m* when they stand in the position of case-endings?

Furthermore, from the word *kim*, by the rule *kimo't* (Pāṇini 5.3.12), the suffix *at* is added; then, the *t* of that suffix receives the designation *it* and is elided by the rule *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Subsequently, by the rule *kvāti* (Pāṇini 7.2.105), *kim* undergoes the substitution *kva*. Thus, the form *kva* is desired. In this context, since the suffix *at* is a *taddhita*, it is designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1).

Regarding the sūtra *5-3-1*, since [the suffix] is designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*), there arises the concern that the letter *t* situated therein would be subject to the prohibition of the *it*-designation by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4). Anticipating this objection, the author of the Vārttika stated: "It should be stated that [the prohibition applies to those] other than *taddhita*. His intention is that the prohibition of the *it*-designation for the dental class (*tavarga*) and so forth is restricted only to those situated in case-endings that are distinct from *taddhita* suffixes; therefore, the *it*-designation does indeed apply to the letter *t* situated in a *taddhita*.

And this *vārttika* was refuted by the author of the *Bhāṣya* after establishing—by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—that there is no prohibition of the *itsaṃjñā* for the *tavarga* sounds and others occurring within a *taddhita* suffix. He stated: "It should be said that [the rule applies] except when it is a *taddhita*. This [statement] is to be construed with the word "refuted" (*pratyākhyātam*). Furthermore, by the rule "idamasthamuḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.94), the suffix *thamu* is prescribed after the word "idam" in the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*), and the letter *u* in *thamu* is marked with the *itsaṃjñā*.

To the objection that the inclusion of the letter *u* here is unnecessary and that the suffix should simply be *tham*, the response must be stated as follows: if that were the case, the letter *m* would acquire the designation *it* by the rule *halantyam*; therefore, the letter *u* has been joined [to *tha*] to prevent this. Consequently, since the letter *m* is not final in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), it does not receive the designation *it*. This is the resolution.

However, even though the suffix *tham* is taught with a final *m*, because it is designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule "prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.27), the letter *m* would not receive the designation *it* by the rule "na vibhaktau tusmāḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.4). Therefore, [the mention of *thamu*] is for the purpose of protecting that *m* from being designated as *it*.

The utterance of the vowel *u* while the suffix is being formed would be redundant. However, since it has been uttered, it indicates that the prohibition of the designation *it* (which applies to suffixes ending in *t*, *tha*, *sa*, *na*, and *m*) does not apply here. Consequently, the *m* of *tham* would otherwise receive the *it*-designation; therefore, the utterance of *u* is purposeful for the sake of prohibiting that. By this very fact, the prohibition of the *it*-designation will not extend even to *at*-beginning *taddhita* suffixes. Thus, the sense is that the *vārttika*—"it should be stated that [the rule applies] when it is not a *taddhita*"—is unnecessary.

Now, one might object: since the prohibition of *itsaṃjñā* for the letters *t*, *u*, *s*, and *m* does not apply to *taddhita* suffixes and case-endings (*vibhakti*), then in the word *idānīm*, the letter *m* at the end of the suffix *dānīm*—which is prescribed by the rule *dānīm ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.18)—would incur the designation *itsaṃjñā*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But *dānīm* will be made to end in *y*. Thus, the suffix is indeed *dānīmy*, ending in the letter *y*.

Furthermore, that *ca* in the form of the *sūtra* [“*cakāra*"] is not heard because it has been elided by the rule “*lopo vyorvali*” (Pāṇini 6.1.66), which applies when a semivowel (*val*) follows. Consequently, since the *m* is not final in its original form (*upadeśa*), it does not receive the designation *it*. Nor should it be argued that if the suffix were to end in *y*, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the *y* in forms such as *idānīm*; for the intention is that the *y* is elided by the rule “*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.2.23). This is understood from the phrase “by the *y* which is indicated as elided,” the remainder being supplied as “by means of the rule *lopo vyorvali*.”

*jhra jñā ṭa*: its [the *ṭ*] elision is by Pāṇini 1.3.9. From the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of Pāṇini 3.1.139, "optionally for the roots *dā* and *dhā*," it follows that dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) is not caused by an *anubandha*. From the indicative power of Pāṇini 1.1.55, "a *śit* [affix] applies to the whole," it follows that having more than one consonant (*anekāltva*) is not caused by an *anubandha*. From the mention of the form with an *anubandha* as having become *āt* in Pāṇini 3.4.19, "of *māṅ* according to the Northern Grammarians," it follows that not ending in a vowel (*anejantatva*) is not caused by an *anubandha*. It is logical that *anubandhas* are exclusively terminal; this is because it is supported by reason.

The rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12), along with the optional provision *anupasargādvā* (Pāṇini 1.3.43), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is stronger than an affix (*vikaraṇa*). This indicates that the restriction applies even when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa*. This point was made clear in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *śadeḥ śitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.60). Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.

In the rule *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), the mention of *ūṭh* in the rule *vāha ūṭh* (6.4.132) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent" (*asiddham*). In the word *indra*, there are two vowels: the *i* and the *a*. Among these, one [the *i*] is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), while the other [the *a*] is replaced by the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) vowel *e*. Consequently, *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*). Since there is no occasion for the application of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in this state, the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] would be redundant; being thus redundant, it indicates that the operation takes place first for the preceding and following members of the compound, and that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not considered internal (*antaraṅga*).

Because of the rule *yasmātpratyayavidhistadādi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 1.4.13), the inclusion of the term *anantaraḥ* ("immediately preceding") in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, it includes a word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. The inclusion of the term *anta* ("ending in") in the rule *suptiṅantam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14) serves as an indicator for the principle that in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the mention of a suffix does not include what ends with it. All of these statements, which are of the nature of *paribhāṣās*, have been explained in detail in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*; therefore, they are not explained here.

We do not know how certain technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) of this kind have come to be included in this *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*. [From the Jñāpakasamuccaya: The mention of the plural number in Pāṇini’s rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Sūtra 1.4.21) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the word *bahu* is understood here as denoting "many distinct substances" (*nānādravya*), and not as denoting "abundance" (*vaipulya*). [Objection: But surely, by the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, the plural number is prescribed for the sense of plurality (*bahutva*).

In that context, plurality (*bahutva*) is twofold: extensiveness (*vaipulya*) and numerical distinction (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*). Since there is no distinguishing factor [between them] in that regard, the plural number would apply to both meanings. Consequently, one might object that in the expression "much rice" (*bahurodana*), the plural would follow because extensiveness is intended by the nature of the word; anticipating this, he says: "the mention of the plural number."

Since it should have been specified as "the plural [is used] for plurality" (*bahutvasyaikatvāt bahau*), the fact that the term "in many" (*bahuṣu*)—itself a plural—is used here indicates that only the word *bahu* which denotes multiple substances (*nānādravyavācī*) is employed in this context, and not the word *bahu* which denotes abundance (*vaipulyavācī*). The intention is as follows: although plurality (*bahutva*) is a single entity according to the sūtra, because the substrata of plurality are many, the plurality residing in those substrata is superimposed upon the plurality itself, and thus the plural designation "in many" (*bahuṣu*) was made.

And thus, the meaning of the sūtra is established as follows: "The plural number occurs when there is plurality whose substratum is manifold. Since the substratum of plurality in the form of extensiveness (*vaipulya*) is singular, the plural number does not occur for that plurality which consists of extensiveness and rests upon a single entity. However, since the substratum of plurality in the form of numerical count (*saṃkhyā*) is multiple, the plural number occurs precisely for that plurality which consists of numerical count.

Regarding these rules for the restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*), since indeclinables (*avyaya*) do not attain the status of being *pada*s, a restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*) must be stated; or else, the restriction of suffixes is dependent upon the meaning of the base form (*prakṛti*). In such cases as "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one" (*dvivacanaikavacane*) and "the plural ending is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*), the status of being restrictive rules (*niyamārthatva*) is accepted. Furthermore, a restriction (*niyama*) is of two kinds: restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) and restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*).

The restriction regarding suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) is that the singular number applies only to a single thing, the dual number only to two things, and the plural number only to many things; whereas the restriction regarding meaning (*arthaniyama*) is that the singular number applies only to a single thing, the dual number only to two things, and the plural number only to many things. In that regard, if one relies on the restriction of suffixes, indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *uccais* and *nīcais* would not obtain the designation of "word" (*pada*), because they do not end in a nominal suffix (*asup*).

Since suffixes (*pratyaya*) are restricted to specific numbers, case-endings (*sup*) would not arise from indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack number; consequently, the designation *pada*—which is contingent upon being a word ending in a *sup*—would not apply. Furthermore, in the absence of *pada*-status, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of rules such as the substitution of *r* (*rutva*). Anticipating this objection, he states, "In that regard, among these," because for this very reason of impossibility, one must abandon the restriction on suffixes and instead adopt a restriction based on meaning. "Among these" refers to the plural and other [numbers]. Even under the view that restricts the suffixes, there is no fault.

A restriction is established without regard for the subject matter at hand. Since "oneness" and so forth are the subject matters under discussion, the restriction on the suffix—that the singular number occurs only when there is one—results in the exclusion of the singular suffix from duality and plurality (which belong to the same genus as oneness) by virtue of their being numbers. However, by that much alone, the singular suffix is not excluded from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number, even when they express the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Therefore, with the intention that the status of being a *pada* (word) is not contradicted even for indeclinables (*avyaya*) because the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*) is established for them, he says: "or [the meaning] is dependent on the context. He recites the *vārttika* which sets forth the two previously mentioned rules: "The meanings of the case-endings (*sup*) are [the objects] such as the *karman* (object), and likewise number; so too for the verbal endings (*tiṅ*). In that regard, the rule is well-known; or, the restriction applies to those [meanings] already under discussion. "In that regard, the rule is well-known" means that there is a restriction regarding the meaning. "Or, the restriction applies to those already under discussion" means...

The meaning is that there is a restriction regarding the suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*). In that context, either by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule "avyayād āpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82), the case-endings (*sup*) are applied after indeclinables (*avyaya*); or else, according to another view stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "taddhitaśca" (Pāṇini 1.1.31), the default singular number (*autsargikam ekavacanam*) applies to indeclinables. Let it be that there is a restriction regarding the suffixes with respect to the general [number]; however, the singular number applies only to singularity (*ekatva*) and not to any other number whatsoever.

Nevertheless, he states—"In that case, the meaning"—to show that the derivation of case endings (*svādi*) from indeclinables (*avyaya*) is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The meaning is: even under the view that the singular number and so forth denote only the sense of oneness and the like, if the case endings (*sup*) were excluded from indeclinables which lack number by a restriction on suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*), then the rule prescribing their elision—*avyādāpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82)—would be purposeless, since no case endings could arise from indeclinables at all. Yet, that rule has been formulated; it therefore indicates that case endings do indeed arise from indeclinables.

The meaning is that, therefore, there is no impossibility of [the suffixes] being *pada*s. Regarding the phrase "sup-s from indeclinables" (*avyayebhyaḥ sup*): *sup* is the nominative plural. The word "arise" (*utpadyante*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In reality, however, not all case-endings arise from indeclinables, but rather only the singular; thus he says, "from indeclinables."

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, having rejected the formulation of the rules as *dvyekayor dvivacanaikavacane* and *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, and instead adopting the arrangement of the rules as *ekavacanam*, *dvayor dvivacanam*, and *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, it is stated that the singular number will be applied as the general rule (*utsarga*), while the dual and plural numbers will serve as its exceptions (*bādhaka*) for the respective meanings of duality and plurality.

Consequently, by the general rule "the singular number," it is obtained that the singular is used when there is an absence of duality and plurality; therefore, since indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack number possess neither duality nor plurality, the singular number prescribed by the general sutra will indeed apply—this is the intended meaning. However, whether the singular of the nominative case alone occurs by virtue of the general sutra, or whether the singular of all case-endings occurs, is another matter. [Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.93: *adhi-parī anarthakau*.

This indicates that even particles (*nipāta*) which are devoid of meaning are treated as having meaning. For this [rule] is intended for the purpose of assigning the designation *karmapravacanīya* by overriding the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*. Alternatively, because they lack any other meaning, these two [particles] denote the action already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus, it serves as an indicator of the meaning that "even those whose meaning has already been expressed may be employed. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "adhi and pari are devoid of meaning," the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the meaningless *adhi* and *pari* is understood without difficulty.
