Nor should it be said that that rule is intended for the purpose of setting aside the technical designations of *gati* and *upasarga*; for the designation of *gati* and the designation of *upasarga* are prescribed based on connection with an action (*kriyā*), and [the rule applies] even to those two when they are meaningless.

Since there is no connection with action (*kriyā*) in the sense of possessing an action as their meaning, those two technical designations (*saṃjñā*) do not apply; anticipating this objection, he states that the Sūtra is purposeful for the sake of providing an indication: "This indicates... It is indicated that even for meaningless elements such as *āṅ* and *pari*, whatever grammatical operation applies to a meaningful word also applies to them. The designations *gati* and *upasarga* occur when they are based on the connection with the action of a meaningful word.

The designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed to prevent those two [words] from becoming *adhi* and *pari* even when they are meaningless; however, the result of this indication is that the statement made in the *arthavat-sūtra*—"the technical name *prātipadika* must be stated even for a particle (*nipāta*) that is meaningless"—is not necessary. In reality, however, *adhi* and *pari* are not meaningless either, for it is the established view that "all prefixes (*upasarga*) illuminate the meaning of the verbal root."

In this regard, other prefixes (*upasarga*) serve to indicate specific distinctions pertaining to the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, *adhi* and *pari* indicate the action expressed by the root itself, but not any distinction therein. It is precisely with this intention that it was stated in the rule "anarthakāḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.93). Thus, the connection with action consists solely in the indication of the action.

Since those two [prefixes] also exist as governing words (*adhipari*), this rule for the designation of *karmapravacanīya* is established in order to set aside the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "preposition" (*upasarga*) that would otherwise apply; thus, there is no inconsistency with the Sūtra. For this very reason, it is not intended to serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned statement. With this intention, he says: "Or rather, because there is no other meaning. This means: because there is no indicated meaning (*dyotya-artha*) in the form of a specific quality belonging to that [action], distinct from the action expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). "They express" (*āhatuḥ*) means they indicate (*dyotayataḥ*).

Now, if the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* express exactly the same meaning as that already stated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then their employment would be redundant, according to the maxim that "that which has already been expressed need not be employed. To this, he says: "even though the meaning has already been expressed. The intention is that it is thereby made known that there is indeed the employment of [prefixes] even when their meaning has already been expressed.

Just as in the expression "bring two Brahmins," although duality is already understood by the dual ending itself, the term is used again for the sake of even clearer comprehension, so too this repeated usage is not contradictory; this is what the rule "adhi-parī anarthakau" indicates. Furthermore, the mention of "parasmaipada" in the rule "halḥ parasmaipadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.2.77), which prescribes *vṛddhi* in the *sic* suffix, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the technical designation "person" (*puruṣa-saṃjñā*) does not sublate the technical designation "parasmaipada."

Objection: In the rule *laḥ parasmaipadam*, the mention of *parasmaipada* need not be made. Rather, the mention of *parasmaipada* should be made right there in the section beginning with *lasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77). If the technical designation *parasmaipada* were stated here in the first chapter, then because of the governing heading *ekasaṃjñādhikāra*, the designations *puruṣa* (person)—such as *ti*, *tas*, and *jhi*—would also be prescribed; consequently, that subsequent designation (*puruṣa*) would subvert the designation *parasmaipada*.

Anticipating the objection that the prescription of the technical term *parasmaipada* would otherwise find no scope in the case of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu*, he says: "In the rule regarding the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] in *sic*. For if the designation *puruṣa* were to sublate the designation *parasmaipada* with respect to *tiP* and the other suffixes, then the mention of *tib* and the others by the word *parasmaipada* in the rule "There is *vṛddhi* in *sic* before *parasmaipada*s" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.1) would be inconsistent. Therefore, the sense is that it is indicated that the designation *puruṣa* does not sublate the designation *parasmaipada*.

The rule *jhr-jñā-ṭa-vibhaktiś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104) occurs while the phrase "three by three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) is still in effect; this is established by such statements as *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.2.84). When that [phrase] ceases to apply, the substitution of *na* is prescribed by *tasmāc-chaso naḥ puṃsi* (6.1.103), and because the expression "of the first two cases" (*prathamayoḥ*) is used instead of "of *au* and *jas*" (*aujasoḥ*), it is indicated that the term "triad" (*trika*) is included in the rule for the long vowel of the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

Objection: In the rule *vibhaktiśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104), does the phrase *trīṇi trīṇi* ("three by three") carry over from the preceding rule *tiṅastrīṇitrīṇi* (Pāṇini 1.4.100), or not? If it does carry over, then the designation *vibhakti* would apply only to a triplet [of suffixes] and not to a single one; this being the case, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the word *aṣṭan* would not occur when followed by each individual suffix beginning with *jas*.

For by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the substitution of *ā* is prescribed when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows. However, there is a difficulty because there is no set of three [case-endings] that occurs simultaneously after the word *aṣṭan*. If the words "three" and "three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) were not supplied as anuvṛtti, then each of the suffixes beginning with *su* would individually receive the designation "case-ending," and thus the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* would be established even before each individual one.

Nevertheless, regarding the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), since the phrase *prathamayor vibhaktyoḥ* does not refer to the two as a collective unit, one might raise the objection that the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* would apply only when the two case-endings *su* and *au*—which possess the technical designation *vibhakti*—are followed by a vowel (*aci*), or alternatively, only when *au* and *jas* follow; it would not apply when *jas* and so forth follow. Anticipating this fault in both these positions, he provides the solution by stating: "when *trīṇi trīṇi* is supplied from the context. This refers to the position where the word is supplied from the previous context.

Even though the designation "vibhakti" (case-ending) applies only to the aggregate consisting of three parts, because the three do not occur simultaneously in usage, the term *vibhakti* is understood to refer to a constituent part of the case-ending by virtue of the force of the rule prescribing the substitution of *āt*. Thus, since the substitution of *āt* is prescribed when a constituent of a case-ending follows, the substitution is established even when each individual part follows; therefore, there is no fault. "Bhavati" [is used] as an example; the remainder of the sense is that the substitution of *āt* occurs for *aṣṭan*.

Regarding the position that the phrase "three by three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) does not recur [to subsequent rules], even though each [of the two sets] is designated as a *prathama* (nominative) case, the author demonstrates that in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, only the first two triads are intended, and not the two suffixes—this is expressed by the words "upon its cessation. This means: upon the non-recurrence of the phrase "three by three. For the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* prescribes the substitution of *na* for the *s* that is a constituent of the suffix *śas*, after having referred back to the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] by means of the word *naḥ*.

In this context, if the word *tasmāt* ("from that") were not included, then in the derivation of *etān gāḥ paśya*—where *go* and *aśas* stand as *go aśas*—the rule *auto'mśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.93) would cause the single substitution of *ā* for both *o* and *a*. At the stage where *gās* is established, the letter *s* would also undergo the change to *ṇ*. To prevent this, the word *tasmāt* is stated [in the rule]. Since the *ā* in *gās* is not a long vowel resulting from the homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the letter *s* does not follow a homogeneous long vowel; therefore, there is no change to *ṇ*.

If it were the case that, by the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, [the long vowel] would not follow from the first two suffixes, namely *au* and *jas*, because of the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), then what would be the purpose of the rule *tasmāt*? That rule being formulated indicates that by the rule *prathamayoḥ*, only the two triplets (of case endings) are intended to be grasped. Therefore, since the homogeneous preceding vowel is established for *am* and *śas* as well, there is no fault whatsoever.

Alternatively, if the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] were intended only for *au* and *jas*, the author would have composed the rule simply as "aujasoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ. Thus, the intention is that by this [rule], the inclusion of only the first two triplets (*trika*)—namely, the nominative and accusative—is indicated. By the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "ityuktyā ca," the prescription of *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *t*) is conjoined. Thus ends the First Chapter.
Now begins the Second Chapter.

In the rule *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* (2.1.18), the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or") indicates that the formation of compounds and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) is optional (*vibhāṣā*). This implies that in the domain of such formations (*vṛtti*), an exception (*apavāda*) is obligatory (*nitya*). However, once this [optional nature] is established, the formation is optional by one rule, while by another rule it is an optional exception within the scope of formation. [Objection: But surely, in the rule *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*, the mention of *vā* is redundant.

It should not be argued that the inclusion of the word *vā* is for the purpose of providing an optional rule (*vikalpa*) for the formation of the compound, such that the correctness of the analytical sentence *pāraṃ gaṅgāyāḥ* (the far bank of the Gaṅgā) is obtained in the case where the compound does not occur; for the optionality is already established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the *mahāvibhāṣā*.

Nor should it be argued that even if the correctness of the analytical sentence is obtained through the *mahāvibhāṣā* in the absence of this compound, the correctness of the genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—such as *gaṅgapāram*—would not be secured by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.2.8), and therefore the mention of *vā* is intended to teach the correctness of the genitive compound.

In the rule for *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* and in the rule "pāremadhye," because the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the principle of optionality) applies to both, the *avyayībhāva* compound "pāremadhye"—which is an exception to the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*—possesses the status of an optional sublater due to its inclusion under the jurisdiction of the *mahāvibhāṣā*. Consequently, in the alternative where this [avyayībhāva] is absent, the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* occurs; and since that too is optional, in the alternative where even that is absent, the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is also grammatically correct. Thus, the desired result is established.

Anticipating the objection that the inclusion of the word *vā* (or) is therefore redundant, he states its purposefulness as an indicator of a specific rule (*vacanaviśeṣajñāpakatayā*)—namely, "the word *vā* [indicates this]. Since it would otherwise be useless according to the reasoning stated previously, the inclusion of *vā* indicates that the formation of a compound occurs optionally by means of the *mahāvibhāṣā*. In that regard, if there is any exception (*apavāda*), that exception applies invariably to the general compound (*utsargasamāsa*).

Therefore, even when the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option) is understood from the *apavāda-sūtra*, it is only the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the sentence that is accepted as an alternative, and not the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Likewise, in the present case as well, if the mention of *vā* were absent, then even with the understanding of the *mahāvibhāṣā*, only the grammatical correctness of the sentence would be obtained in the alternative where this [rule]—which is an exception to the genitive compound—is not applied, and not the genitive compound itself. For that purpose, the mention of *vā* is made.

And when that [Mahāvibhāṣā] exists, the grammatical correctness of the sentence is established through the term *vā*; by the inclusion of *vā*, the general rule (*utsarga*) is also permitted as an alternative option. Thus, the correctness of all three—the sentence, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*)—is secured. Furthermore, it should be noted that if the term *vā* is absent in an exception rule (*apavādasūtra*) falling within the jurisdiction of the Mahāvibhāṣā, it is determined that the general rule is not accepted because the exception invariably subverts it.

In this context, it should be understood that the result of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory rule) is that even though [the rule] is an optional alternative (*vaikalpika*) serving as an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it nevertheless permits the grammatical correctness of the analytical sentence (*vākya*) when it does not accept the genitive compound. Regarding the phrase "but when this is done" (*kṛte tvasmin*): the meaning is "when the word *vā* is employed. Thus, because there exist two words expressing optionality—namely *vibhāṣā* and *vā*—the compound is prescribed optionally by one of them; consequently, it is established that the analytical sentence is also correct in the alternative case.

Furthermore, an exception (*apavāda*) is stated by means of an alternative formulation (*vikalpa*). By that, it is understood that the general rule (*utsarga*) also applies; this is the meaning. Regarding the term *tadarthārtha* [in the rule *caturthī tadarthārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.36)], the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound] occurs only when there is a relationship of material cause and its product (*prakṛtivikṛtibhāva*), as evidenced by the inclusion of the word *arthe* in the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.43), and by the inclusion of the word *arthe* in the rules *arthe* (6.2.44) and *kte ca* (6.2.45).

Thus, because of the grasping of benefit and happiness, the compound *tadartha* is formed precisely with a dative case ending in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tad-artham*). [Objection: But surely, according to the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), it must be stated that a compound is prescribed between a word ending in a dative case expressing the "modified" (*vikṛti*) and a word ending in a case suffix expressing the "original material" (*prakṛti*), when there is the sense of being for the sake of that. Otherwise, there would result the undesired application of the *tadartha* compound even in cases such as *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking").

And thus, compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* would not be established, because there is no relationship of "original material" (*prakṛti*) and "modification" (*vikṛti*) between a horse and fodder. Nor can it be argued that *aśvaghāsa* will take the form of a compound consisting of a word ending in the genitive case—expressing a relationship characterized by purpose—as in "the fodder of a horse," and that therefore there is no harm even in the absence of a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*).

In the case of a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) applies by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.43); whereas in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), the final syllable of the compound receives the acute accent (*samāsāntodātta-svara*) by the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223). Thus, because there is a difference in accent, it cannot be said that the grammatical operation of a dative compound is accomplished by means of a genitive compound.

Anticipating the objection that [this would be] impossible, [the author] provides the following resolution: the *prakṛtisvara* (original accentuation) of the first member of a compound applies only in cases where there is a relationship between an original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*). Consequently, even in the case of the compound *aśvaghāsaḥ*, since it results in an *antodātta* (acute accent on the final syllable) due to being a *samāsa*, there is no difference in accent; thus, considering that words such as *aśvaghāsa* are correct only as genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the *prakṛtisvara* of the first member—which is prescribed by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36)—[does not apply here].

He provides the evidence for the claim that this occurs *only* in cases of the relationship between material cause (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) by citing the rule "The fourth case [is used] in the sense of 'for that'" (*caturthī tadarthe*), etc. This is the underlying intention: if the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), which is prescribed by the rule "The fourth case [is used] in the sense of 'for that'," were to apply even in cases where the relationship of material cause and modification is absent, then the two subsequent rules—"in the sense of 'for' (*arthe*)" (Pāṇini 6.2.44) and "and when ending in the suffix *kta*" (Pāṇini 6.2.45)—would be rendered useless.

In examples such as *devatārtham*, when a word ending in the dative case—such as *devakata*—is followed by the word *artha*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member is prescribed by the rule "arthe" (Pāṇini 6.2.45). In examples such as *go hitam*, when a word ending in the dative case is followed by a word ending in the suffix *-kta*, the original accent of the preceding dative member is prescribed by the rule "kte ca" (Pāṇini 6.2.150). In both these instances, since the original accent of the preceding member would already be established by the rule "caturthī tadarthe" (Pāṇini 2.1.36), the repeated prescription [in the aforementioned rules] should not have been made.

And that [usage] has been established; it indicates that the accent prescribed by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* applies only when there is a relationship between an original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*). Consequently, in cases such as *devatārthagohitam*, since there is no relationship of original material and modification, the accent would not apply; therefore, the two rules *arthe* and *kte ca* are formulated to ensure its application. Thus, the meaning of this section is that even in the case of compounds like *aśvaghāsa*, the accent and other properties are successfully established through their status as genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

In the Mahābhāṣya, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) was made for the purpose of refuting the Vārttika which states, "it should be stated that [the word] *artha* is always in a compound. One sūtra is "caturthī" (P. 2.1.36), and another is "tadarthārtha" (P. 2.1.37). Therein, the meaning of the sūtra "caturthī" is that a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthyanta*) is compounded with a word ending in a *sup*-suffix. And the meaning of "tadarthārtha" is that the word "artha" is substituted for the final member (*uttarapada*) when its referent is that [referent] of the preceding word.

Furthermore, when the compound *brāhmaṇāya payaḥ* is formed, the repetition of the word *payaḥ* as *paya* serves to indicate that the word *artha* is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the word *payaḥ*. This is the resulting implication.

If the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) is performed in this manner, then one might raise the objection that in the example *chātrāya rucitam*, the word *rucita* would also undergo the substitution of the word *artha*. In response to this doubt, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "The activity of the Teacher indicates: 'That dative case which occurs in the sense of *tadarthya* (for the sake of that) is compounded, but not every dative case. This is because he [the Teacher] makes the inclusion of the words *hita* and *sukha*. Even under the view of *yogavibhāga*, by the rule "the fourth case" (*caturthī*), only that dative case which occurs in the sense of *tadarthya* is subject to compounding.

Nor does this apply to the general category of the fourth case (caturthī). Otherwise, since the compound *go-hitam* ("beneficial for cows") would already be established by the rule regarding the fourth case alone, the inclusion of the words *hita* and *sukha*—which serve as the means for establishing that specific compound—would result in futility. Consequently, in the example *chātrāya rucitam* ("pleasing to the student"), the fourth case is not one denoting the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādṛśārthatve*).

Therefore, since there is no compound at all in that case, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the substitution of *artha* for the final member of the compound—which is prescribed by the rule *tadarthārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.36)—does not occur either. Bearing this context in mind, he says: "For instance... (*tathā hi*). [Under the rule] *taddhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.51): even when the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has already been expressed by a compound, a secondary derivative suffix is still applied.

This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) in *dvigor lug-anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88), which prescribes the elision (*luk*) of the subsequent *taddhita* suffix after a *dvigu* compound. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*, a compound of cardinal numbers and directions with a *sub*-ending word is prescribed in the sense of a *taddhita* derivative, or as a final member, or in a collective (*samāhāra*).

And this is the conclusion reached: since there would be no meaning of the suffix distinct from the meaning of the base in that which constitutes the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix, a *taddhita* suffix would not apply in cases such as *pāñcanāpitih*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "even though it is expressed by a compound. By the rule "dvigor lug anapatye," the elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix following a *dvigu* compound is prescribed when its meaning is not that of a descendant (*anapatya*).

For example, in the case of *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared in five potsherds"), since the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed by the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16) in the sense of "prepared [as a sacrificial cake]," when the compound *pañcan-sukapāla-su* is formed in the sense of that *aṇ* by the rule *taddhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), and then the *aṇ* is elided by the rule *dvigorluganapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88), the form *pañcakapālaḥ* results. Here, in the sense of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [the number is expressed].

Because the meaning [of the suffix] is already expressed by the formation of the *dvigu* compound, the prescription of elision (*luk*) for the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) *aṇ* would be purposeless; for the prescription of its elision is meaningful only when *aṇ* actually arises. Therefore, the prescription of elision indicates that a secondary derivative suffix occurs even when its meaning has already been expressed by a compound. Consequently, the rule is purposeful as it prescribes the elision of the secondary derivative suffix once it has arisen.

The intention is that, therefore, in cases such as *pāñcanāpitir*, even though the sense of offspring (*apatya*) is already expressed by a compound, the formation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) remains unimpeded. In reality, however, if one were to explain the rule *taddhitārthe vācye* as *taddhitārthe viṣaye* ("when the domain of the secondary suffix is present"), this fault would not arise. Nevertheless, the underlying point is that the very prescription of elision (*luk*) indicates that what is intended is "in the domain of the secondary suffix. As it has been stated in the Udyota: "In this way, it is also established by taking the meaning to be 'when the domain of the secondary suffix is present.'"

"In fact, it should be understood that this very meaning is indicated by the *jñāpaka* [the evidence]. (Udyota on Pāṇini 2.1.51). Regarding the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.56): Since a compound would not apply due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*)—because there would be a state of mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*) when a common attribute is used—that prohibition [of compounding] indicates that a compound can indeed occur even for a principal word (*pradhāna*) that is dependent on something else. [Objection: But surely, in the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.1.56), the phrase "when a common attribute is not used" (*sāmānyāprayoge*) is redundant.

One might object: "In the case of *na ca puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ* ('And the man is not a hero like a tiger'), since the word *śūra* (hero), which expresses a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), is employed, the formation of a compound should be prevented by that [rule]. To this, one should reply: even without that rule, the formation of a compound can be prevented here precisely because the word *puruṣa*, which is being compounded, is dependent upon the word *śūra*, which is not a constituent of the compound; thus, the condition of "independence from words not constituting the compound" (*samāsāghaṭakapadanirapekṣatva*) is absent. Anticipating this objection, he states its purpose as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words beginning "in the case of the employment of a general term" (*sāmānyaprayoge*).

It is indicated that a compound is formed even when, between two words being compounded, the word expressing the substantive (viśeṣya) is dependent upon a word not included within the compound itself. Thus, in the case of *puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ* ("A man is brave like a tiger"), although the word *puruṣa*, which provides the substantive, is dependent upon the word *śūra*, a compound would otherwise result; therefore, the rule *sāmānyāprayoge* ("when the general term is not used") is stated to prevent that. The sense is that because of the use of the word *śūra*, which expresses a general quality (*sāmānya*), no compound is formed there.

The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is that in examples such as *rājapuruṣo 'bhirūpaḥ* ("the king's handsome servant"), the compound is established even when the word expressing the substantive (*viśeṣya*), namely *puruṣa*, is dependent on words like *abhirūpa* which are not constituents of the compound. Regarding the term *vṛtti*: it means "compound" (*samāsa*). This is because we see the very wording in the Bhāṣya: "Indeed, a compound does take place even for a principal element (*pradhāna*) that is dependent. [Now, regarding the rule] *yuvā khalati* (Pāṇini 2.1.67).

This indicates that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned [in a rule], that which is qualified by gender is also included. This *paribhāṣā* has been explained in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*; therefore, we shall leave it aside here. Regarding *dvitīyatṛtīya* (Pāṇini 2.2.3): when the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option) is in force, the mention of *anyatarasyām* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that where a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*) are both made optional by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, the general rule does not apply once the exception has already taken effect.

This statement, *jhrvi.ṭa*, was previously cited as having been indicated by the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or") in the rule *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* (P. 2.1.18), and its explanation is largely complete. Its purpose, however, is to establish the correctness of forms such as *bhikṣādvitīya* by allowing for the optional formation of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) as well. *jhrjñā.ṭa*: The rule *upapadam* (P. 2.2.19) [is understood]. The prohibition regarding *atiṅ* (P. 2.2.19) indicates that the rule *sup supā* (P. 2.1.4) has ceased to apply to these two rules. By this, the principle *gatikārakopapadānām kṛdbhiḥ saha samāsavacanam prāk subutpatteḥ* ("the statement that prepositions, kārakas, and upapadas form compounds with kṛt-derivatives prior to the addition of case-endings") is established.

The rule *jhrvi.ṭa* is not explained here, as it is a general metarule (*paribhāṣā*). Regarding *jhrjñā.ṭa*: "When more than one [word] is used in the sense of another word-meaning" (Pāṇini 2.2.24). By the force of the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*), the "word-meaning" (*padārtha*) is understood here as being complete—that is, possessing substance (*sadrvya*), gender (*saliṅga*), and number (*sasaṃkhya*).

Regarding the sūtra *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24), a solution was stated: if the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) is denoted by the bahuvrīhi compound itself, then in an expression such as *citragur devadattaḥ*, the subsequent employment of the word *devadatta* would be untenable; for since the other referent—Devadatta—is already denoted by the bahuvrīhi alone, there would be no need for further mention. To resolve this, it was argued that because the other referent is not denoted in its specific form [as Devadatta], the employment of the word *devadatta* is justified. Alternatively, it is maintained that the case-ending meaning (*vibhaktyartha*) is what is denoted.

Thus another alternative view has been stated in the Bhāṣya: that the meaning of the suffix, qualified by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is denoted by the word; and because the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) alone is predominant, it is included by the mention of the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*). And so, by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the meaning of the case-ending—such as the relation (*saṃbandha*) and so forth—is expressed.
Now begins the third chapter.

Pāṇini 3.1.3 states: *jhrjñā.ṭa ādyudāttaśca*. Although this could have been established by the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣvapicca liṅ* (3.4.103), the specific formulation *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca* indicates that suffixes (*āgama*s) are unaccented (*anudātta*). It has been stated that this very point also serves as an indicator for the principle that suffixes (*āgama*s) are as if non-existent. However, both of these [interpretations] are merely the assertions of partial authorities (*ekadeśin*).

JHRVIṬA: Now, in the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca*, what is the purpose of including the mention of *udātta* (acute)? For the acute nature of *yāsuṭ*, which is a part of the suffix, would be established by the accent of the suffix itself. Nor can it be argued that the mention of *udātta* is for the purpose of setting aside the fact that *yāsuṭ*—which is a part of the *liṅ* substitutes *ti*, *sip*, and *mip*—would otherwise be *anudātta* (grave) according to the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.1.4).

If that were the case, one could have formulated the rule simply as *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣvapicca liṅ*; for in that formulation, since all substitutes of *liṅ* would be designated as having the property of being *apit* by the phrase *apicca liṅ*, the property of being *pit* would not apply to them, and consequently, the low-pitched (*anudātta*) quality conditioned by *pit*-ness would not be established. Since the high-pitched (*udātta*) quality would then necessarily result from the accent of the suffix itself, the mention of *udātta* (in the original rule) would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he states that the mention of *yāsuṭ* is purposeful because it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the metarule *āgamā anudāttāḥ* ("augments are unaccented"). Thus he says: *yāsuḍiṭ*.

The sense is that since verbal suffixes (*āgama*) are *anudātta* (unaccented), the rule for *yāsuṭ* might otherwise result in it being *anudātta* as well; therefore, the explicit statement that it is *udātta* was made. Regarding the phrase "this very [rule]" and so forth: the word "stated" refers to the *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) mentioned in the context of the sūtra *ādyudāttaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.3). Since *yāsuṭ* would already be established as *udātta* by the accentuation of the beginning of a suffix—given that it is a suffix qualified by *yāsuṭ*—the specific mention of *yāsuṭ* as *udātta* serves as an indicator of the principle that "verbal suffixes (*āgama*) are as if non-existent."

Furthermore, it has been established therein that when [the suffix] is non-existent, since the pratyaya itself—devoid of that [augment]—is acute-accented (udātta), the grave-accent (anudātta) of the augments is established by the rule of "grave accent for the remainder" (śeṣanighāta). Thus, his intention is that the mention of "acute" (udātta-grahaṇa) serves its purpose as an exclusion of the grave accent that would otherwise result from śeṣanighāta.

One might object: "Since *yāsuṭ* is conditioned by the *parasmaipada*, it applies after the substitution of the *l*-suffixes; therefore, because it is either *antaraṅga* or *para*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the beginning of the suffix would apply first. Consequently, the accent of *yāsuṭ* would be either the acute (*udātta*) or, by the rule of *śeṣanighāta*, the grave (*anudātta*). Thus, how can the explicit mention of the acute (*udāttavacana*)—which is performed for the purpose of establishing an acute accent—be considered an *jñāpaka*? Anticipating this doubt, he states that this is merely the opinion of a partial exponent (*ekadeśin*), saying: "Both of these... [The sūtra: *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).

Regarding the rule *aśvāghasyāt* (Pāṇini 7.4.37), because the prescription of the vowel *ā* is intended to override the substitution of *ī* in the *kyac* suffix, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *kyac* suffix occurs after the word *agha* in the Vedic language (*chandas*) when expressing the desire of another. Now, an objection is raised: in the sūtra *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the term *ātmanaḥ* is construed with *supaḥ*. Consequently, the meaning of the sūtra is obtained as follows: the *kyac* suffix occurs after a nominal stem (*subanta*) that expresses a thing related to oneself, in the sense of "desire."

This being the case, regarding the Vedic passage "mā tvā vṛkā agāyavaḥ," one might object that the suffix *kyac* would not apply after the word *agha* in the sense of "desiring evil" (*aghamicchanti*), because the wolves do not desire evil pertaining to themselves, but rather the evil of another. Furthermore, since the word *agha* lacks the capacity to denote evil connected to the wolves who are the desirers, how could *kyac* arise from it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the rule *aśvāghasyāditi*. In the Veda, the suffix *kyac* occurs even when the desire concerns something belonging to another.

In this regard, the indicative authority (*jñāpaka*) is the rule *aśvāghasyāt*. The meaning of that rule is that when the suffix *kyac* follows the words *aśva* and *agha*, the substitution of *ā* occurs [for the final vowel]. In that context, the suffix *kyac* can only occur after the word *agha* when expressing the desire of another; for in the world, no one would ever desire their own misfortune (*agha*), but rather desires the misfortune of another. Thus, by prescribing the substitution of *ā* for the word *agha* when *kyac* follows, Pāṇini implies his approval of the occurrence of *kyac* after the word *agha*.

The point is this: from this *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), namely the word *agha*, it is established that in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *kyac* occurs even in the sense of "desiring something undesirable" (*agham icchati*). This is because of the *jñāpaka* in the rule *namovarivaścitraṅaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.19). Since the suffixes beginning with *kyac* denote actions (*kriyāvacana*), they receive the technical designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32). The purpose of this is that these [suffixes] trigger the grammatical operations associated with verbal roots, such as the suffixes *tavyat* and others. Furthermore, the suffixes *tavyat* and others occur in relation to the "means" (*sādhana*, i.e., the agent or instrument). And since the "means" belongs only to an action, it follows that even a "state" (*bhāva*) is indeed an action.

However, in the case of an external means (*parasādhana*), there is no production [of a suffix] from these [roots]. This is because the term "means" (*sādhana*) is inherently relational; for when a root has a particular means, the suffix is produced from that very root. This is stated in the rule *vi-ṭan-mo-vaś-vaś-vaś-citraṅaḥ kyac*, which indicates that in the case of suffixes such as *kyac* and others, the meaning of the suffix is specified [in relation to the root].

Thus it was stated by the author of the Vārttika. Its meaning is as follows: the suffix *kyac* occurs after the word *namas* in the sense of "worship," after the word *varivas* in the sense of "service" (*saparyā*), and after the root *citraṅ* in the sense of "wonder"; in this way, the meaning of the suffix *kyac* must also be specified. Otherwise, that which ends in *kyac* would not be expressive of an action (*kriyā*). This Vārttika was refuted by the author of the Bhāṣya through a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark), whereby the fact that forms ending in *kyac* and others are expressive of action was established.

Thus he says: "those ending in *kyac* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the suffix *ṇiṅ* is included. By the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.1.32), the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is prescribed for that which ends in *kyac* and so forth. The purpose of this is the establishment of forms such as *tavyat* and others, which are prescribed under the governing heading "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*). Furthermore, *tavyat* and other suffixes are prescribed when there is a "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) in the form of an object (*karman*) and so forth; and a means of accomplishment belongs to an action (*kriyā*).

The point is this: if that which ends in *kyac* and so forth were not expressive of action (*kriyā*), then because the action denoted by it would be absent, suffixes such as *tavyat*—which are prescribed for the accomplishment of action (*kriyāsādhana*)—would not occur after those ending in *kyac*. Consequently, the rule prescribing the technical designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) for the purpose of [applying] *tavyat* and other suffixes would be rendered meaningless. Since the designation "root" has been stated, it is understood that that which ends in *kyac* and so forth is expressive of action. [Objection: But how can it be said that *tavyat* and the others occur in relation to the "accomplisher" (*sādhana*)?

Having raised the objection that the suffixes *tavyat* and others are prescribed even in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70), [the author] replies: Let it be so. Nevertheless, since the suffixes *tavyat* and others occur after the word *bhāva*, they must refer to the action expressed by that [word]; and because a word ending in *kyac* and the like lacks the capacity to denote an action, the suffixes *tavyat* and others would be difficult to obtain even in the sense of the abstract action after such a word. Thus, the prescription of *tavyat* and others in the sense of the abstract action, as well as the prescription of the technical term "verbal root" (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) for its result, necessarily implies that a word ending in *kyac* and the like does not denote an action.

He provides the resolution by stating that "even a state (bhāva) is indeed an action (kriyā). Now, one might object: even if forms ending in *kyac* and so forth lack the capacity to express an action, they may denote a substance (*dravya*) due to their being suffixes that do not alter the meaning (*svārthika*). Furthermore, the result of the technical designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is the derivation of suffixes such as *tavyat*, which express the action or the factors of action (*kāraka*) denoted by other words—just as, for example, from the word *vṛkṣa* (tree), which denotes a substance, the accusative case ending is applied in expressions like *vṛkṣaṃ paśya* ("see the tree") when one intends to express its status as the object of the action of seeing. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But in the case of the means belonging to another (*parasādhane*)."

Since the word *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is inherently relational, when the expectancy arises as to "in the accomplishment of what," the understanding is obtained that the suffixes such as *tavyat* apply to that verbal root whose meaning possesses the means of accomplishment in question. This is just as when it is said, "one must behave toward one's mother," and upon the doubt arising as to "toward whose mother? it is understood to mean "toward one's own mother."

Furthermore, since the suffixes beginning with the second case (dvitīyā) are prescribed after nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and since a nominal stem denotes a substance (*dravya*), these suffixes arise for the sake of another (*parasādhana*) by virtue of the authority of the grammatical rule. However, suffixes such as *tavyat* and others have their scope for application in expressing action (*kriyā*) when they follow other verbal roots (*dhātu*) for the sake of themselves (*svasādhana*). They do not arise for the sake of another when following forms ending in *kyac* and so forth. Thus, the point is that the very prescription of the technical term "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) for these forms ending in *kyac* etc., resulting in suffixes like *tavyat*, is the proof that they denote action.

*Muṇḍamiśra* (Pāṇini 3.2.21). Because of the rule prescribing the substitution of *a* for *hal* and *kala*, it is indicated (*jñāpaka*) that when the *vṛddhi* [vowel] has been applied, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant]. [Objection]: But surely, by the rule *muṇḍamiśraślakṣṇalavaṇavratavastrahalakalakṛtatūstebhyo ṇic* (Pāṇini 3.2.21), the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed after words such as *muṇḍa* in the sense of "he makes [someone] so"; and in that rule, the two words *hala* and *kala* are recited.

It is understood from that [rule] that *ātva* (the substitution of /a/) is prescribed for these two, *hali* and *kali*, which end in /i/, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). This is illustrated by the examples: "he causes the *hali* to be seized" (*halayati*) and "he causes the *kali* to be seized" (*kalayati*). In this regard, let it simply be that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied directly to the forms ending in /i/, namely *hali* and *kali*. For what purpose is it explained that the causative suffix is applied to *hali* and *kali* after they have already undergone the substitution of /a/ (*ātva*)?

Nor is it explained in that way for the purpose of prohibiting *saṇvad-bhāva* (the treatment as having a penultimate *s*); for instance, from the roots *hal* and *kal*, when followed by *ṇic* and *luṅ* with *caṅ*, the forms *acakalat* and *ajahalat* are desired. And these two are possible only when *ṇic* is present, because they are treated as nipātana (irregularly formed) items.

In the case of *ahala i at*, after the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat*, and after doubling [the root] by the rule *caṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.11) and the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the form *ajahalat* is established. Because the stem (*aṅga*) has lost its vowel (*aglopi*), the rule *anaglope* (8.4.93) prohibits the treatment as if it were followed by *san* (*sanvadbhāva*). Consequently, the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *sanyataḥ* (7.4.89) does not take place. Furthermore, if the *ṇic* affix were added to the form ending in *ikāra* (*hali*), then, due to the extended application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat*, the *ikāra* would be elided by the rule *ṭeḥ* (6.4.155), and [the subsequent rules such as] *aco ñṇiti*... [would apply].

Since both [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* and [the substitution of] *aikāra* would apply [by Pāṇini 7.2.115], *vṛddhi* takes precedence due to its higher status; thus, when *aikāra* is substituted, the *ṭi*-portion is elided by the rule "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.143). Because the *aikāra* no longer possesses the quality of being a vowel (*aktva*), the elision of that [vowel] does not constitute an "elision of a vowel" (*aglopa*). Consequently, since the prohibition "in the case of non-elision of a vowel" (*anaglope*) does not apply, the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *saN* suffix) applies by the rule "sanvallaghuni" (Pāṇini 7.4.93), and the *itva* (substitution of *i*) of the reduplicated syllable occurs by "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79), resulting in forms such as *ajīhat* and *acīkalat*. Therefore, it must be stated that the *ṇic* suffix is applied to the roots *hal* and *kal*, which have already undergone the substitution of *ātva*.

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* (Pāṇini 7.4.2), it is indicated that elision (*lopa*) is stronger than vṛddhi because of the mention of *aglopi*. Consequently, even in the case of *ahali i at at*, elision of the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the *ikāra* by the rule *hali* would take precedence over vṛddhi; thus, since the base (*aṅga*) would still be *aglopi*, the prohibition *anaglope* would prevent the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule. Anticipating the objection that the specific mention of the short *a* (*adantatva-nipātana*) is therefore redundant, he says: *halikalyoḥ*.

The purposeless prescription of the suffix *sad* ending in *at* (in the rule *sadisvidisādhigaḍirudhi*) indicates that, in the case of the words *halika* and *kalika*, after the application of *vṛddhi* and the subsequent elision (*lopa*), [the resulting form] is not treated as having its penultimate vowel elided (*aglopi*). Consequently, when a *ṇic* is added to a word ending in *i*, if *vṛddhi* were applied first and then the *i* were elided, the *ṇic* would lack the status of being *aglopi*. In such a case, when *saṇvadbhāva* applies, the substitution of *it* by the rule *sanyataḥ* would occur; therefore, the *ṇic* is stated here with the *ātvam* already applied.

And thus, when the suffix *ṇic* is added to roots ending in short vowels such as *hal* and *kal*, and the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied to produce the vowel *ā*, even though that *ā* is subsequently elided, there is still an elision of an *ak* vowel (*aglopa*). Consequently, because of the prohibition "in the case of non-elision of an *ak* vowel" (*anaglope*), the treatment as *sanvadbhāva* does not apply; therefore, the substitution of *it* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not occur—this is the underlying intention. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, it is observed: "The specific mention of the forms *halika* and *kalika* is for the purpose of prohibiting *sanvadbhāva*. One should understand that this statement also somehow intends the same meaning already explained. [Now follows the rule: *jñā-ṭa cleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44).

Because of the *kit*-marker attached to *sic*, it is indicated (*jñāpaka*) that there is no elision of the final *n* of a stem ending in *sic*. Consequently, the *it*-marker on *sic* may be rejected; for its status as having an *it*-marker is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original). [Objection: But surely, regarding the substitute *sic* that takes the place of *cl-* (the aorist suffix), both the letter *c* and the vowel *i* are intended to be marked with the *it*-designation. In that case, the addition of the secondary marker (*anubandha*) called *i* would be useless. Nor can it be argued that the addition of that marker is for the sake of an operation triggered by the *it*-status of the stem ending in *sic*.

For instance, regarding the form *amaṃsta*, one might argue that since the suffix *sic* lacks the marker *it*, the *sic*-ending stem would not be considered *anidit* (having no *it* as its final vowel), and consequently, the *n* of its penultimate (*upadhā*) syllable would be elided by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). However, this objection is refuted because the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14)—which prescribes that *sic* following the root *han* is marked with *kit*—serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of *n* does not apply to *sic*-ending stems; thus, the absence of *n*-elision in *amaṃsta* is established.

To explain: from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *ā*, in the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is applied; *cli* becomes *sic*, and [the ending] *ta* is added. When the form *ā han s ta* is established, because the *sic* suffix is *kit* by the rule *hanaḥ sic*, the nasal *n* is elided by the rule *anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), which prescribes the elision of the nasal of roots taught with an *anudātta* accent, as well as *van* and *tan* etc., when followed by a *jhal* consonant or a *kṅit* affix. Then, by the rule *ḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍanasvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.27), the *s* is elided, resulting in the form *āhata*.

In this context, the prescription of *kittva* for the suffix *sic* would be redundant if it were *anidit* (lacking an *i* or *t* as its *it*). For if that were the case, then in the form *āhan* (from *āhan-s*), the *n* of the stem ending in *sac* would be elided by the rule "aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.24), thereby achieving the desired result; what then would be the purpose of prescribing *kittva* for *sic*? Yet, that very prescription is made, and it serves to indicate that the *n* of the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a stem ending in *sic* does not undergo elision by the rule "aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ."

And thus, the prescription of *kit*-status for *sic* is purposeful for the sake of establishing the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* in the root *han*. Furthermore, since the absence of *n*-elision is established by the statement that it does not occur for the form ending in *sic* in *amaṃsta*, the *it*-status of *sic* is not necessary for that purpose. Consequently, let there be no *it*-status for *sic*; let it simply be *sac*. This is the conclusion. He states this very point with the words "because of the making of *sic* a *kit*" and so forth.

Because the root *cli* has the marker *it*, the *sic* that arises in its place obtains the status of having the marker *it* precisely through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, he says—namely, "by way of *sthānivadbhāva*"—that the *it*-marker of *sic* is entirely useless. However, in reality, since it has been demonstrated that all desired results are established even without the *it*-marker, the attempt to establish the *it*-marker of *sic* by means of *sthānivadbhāva* is superfluous.

Therefore, it should be noted that the author himself stated in his *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota* that the Vārttika "because of being like the substitute for what stands in the place of *it*" (*ididvāsthānivattvāt*) is the statement of a partial view (*ekadeśyukti*). Regarding the rule *vāsarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94): due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *dadātidadātyor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.139), dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) is not caused by an *anubandha* (indicatory letter). [This applies to forms such as] *haśaśvator laṅ*.

By the *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) of the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.116), it is understood that the rule of non-homogeneity (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply to substitutes for *loṭ*. These two rules (*vi.* and *jñā.*) are not explained here because they are of the nature of *paribhāṣās* (technical maxims). Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter. Regarding the rule *ṭhacareṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16), [the suffix] is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and not the object (*karman*), as indicated by the inclusion of the word "alms" (*bhikṣā*) in the rule *bhikṣāsenādāyeṣu ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.17).

Objection: Why does the suffix *ṭa*, prescribed by the rule *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16), not occur in the case of *kurūṃścarati* when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is the *upapada*? It cannot be argued that because the term *adhikaraṇe* ("in the sense of locus") from the preceding rule *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* (3.2.15) is understood to carry over into *careṣṭaḥ*, the suffix does not apply when the *upapada* is an object (*karman*). For the term *karmaṇi* ("when the object is the *upapada*") is also understood to carry over [from the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*].

Otherwise, there would be no possibility of the application of the suffixes prescribed by the subsequent sūtras when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). Anticipating this objection, he establishes [the point] by means of the following: "The rule *careṣṭaḥ* applies only when the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) is the co-occurring word, not when the direct object is," as indicated by the statement "and in the case of *bhikṣā*, *sena*, and *ādāya*" (*bhikṣā-senādāyeṣu ca*).

If the rule *careṣṭaḥ* were to apply even when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a co-occurring word (*upapada*), then in the case of *bhikṣāṃ carati*, the form *bhikṣācaraḥ* would be established by this very suffix *ṭa*; consequently, the mention of *bhikṣā* in the rule *bhikṣā-senā-dāyeṣu ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.16) would be redundant. Yet, that [mention] has been made; it serves to indicate that the rule *careṣṭaḥ* applies only when there is a locative (*adhikaraṇa*) as the co-occurring word.

And thus, the inclusion of *bhikṣā* [in the rule] serves its own purpose by providing for the suffix *ṭa* when *karmaṇi* is the upapada; however, the practical utility is that in examples such as *kurūṃścarati*, the suffix *ṭa* does not occur after the root *car* when *karmaṇi* is the upapada—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the rule *satsūdviṣa...* (Pāṇini 3.2.61): here, the mention of *su* indicates that even when an upasarga is present, [the suffix applies]; otherwise, in other rules where *su* is mentioned, an upasarga would not be included. Consequently, the requirement to explicitly state "when there is no upasarga" (*anupasarge*) in the case of the root *vad* (as in *vadaḥ supyanupasarge*) becomes unnecessary.

In the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhasatsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājāmupasarge'pi kkip* (Pāṇini 3.2.61), the author of the Vārttikas stated: "The term *sub* is to be included among *sad* and the others. The meaning of this is that the suffix *kkip* occurs after roots such as *sad* when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is present as an upapada. For example, in the phrase *vedyāṃ sīdati* ("he sits on the altar"), when the word *vedi* ending in a case-suffix is present as an upapada, the root *sad* takes *kkip*, resulting in the form *vediṣat*.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, raised the objection: "If it is stated that *kvip* occurs when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is the *upapada*, then since a prefix (*upasarga*) is also a word ending in a case-suffix, it would already be included by the rule *supi*; therefore, it need not be stated in the sūtra that 'also when there is a prefix'. Anticipating this, he stated that this must be stated for the sake of providing a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since the inclusion of the prefix (*upasarga*) is already established by the very mention of *sup* (in the rule *supi*), the fact that the term *upasarga* is explicitly mentioned serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Its intended meaning is this: wherever a suffix is prescribed with *sup* as the governing word (*upapada*), it does not apply when a prefix is the governing word. This is confirmed by the fact that the term *upasarga* is included in the rule *satsūdviṣa...* for the purpose of forming the *kvip* suffix even when a prefix is the governing word; thus, its purpose is fulfilled.

The purpose, however, is this: by the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.106), which prescribes the suffix *kyap*, it is established that the suffix *kyap* does not occur when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*). Consequently, it is proven that the Vārttika stating "the mention of 'not being preceded by a prefix' (*anupasarga*) must be made" for that rule need not be composed. For this very reason, in forms such as *pravādyam*, the suffix *kyap* does not occur after the root *vad* when a prefix is present as an attendant word. Having intended all of this, he says: "even here, despite the prefix."

The rule *jhrjñā.ṭa ātmamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.83) teaches that the prescription of the anudātta accent for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following the root *tās* (the third person singular ending) indicates that the accent of the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational affix), even when it is subsequently applied (*sati śiṣṭa*), does not supersede the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*. Regarding the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhaātamamāne khaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.82), it is stated by the *vārttika* "karmakartari ca" that the affix *khaś* occurs after the root *man* when it is used in the sense of self-reflection (*ātmakarmakamanana*) with a nominal stem (*sup*) as its attendant word (*upapada*), provided the meaning is that of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*).

The intention of the speaker is this: when the suffix *khaś* follows, the suffix *yak* is applied by the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67), because the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) applies due to the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87). Thus, in the form *darśanīyamānī*, the audible presence of the letter *y* is the result. Regarding this, the following objection arises: let there be no mention of the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) here; let this suffix *khaś* be prescribed for the agent alone.

Because the root *man* belongs to the *divādi* class, when the suffix *khaś* follows in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) before a sārvadhātuka affix, the form *darśanīyammanya-*—containing the letter *ya*—is indeed established by the application of *śyan*. Now, although the form is established, there is nevertheless a difference in accent (*svara*). If *yak* were applied, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) would result from the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). However, if *śyan* is applied, the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) results according to the rule *ñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197).

This must be stated: because the accent of *śyan* is superseded by the accent of *khaś*, the desired final acute (*antodātta*) is established. Even so, since *khaś* and its accent occur first, followed by *śyan* and its associated accent, the accent of *śyan* would be stronger—because it is prescribed in the presence of the accent of *khaś*—and thus the initial syllable would necessarily be acute. To resolve this doubt, he provides a solution based on a rule established by implication (*jñāpaka*), stating: "of that which follows *tās*."

The intention here is as follows: by the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) is prescribed for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes that follow the element *tās*. For example, in forms such as *kartā*, the *ā*—which is the substitute for the *luṭ* ending following *tās*—becomes unaccented. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accentuation of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).

If a *sati-śiṣṭa* accent were stronger, then, since the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) is *sati-śiṣṭa*, the accent of *tās* would subvert the accent of the suffix; thus, the anudātta status of the suffix being already established by that alone, the prescription of anudātta for the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās* would not be necessary. Since this anudātta is prescribed, it indicates that even a *vikaraṇa-svara* which is *sati-śiṣṭa* does not subvert the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*.

Furthermore, in forms such as *kartā*, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would apply; therefore, to prevent that, the rule prescribing an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel for what follows the suffix *tasi* is established. Thus, in cases like *darśanīyamānyaḥ*, if the suffix *śyan* is used, it does not subvert the *khakhsvara* (the accent of the *khaś*), and consequently there is only the final acute (*antodāttatā*). Since even with the suffix *yak* there is only the final acute, there is no difference in accent; thus, since the desired result is achieved by *śyan* alone, it is logical that this *khaś* applies only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, it is concluded that the mention of the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) need not be made.

*Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.118*: *laṭ sme*. This indicates that the [suffixes] characterized by *purā* and those characterized by *sma* do not occur in the sense of the recent past (*adyatana*). The meaning of the rule *laṭ sme* is that when the word *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *laṭ* occurs in the sense of the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa*); this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *liṭ*. Examples include: *nalena sma purādhīyata* ("Nala was studying in the past"). Regarding that sūtra, there are two Vārttikas: "In the case of *sma* and *purā*, [the suffix is used] for the mere past (*bhūtamātra*); in the case of *sma* and *purā*, [it is] not for the recent past (*adyatana*)."

And this is its meaning: by means of the words *sma* and *purā* at the beginning and end of the first *vārttika*, the group of five sūtras (*sūtra*-pañcakam) from Pāṇini 3.2.118 to 3.2.122 is indicated—namely, "The present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is used with *sma*" (3.2.118), "Also when not immediate" (3.2.119), "With *na* or *nu* in response to a question" (3.2.120), "Optionally with *na* or *nu*" (3.2.121), and "The aorist (*luṅ*) is used with *purā*, except with *sma*" (3.2.122). In that context, the suffix occurs for mere past time (*bhūtamātra*). However, a suffix characterized by *sma* or *purā* does not occur in the sense of the current day (*adyatana*).

That is to say, by the three rules—"*laṭ sme*," "*aparokṣe ca*," and "*puriluṅ cāsme*,"—an affix is prescribed for a specific past tense (*bhūta-viśeṣa*) that is not of today (*anadyatana*). However, by the two rules—"*nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane*" and "*nanvor vibhāṣā*"—an affix is prescribed for the past in general (*bhūta-mātra*). Thus, one must adopt this systematic distinction (*vyavasthā*). And the intention of the author of the *Vārttika* is that this systematic distinction is not obtainable from the Sūtras themselves.

In fact, this very rule is obtained from the Sūtra itself; thus he says: "it makes this known. Because of the commencement of the subsequent Sūtra, "aparekṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.119), it is understood that the term *parokṣa* (past not witnessed by the speaker) is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the Sūtra "laṭ sme" (3.2.118). Consequently, since the mention of *anadyatana* (not of today) is also connected with the mention of *parokṣa*, it follows that the Sūtra "laṭ sme" pertains to the domain of the *parokṣa-anadyatana* (past not witnessed and not of today).

The rule *aparokṣe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.119) concerns the non-perceptual and non-immediate past; however, in the rule *puri luṅ cāsme* (Pāṇini 3.2.122), the mention of the *luṅ* suffix itself establishes that its scope is restricted to the non-immediate past.

For if this were a rule [applying] merely to the past (*bhūtamātra*), then, by the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* from the rule "nanvor vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 3.2.121), the present tense (*laṭ*) would be prescribed optionally; consequently, in the alternative where that is absent, the aorist (*luṅ*)—which is prescribed for the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*)—would occur anyway. Thus, the mention of *luṅ* would be redundant. However, since the aorist is not prescribed for what is not of the current day (*anadyatana*) by the rule "puri," the mention of *luṅ* is made in order to ensure the occurrence of the aorist in that specific case.

Thus, it is established that this triad of rules pertains to the past tense excluding the immediate past (*anadyatana*). Regarding the middle two rules—*nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* (Pāṇini 3.2.120) and *nanvor vibhāṣā* (3.2.121)—since the mention of "the remote past" (*parokṣa*) and its negation, "not the remote past" (*aparokṣa*), are removed, the mention of "the immediate past" (*anadyatana*), which is invariably associated with them, is also removed. Consequently, these rules have as their scope the past in general. Since this distinction of scope is obtained by the rules themselves, the sense is that the Vārttika is unnecessary.

Regarding *jhr-jñā-ṭa* [Pāṇini 3.2.146]: Because of the rule prescribing the suffix *vuñ* after words such as *nindā*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in the case of suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), suffixes such as *tṛc* do not occur by way of the *vā-sarūpa* rule. [Objection: But surely...

The prescription of the suffix *vuñ* after words such as *nindā* by the rule *nindahiṃsa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.146) is redundant, because the desired form is already established by the suffix *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (Pāṇini 3.2.133). This is because there is no difference between the two forms in terms of their appearance (*rūpa*) or accent (*svara*). In the case of the word *nindaka* under the *ṇvul* alternative, by the rule *liti* (Pāṇini 6.2.193), the syllable preceding the suffix becomes acute; thus, the vowel *i* of the root is acute.

Even in the case of the suffix *vuñ*, there is no difference in accent, because by the rule "the first syllable of that which begins with *ñ* is always acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.197), that very same [initial syllable] of the whole word becomes acute. Although there is no difference in accent regarding monosyllabic verbal roots (*ekācdhātu*), nevertheless, a difference in accent certainly occurs regarding polysyllabic verbal roots (*anekācdhātu*). In this rule, the root *asūya* is specified; therefore, when the suffix *vuñ* is applied, in the word *asūyaka*, the beginning of the whole word is acute.

However, since there is a difference in accent—namely, that in the case of the *ṇvul* suffix, the vowel *ū* preceding the suffix and following the letter *s* is acute—one must say that the rule exists for that purpose. Then, one might object: "In that case, let the rule simply be 'asūyovun,' for the mention of 'censure' (*nindā*) and so forth is redundant. Anticipating this, he states that the rule is meaningful as a *jñāpaka* (indicator) for a specific grammatical statement: "from censure and so forth" (*nindādibhyaḥ*). This is the meaning: in the absence of the mention of "censure" and so forth, forms such as *nindakaḥ* would not be established.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṇvul* is established optionally by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), since *tṛn* would otherwise invariably supersede *ṇvul*. For if that were the case, the desired result would be achieved through that very rule alone, making the inclusion of the term "censure" (*nindā*) and so forth in the sūtra redundant. This redundancy serves to indicate that the rule of "non-identity of form" does not apply in the sense of "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*) and other such meanings; thus, *ṇvul* would be invariably superseded by *tṛn*. Consequently, the inclusion of "censure" and so forth in the *vuñ*-sūtra is for the purpose of establishing forms such as *nindaka*, thereby fulfilling its own specific function (*svāṃśe cāritārthya*).

In other words, regarding the scope of suffixes prescribed by the *tācchīlika* section, the general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*) does not apply. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the suffixes *tṛc* and others, which would otherwise be obtained by the principle of *vāsarūpa*, do not occur in the case of *tācchīlika* suffixes. By the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) of the word *pada* in the rule *jucaṅkramya* (Pāṇini 3.2.150), it is understood that *tācchīlika* suffixes do not coexist with other *tācchīlika* suffixes by virtue of the *vāsarūpa* principle. However, by the indicative mark of the inclusion of the word *dīpa* in the rule *sūdadīpa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.148), there is a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *yu* with the suffix *reṇ*.

Objection: But surely, by the rule *ju-caṅkramya-draṃsya-sṛ-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ*, the suffix *yuc* is prescribed after roots beginning with *jup* when the agent possesses the qualities of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth. In that context, the inclusion of the root *pad* is redundant; for since it is both *anudātta-it* (having an indicatory vowel with a low pitch) and begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), the suffix *yuc* is already established by the general rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149).

Nor should one argue that, since the suffix *ukañ*—prescribed by the specific rule "laṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣahanakamagamaśṝbhya ukañ" (Pāṇini 3.2.154)—would otherwise sublate the suffix *yuc* prescribed by the general rule, the inclusion of the root *pad* in this *yuc*-rule is intended to establish their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). For, by the principle of *vāsarūpa*, the dissimilar suffix *ukañ* optionally sublates *yuc*, so that *yuc* is established in the alternative case anyway. Anticipating this objection, he states: "Because of the mention of *pada* here," meaning that the mention of *pada* is for the sake of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*).

The inclusion of the word *pada* in the rule is otherwise redundant according to the principle stated above; however, it serves to indicate that when there are apavāda (exceptional) rules involving *tācchīlika* suffixes, the corresponding *utsarga* (general) rules involving *tācchīlika* suffixes—which would otherwise apply by the *vāsarūpa* principle—are prohibited. Thus, since *ukañ* would otherwise supersede *yuc*, the inclusion of *pada* is meaningful for the sake of establishing *yuc* as well; this is the underlying intention. But if this is what is being indicated, then the mention of *dīp* in the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.153) would be redundant.

By that rule [sūtra], the suffix *artha* is prohibited for the root *dīp*, which would otherwise have been applicable by the rule "anudāttetaśca halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.149). The suffix *ra*, prescribed by the rule "namikampiramyajasakamahiṃsadīpo raḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.167), serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

Since both [suffixes] denote habitual action (*tācchīlika*), one might suspect that the mention of *tī* in the rule "sūdadīpadīkṣaśca" is redundant; for, by the power of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), the general suffix *yuc*—which is the subject of the exception to the *tācchīlika* suffixes—does not apply in the domain of the apavāda suffixes, and thus its prohibition would already be established. Anticipating this objection, he states "in the rule 'sūdadīpa... etc., explaining that it is indeed purposeful because it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the statement: "there is co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *yuc* with *re*."

The intention is that because of the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *yuc* with the suffix *rapratyaya*, the suffix *yuc* might occasionally also apply to the root *dīp*. Therefore, the mention of *dīp* is for the purpose of obtaining its exclusion. The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is that in cases such as "the desiring girl" (*kamrā kanyā*), the suffix *yuc* may optionally occur; by means of this, forms such as *kamanā kanyā* are established. Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter. [Note: *tumunṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10)] The prescription of the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* indicates that when a verbal action intended for the sake of another action is the governing word (*upapada*), [the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are applied].

[The objection is: "By the rule *vāsarūpa*, forms such as those ending in *-tṛc* are not excluded. [The reply is: Even so, that [rule] is for the sake of the suffix *ṇvul* in cases where *luṅ* and *lṛṅ* would otherwise apply. [Objection: But then, the prescription of *ṇvul* by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām* is redundant. Since the suffix *ṇvul* is already established by the general rule *ṇvul-tṛcau* when a verbal root meaning an action is used as an upapada and the time is future, forms such as *bhojako vrajati* ("he goes to eat")—meaning *bhoktuṃ vrajati* ("he goes in order to eat")—would be correctly formed even without the specific rule.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *ṇvul* in the rule is intended to prevent its sublation by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.23), which prescribes the suffix *lṛṭ* for the future tense when another action is present as a subordinate factor (*upapada*) for the sake of another action; for by the principle of "optionality due to dissimilar form" (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), *lṛṭ* would optionally sublate *ṇvul*, and thus *ṇvul* would be established even in the alternative case. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But [the suffix] *ṇvul* is prescribed again."

And thus, because it is indicated that the rule of *vāsarūpa* (the optionality of different suffixes) does not apply when one action is the object of another action used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed once again so that its application by *lṛṭ* may not be barred. Consequently, *ṇvul* is established even in cases where *lṛṭ* would otherwise be the sublater. By this, suffixes other than *ṇvul*, such as *tṛc* and others, are always superseded by *lṛṭ*.

The point is that expressions such as *kartā vrajati* ("the agent goes") are not used, because the sense [of the sūtra] is "he goes intending to do," just like *kārako vrajati* ("the doer goes"). Regarding the rule *grahavṛdṛniści* (Pāṇini 3.3.58): since the suffix *ghañ* is prohibited in the case of theft (*steya*)—as indicated by the mention of *steya* in the rule for the suffix *suṅ*—and because it is undesirable when not referring to theft, the inclusion of the term *niści* (from the root *ci* with the prefix *ni*) indicates this: namely, that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule *thāthaghañktātritrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) does not apply to the root *ci* preceded by *ni*.

Objection: In the rule *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.58), which prescribes the suffix *ap*, the inclusion of the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *nis-* is redundant. This is because the form *niścaya* is already established by the suffix *ac* according to *erac* (3.3.56). Furthermore, there is no difference in accent: in the case of the suffix *ac*, the word is oxytone due to its being marked with *cittva*; and even in the case of the suffix *ap*, it would be oxytone by the rule *thāthadhañktābitrakāṇām*. Thus, there is no distinction in accent either.

Nor should it be argued that the prescription of *ap* is for the purpose of overriding the application of *ghañ*—which would otherwise occur by the rule *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40)—on the grounds that this applies when there is no theft. For by the prohibition "when there is no theft," *ghañ* does not apply in the case of theft. Furthermore, in the case of taking with the hand where there is no theft, only *ghañ* is desired, as in *niścāya*, and not *ap*.

Thus, having raised the objection that the prescription of the suffix *ap* after the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *nis* would be purposeless, [the author] suggests that this very fact indicates that the final acute accent (*antodātta*) prescribed by the rule "thā-tha-... does not apply to the root *ci* when preceded by *nis*. Consequently, in the alternative where the suffix *ap* is applied, since the accent of "thā-tha-... does not take effect, the vowel following the letter *ca* in the word *caya* becomes acute by virtue of the root accent (*dhātusvara*).

The word *niścaya* is also derived from the same root by means of the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), whereby it becomes *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable). In the case of the suffix *ac*, it would be *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable); thus, due to this difference in accent (*svarabheda*), since the desired result cannot be achieved through *ac* when the object is the taking of something with the hand in the sense of theft, he provides the solution by stating "of theft" (*steyasya*) and so forth, namely that the suffix *appratyaya* is prescribed after the prefix *nis* [along with the root *ci*]. The phrase "in the rule for *ghañ*" means: in the rule *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40).

"Because it is undesirable"—this is the remainder [of the sentence], referring to the suffix *ap*. [The rule] *jñā-praiṣātisarga* (Pāṇini 3.3.163) is a statement regarding the *kṛtya* suffixes; its purpose is to ensure that there is no sublation by the *loṭ* suffix. By being situated after the section on feminine suffixes (*strī-adhikāra*), it indicates that the *vā-sarūpa* rule does not apply here. [Objection: But surely, in the rule *praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca*, the mention of *kṛtya* should be omitted. Since *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed generally for the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), they will apply to the cases of *praiṣa* and so forth, as well as elsewhere.

Nor should it be said that the mention of *kṛtya* [suffixes] is for the purpose of preventing the sublation of *kṛtyas* by this *loṭ* suffix prescribed as a specific rule in cases such as *praiṣa*; for, by the maxim of *vāsarūpa*, the *loṭ* would optionally sublate them, and thus the *kṛtyas* would still be established in the alternative case. Anticipating this objection, he states: "In that case, then, it is for the purpose of indicating that the rule of *vāsarūpa* does not apply after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*)."

And thus, since this rule *praiṣātisarga* exists after the governing heading *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the maxim of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*) does not apply here; consequently, since the *loṭ* suffix would invariably supersede the *kṛtya* suffixes, he states—"this mention of *kṛtya*"—in order to establish their coexistence.
