Regarding these two views, in the first case, by carrying forward the word *anta* ("end") from the rule *karṣātvato ghaño'nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), the meaning of the sūtra becomes: "the end of that which lacks an acute accent is acute."

In the second alternative (*pakṣa*), however, because an acute accent (*udātta*) is prescribed for the grave (*anudātta*) syllable itself, the word "end" (*anta*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], as there would be no purpose for it. Thus, in the second alternative, the result is that the initial [syllable] of the grave becomes acute; whereas in the first alternative, the result is that the end of the grave becomes acute. When the doubt arises as to which of these two alternatives is superior, he states that the second alternative alone is superior: "because of the *cit* designation applied to *ayac*."

In the sense of "this has two parts" or "this has three parts," the suffix *tayap* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* (Pāṇini 5.2.42) after the words *dvi* and *tri*. Furthermore, for the suffix *tayap*, the substitution of *ayaj* is prescribed by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyaj vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.43). Since *tayap* is marked with the indicator *p*, it is *anudātta* (unaccented).

The *ayac* substitute in place of that [suffix] is also considered *anudātta* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. When this [anudātta] follows, the *ikāra* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). In the cases of *dvayaṃ* and *trayaṃ*, the present sūtra—*anudāttasya ca yatro dāttalopaḥ*—would result in the initial vowel of *aya-* becoming *udātta*. To ensure that the word ends with an *udātta* (antodātta), the *ayac* suffix is marked with the *cit* accent.

Furthermore, if the word *anta* were to carry over (*anuvarteta*) from the rule *anudāttasya ca*, then by the rule *anudāttasya ayaḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) would apply only to the very end of the suffix *aya*; since the desired result would thus be established, what would be the purpose of applying the *cit* marker to *ayaC*? Therefore, the application of the *cit* marker indicates that the word *anta* does not carry over into this rule. If it does not carry over, then when it is stated that for an unaccented [suffix] *aya* there is an acute accent, because there is no reason to skip the first [element], it follows by implication that the accent applies to the very beginning (*ādi*).

The intention is that the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ayac* is purposeful, so that the final syllable may be acute (*udātta*). The result of this rule-statement is the establishment of the acute accent for the vowel *ā* in the form *vindāte*; otherwise, the final *e* would be acute. In the case of the root *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇe*), the suffix *āte* following it is rendered grave (*anudātta*) by the rule "tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttaṃ" (Pāṇini 6.1.186). Since *śnam* is a suffix (*pratyaya*), it is acute.

Consequently, when the *śna* and *as* suffixes undergo elision (*lopa*), it is desired that the vowel *ā* be acute according to the aforementioned rule; for if the term "end" (*anta*) were to carry over [from the previous rule], only the *e* would become acute. Regarding *aṣṭano dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.182): the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the case of *aṣṭan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *nuṭ* applies to forms ending in *ā*, and it is also an indicator for the optional application of the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan*).

Objection: The meaning of the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt* is that a case-ending beginning with *śas* following the long-vowel form of the word *aṣṭan* is acute-accented; *aṣṭāsu* is the illustrative example. In this regard, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) need not be included. Nor should it be argued that if it were absent, the case-ending *su* in *aṣṭasu*—following the short-vowel form of the word *aṣṭan*—would become acute-accented, and thus the mention of "long" is for the purpose of preventing that.

Regarding the word *aṣṭasu*, by the subsequent rule *jhalyupottamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.180)—which means that when a case-ending beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows, the penultimate syllable of the word ending in that suffix becomes acute—the penultimate vowel, namely the *ā* following the *ṭ* in *aṣṭa*, would indeed be acute. Consequently, the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.172), which occurs earlier in the sequence, does not apply to make the syllable *su* acute.

Furthermore, regarding the question as to why the *upottama* accent would not prevail even in the case of *aṣṭāsu* due to its subsequent status, the reply must be given by means of the *yenanāprāpti*-rule (the rule that applies when another rule would otherwise apply): namely, that the accent prescribed for *aṣṭan-* supersedes the *upottama* accent. And thus, by the same logic, one might argue that in *aṣṭasu* as well, the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*)—being an exception (*apavāda*)—would supersede the subsequent *upottama* accent; therefore, it must be said that the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule is meaningful precisely to prevent that [application of the case-ending accent].

For in the case of *aṣṭasu*, since the substitution of *ā* for *n* would result in a form ending in *a*, the designation *ṣaṭ* (six) would be absent; consequently, the accent prescribed by the rule *jhalyupottamam*—which depends upon the designation *ṣaṭ*—would not apply at all. Since that [accent] would necessarily have occurred [in its absence], it is impossible to say that the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* was formulated [merely] to prevent it, as there would be no status of an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, in *aṣṭasu*, because of its superior force (*paratva*), the accent of the penultimate syllable (*upottama-svara*) alone will take effect.

Even if the elision (*lopa*) of *n* were not performed, because it would remain unestablished (*asiddha*), the word would still possess the designation *ṣaṭ* by virtue of ending in *n*, and thus the penultimate accent (*upottama-svara*) would apply. Consequently, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha-grahaṇa*) would be redundant; therefore, he says: "The mention of the long vowel in the case of *aṣṭan*. Thus, the mention of the long vowel serves to indicate that the designation *ṣaṭ* applies even when the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) has been made.

And likewise, in the case of *aṣṭāsu*, since it possesses the designation *ṣat* (six), the *upottama-svara* (penultimate accent) would have applied; however, because the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* is formulated, this rule takes precedence as an exception (*apavāda*) according to the principle of "that which applies where another does not" (*yena nāprāpti*). Thus, the *upottama-svara* does not apply in *aṣṭāsu*. By the same logic, in *aṣṭasu* as well, the *vibhakti-svara* (case-ending accent) would have applied due to the force of the exception; therefore, the inclusion of the term *dīrgha* (long vowel) serves to prevent that, thereby fulfilling its purpose within its own scope.

He states the purpose of this indication elsewhere: "for the sake of [the application of] *nuṭ* to that which ends in the vowel *ā*. In the case of *aṣṭan + ām*, when the substitution of *ā* for the *n* is effected by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.84), the form *aṣṭānām* is established because, by virtue of the aforementioned indication, that which ends in *ā* is also designated as *ṣaṭ*; thus, by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55), *nuṭ* is added to *ām*. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, one might raise the objection that since the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan-* prescribed by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* is obligatory, the form in the locative plural would necessarily be *aṣṭāsu* (containing the long vowel) and not *aṣṭasu* (containing the short vowel). Consequently, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) as a qualifier for that [form] would be redundant. Anticipating this, it is explained that the mention of the long vowel is intended to indicate that the substitution of *ā* prescribed for *aṣṭan-* is optional.

And thus, since the form *aṣṭasu* also exists in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* (*ātvābhāvapakṣe*) does not apply, he states that the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) in that rule is purposeful, so that the accent prescribed by the rule "aṣṭanaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.172) does not apply there: "And because of the optionality of the substitution of *ā*" (*ātvavikalpasya ca*). The intention is that a single instance of the mention of the long vowel serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for both statements, since it is possible for a single [mention] to indicate multiple meanings through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used to indicate this very point.

In reality, however, in the case of *aṣṭanām*, because the designation *ṣaṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) in relation to the substitution of *ā*, when the designation *ṣaṭ* is to be applied, the substitution of *ā* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being external (*bahiraṅga*).

Since the designation *ṣaṭ* is established by the very fact that [the word] ends in *aṣṭan*, the desired form *aṣṭānām* is accomplished through the addition of the *nuṭ* augment conditioned by that designation, followed by the lengthening of the penultimate vowel according to *nopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.7) and the elision of *n*. Therefore, because there is no fruit for such an indication (*jñāpana*), it need not be taught that "the designation *ṣaṭ* applies once the substitution of *āt* has been made. The inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is solely for the purpose of indicating the rule that the substitution of *āt* is optional (*vibhāṣā*). The practical utility [of this indication] is the establishment of the two forms, *aṣṭābhiḥ* and *aṣṭābhiḥ*, and so forth.

Furthermore, in the rule *ātva-vikalpasya ca*, it appears that the particle *ca* has the sense of *vā* (or). The rule *tit-svaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185) indicates—by means of the *tapara* notation—that when the *ū* of *diva* (from *diva aut*) is replaced by *ūt* (from *ūt-ṭa*), the *ū* is intended to include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Thus, the *tapara* notation serves to exclude the long vowel in the case of *ūṭ*. As for the requirement that the term *ti* must be understood as referring to an affix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), this has been rejected on the grounds that the letter *d* in the substitutes (*ādeśa*) suffices [to indicate the affix].

In the *tapara* rule (*aṇ udit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*), the letter *d* is also included as having the nature of *ṛ*. Regarding the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhatitsvaritam*, there is the Vārttika: "In the [rule] *titi*, there must be a mention of 'affix' (*pratyaya*). Its meaning is this: it must be stated that only an affix ending in *ti* is *svarita*. Otherwise, in the word *kirati*, the vowel *i* prescribed by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) would also become *svarita* because it possesses the property of being *ti*.

Desiring to refute this *vārttika*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated that since the substitution of *it* for *ṛt* would not be marked with *ti*, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent would not apply. Furthermore, if the division were made as *ṛtaḥ it*, then the substitute *ikāra* would be a long vowel, being the most similar (*antaratama*) to its original (*sthānin*), which is also long.

Anticipating the objection that by including the *tapara* marker (the *ṛ*), the substitution would apply only to those sounds of the same duration as *ḍha*, *ḍha*, *ṭha*, and *ṭha*—namely, the short *ik* vowels—the author provides the resolution: by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "an element being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)," the *ik* vowel here refers only to the short [vowels]. Therefore, the substitute *id* possesses the *dakāra* (the letter *d*) as its *anubandha*. Having thus established this, he addresses the following point: if it is maintained that "an element being taught does not include its homogeneous counterparts," then in the derivation of *amūbhyām*—at the stage *ad-ā bhyām*—the long *ākāra* following the *dakāra* would be subject to the rule *adaso 'ser dād u do maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80).

The vowel *u* prescribed by the rule *maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80) would not include its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterpart *ū*, because it is itself being prescribed [as a substitute]. Consequently, in the form *amūbhyām*, there would only be the short *u* (as in *ḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍanasva*). Having raised this objection again, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In that case, the activity of the Teacher indicates that a vowel being prescribed as *u* does include its homogeneous counterparts; for he makes the *u* in the rule *diva ut* (6.1.131) a *tapara* [to indicate its short duration]."

Having taken this into consideration, he says: "Thus it makes known the *tapara* status," and so forth. He states that [the rule] finds its utility within its own scope: "And thus, in the case of *ūṭh*. In the derivation of *dyubhyām*, when *div* + *bhyām* is established, because the letter *v* is followed by a *jhal* sound, the rule "The substitution of *ūṭh* occurs for *ch* and *v* before a nasal or a *śuṭ* sound" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.19) applies, resulting in *diūbhyām*. Then, for the *ū* in *diūbhyām*, the rule "For *div*, *ut*" (*Pāṇini* 6.1.131) applies, and after the substitution of *u*, the *yaṇ* sandhi results in the form *dyubhyām*.

The point here is that since the substitute *u* (in *amūbhyām*) would, by virtue of being a homogeneous sound (*savarṇagrāhaka*), include the original *ū*, the long vowel *ū* would result; therefore, the use of the *tapara* marker *ut* is meaningful as it serves to exclude that [homogeneous inclusion]. However, its purpose elsewhere is seen in forms such as *amūbhyām*. Now, one might object: "Since the *u* prescribed by the rule *diva ut* is a *tit* (having *t* as its marker), the term *tit* must necessarily be understood as referring to an affix (*pratyaya*) in order to prevent the circumflex accent (*svarita*) from applying via the rule *titsvaritam*"; to this, he replies: "The mention of the affix in the rule regarding *tit*..."

And likewise, even in the rule *diva ud* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), the substitute is indeed *ud*. Thus, since the circumflex (*svarita*) accent would not apply simply by virtue of the absence of the *tittva* property [of the suffix], the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) is unnecessary; this is the intended sense. Now, one might object: if the substitute is *ud*, then by the non-application of the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), the long vowel *ū* could also become the substitute. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the rule concerning *tapara*. Consequently, in the expression *dtaparaḥ*, because the letter *d* is a *repha* (r), the rule is actually *ttaparaḥ*.

The meaning of the rule is that a vowel followed by *d* or *t* is the designation (*saṃjñā*) for its own duration. Consequently, the implication is that the substitution of *ud* would apply only to that [vowel] of its own duration, and not to the long [vowel]. In the rule *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-vas-tav-as-pratyaya-āt* (Pāṇini 6.1.192), the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), a composite unit (*saṅghāta*) is the locus of the operation. Furthermore, the mention of the word *pūrva* (preceding) is an indicator that in rules concerning accent, locative cases denote the end of a preceding element (*tadanta-saptamī*).

Objection: But surely, by the rule *bhīhrībhṛhumadajanadhanadaridrājāgarāṃ pratyayātpūrvaṃ piti* (Pāṇini 6.1.192), for the roots beginning with *bhī* that are abhyasta, the syllable preceding the affix is acute when followed by a *pit* sārvadhātuka affix.

The word *syāt* is prescribed [as an example]. *juhoti* is the illustration. Here, the vowel *o* preceding the affix (*pratyaya*) is acute (*udātta*). In the absence of this sūtra, the acute accent would instead apply to the beginning of the word by the rule "anudātte ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.190). In that case, what is the purpose of including the term *pratyaya*? It is not so that, in the absence of it, the vowel *ā* in *bibhayāni*—where *ni* follows a *pit* affix—would become acute; for it is desired that the acute accent belong only to the vowel preceding *ā*. For that reason, the term *pratyaya* is included.

And since that [suffix] exists, according to the logic of the traditional rule (*āgama-nyāya*), because the suffix is accompanied by the augment *āṭ*, it is stated that the vowel preceding the suffix is acute (*udātta*). To ensure that the acute accent falls specifically on the vowel *ā* following the letter *bh* (i.e., in the syllable *āni*), the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) must be mentioned in the rule. This is what should be said.

One might raise the objection that even in the absence of the mention of "an affix" (*pratyaya*), when it is stated that "that which precedes *pit* is acute," the augment *āṭ*—which is a part of the *nit* [root]—will also be included by the mention of *pit*; thus, when *āni* follows, the preceding element alone would become acute. Consequently, since the acute accent for *āṭ* would not be obtained, the mention of "affix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) would be rendered useless. Anticipating this, he states its purpose as being indicative (*jñāpaka*): "The mention of 'affix' here... [is for the sake of indicating that rule].

And thus, being otherwise redundant according to the aforementioned reasoning, the inclusion of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) indicates that in the rules governing accent (*svaravidhi*), a "group" (*saṃghāta*) is intended as the object of reference. Consequently, the intention is that the inclusion of *pratyaya* serves to ensure that the acute accent (*udāttatva*) does not apply to the preceding group starting from *āni*, but rather that the acute accent falls on the vowel immediately preceding the suffix. This is the underlying sense.

The result of this indication (*jñāpanaphala*) is stated in the Bhāṣya as follows: "What was said—that due to the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) prevails over the high-pitched final accent (*cita*) for roots such as *ās*—is thereby justified. This is the intended meaning: in forms such as *āsīnaḥ* and *śayānaḥ*, the suffix *śānac* is *cit* (marked with *C*); consequently, by the rule "the end of a *cit* [suffix] is high-pitched" (*citaḥ anta udāttaḥ*), a high-pitched accent would first apply to the final syllable. However, by the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a root that ends in *tās*, or is marked with *N* or *K*, or is taught with an indicatory *Ṅ*, are low-pitched" (*tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttaṃ*), a low-pitched accent is also applicable to *śānac*. [Thus, there is a conflict between the two rules.]

When both [rules] apply simultaneously, the author of the Vārttika stated in the rule *tāsyanudāttet* that "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam*, Pāṇini 1.4.2), and thus the anudātta alone occurs. This is only logical if, in the prescription of accent, the entire complex [of the suffix] were the subject of the operation;

otherwise, by the paribhāṣā *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), there would be no conflict—since the initial *ā* of the suffix *śānac* would receive the anudātta and its final syllable would receive the udātta by the rule *citaḥ*—and consequently, the application of the rule on conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*) would not be justified.

However, if the *saṃghāta* (the entire cluster) were intended to have its own accent, then the statement that the *saṃghāta* is unaccented (*anudātta*) would contradict the fact that its final element is accented (*udātta*); thus, due to this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), according to the method of the Vārttika, the statement regarding its unaccented nature is correctly established by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratva*).

Since the word *piti* is heard in the locative case in the very sūtra *bhīhrī* (Pāṇini 6.1.192), one might object: "By the paribhāṣā *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), the term 'of the preceding' (*pūrvasya*) will be understood; therefore, what is the purpose of including the word *pūrva* in [the sūtra] *pratyayātpūrvaṃ piti* (Pāṇini 6.1.192)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The inclusion of the word *pūrva*... Thus, the inclusion of *pūrva* is for the purpose of indicating that in the formulation of rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), locative cases denote the end of that which precedes (*tadantasaptamī*).

Furthermore, in the view that [the suffix] follows the final vowel (*tadanta-pakṣa*), the meaning of the sūtra would be: "That which has *pit* prescribed after [a root] beginning with *bhī* and others becomes udātta at its end. In this case, all vowels would alternately become udātta. Since it is desired that only the single vowel preceding the suffix be udātta, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for that purpose; thus, it serves its own function within the rule itself. However, its purpose as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies to rules such as "upottamaṃ riti" (Pāṇini 6.1.216).

For in that context, when the suffix *rit* follows, it is not intended that the penultimate syllable [of the base] be acute; rather, it is intended that the penultimate syllable of the word ending in the suffix *rit* be acute. The rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204), which prescribes that the first syllable of a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is acute, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is a prohibition of the application of the accentual rules based on suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when the accent is determined by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*).

Objection: Is not the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 2.1.55), which prescribes that the first syllable of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is acute when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*), redundant? Nor should it be argued that in the absence of this rule, how could the word *cañcā*—derived from *cañcā iva cañcā* where the suffix *kan* prescribed by *saṃjñāyām* (5.3.96) is elided by *lum manuṣye* (5.3.98)—be established as having an acute accent on its first syllable.

[The author] raises an objection: since the elision of the *kan* suffix is subject to the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (as if the suffix were still present), the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is established by the very sūtra *ñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.198); and because this initial acute accent does not fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) does not apply. Anticipating this, he says: "of the standard of comparison" (*upamānasya*). Thus, in cases such as *cañcā*, [the accent is established] precisely by means of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*.

Since the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* would otherwise be redundant once the accent has been established, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the status of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply to an accent caused by an *anubandha*. Consequently, because the accent prescribed by the rule *ñ-nity-ādir nityam* is caused by the designation *it*, when that accent is to be applied, the status of being a suffix does not apply to the suffix *kan* (which is elided by *lup*). Thus, the word *cañcā* lacks the quality of having a *ñ* as its final element; consequently, the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) would not apply. It is for the purpose of securing that accent that the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* is meaningful—this is the underlying intention.

The purpose of this *jñāpaka* (indicatory rule), however, is as follows: in the case of forms such as *gargāḥ*, where the meaning is "the descendants in the lineage of Garga," the suffix *yañ* prescribed by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105) undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64). Based on the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating the suffix as present despite its elision), the rule *ñnityādir nityam* would result in the initial vowel being acutely accented (*udātta*). However, because of the *jñāpana* that "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* with respect to an accent conditioned by an *anubandha* (indicatory letter)," that acute accent does not occur.

In rules such as *jhrjñā.ṭa ṭhanottarapade'nudāttādāvapṛthivī* (Pāṇini 6.2.142), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word *apṛthivī* and others serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "in a rule prescribing an accent, a consonant is as if non-existent. In the rule *yato'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.213), the prohibition *anāvaḥ* serves as an indicator that "when an accent for a vowel is to be applied, a consonant is as if non-existent. In the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.59), the inclusion of the term *anantara* ("immediately preceding") indicates that when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned [in a rule], it includes a word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*.

*Jhrvi.ṭa*: These three *paribhāṣās* are not explained here because they are recited in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*. *Jhrjñā.ṭa*: [The rule] *dvitribhyāṃ pāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.197). The mention of *mūrdhasu* in this rule indicates that the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is optional. *Jhrvi.ṭa*: By the rule *advitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197), an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta-svara*) is prescribed for the words *pād*, *dan*, and *mūrdhan* when they follow *dvi* or *tri* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

In this regard, the examples for the word *mūrdhan* are *dvimūrdhaḥ* and *trimūrdhaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ṣ* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule "dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.115). Since that compound-final suffix is obligatory, it is appropriate to refer to the word using its form with the compound-final suffix applied, namely *mūrdha*, according to the rule "pāddanmūrdheṣu" (Pāṇini 6.2.197).

Having raised the objection that since the rule begins with *pādi*, which includes the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), it would be appropriate to refer to the word *mūrdhan* in the same way, [the author] considers that because the word *mūrdhan* is cited in the sūtra as *mūrghasu* without the compound-ending suffix—according to the rule *pāddanmūrghasu*—it thereby indicates that the compound-ending suffix is optional. Thus, the sūtra cites *mūrghasu* by relying on the alternative case in which the compound-ending suffix is absent.

And for this reason, with the intention that the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is established by this rule even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the *samāsānta* suffix has not been applied—as in *dvimūrdhā* and *trimūrdhā*—the author says: "The mention [of the word] *mūrdhasu*. However, the purpose of this indication is that in cases such as *supathī nagarī*, the suffix *kap* prescribed by the rule "inaḥ striyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.152) does not occur because it is optional. Furthermore, this statement is already covered by the maxim (*paribhāṣā*): "The rules concerning *samāsānta* suffixes are not mandatory."

In the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, it is stated that the inclusion of the word *rājan* in the *aśvādi* group (Pāṇini 6.2.193)—which prescribes an udātta accent on the final syllable for a *tatpuruṣa* compound—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this rule. Regarding Pāṇini 6.3.50, *hṛdayasya hṛt-lekha-yat-aṇ-lāseṣu*: because of the mention of *lekha*, it is indicated that within the governing context of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, it refers to the specific form (*rūpa*) [of the suffix]. This is because in the rule *khityanavyayasya* (6.3.66), the term *anavyayasya* ("not being an indeclinable") is used; had it been intended to refer to the suffix *khit* in general, the mention of *anavyayasya* would have been unnecessary. Thus, the mention of *anavyayasya* indicates that the reference is to the specific form ending in *khit*.

Objection: In the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekha-*, since the suffixes *yat* and *aṇ* are mentioned, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed and ends with it"—applies. Consequently, the substitution of *hṛd-* for *hṛdaya-* would occur only when followed by a word ending in *yat* or *aṇ*, but not after the suffixes *yat* and *aṇ* alone. Thus, forms such as *hṛdyam* and *hārdam* would not be established. Anticipating this objection, he says: "because of the mention of *lekha*."

If the inclusion here were of that which ends in *aṇ*, then since the word *lekha* itself ends in *aṇ*, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* would already be established when that [suffix] follows; thus, the specific mention of *lekha* would be redundant. Because the Teacher makes the mention of *lekha*, he indicates that by the term *aṇ*, only the suffix itself is understood, not that which ends in *aṇ*. And so, because it is impossible for the word *lekha*—which ends in *aṇ*—to be included by the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *lekha* was made.

Alternatively, because an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon its context, it is indicated that within the governing rule for the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix (*tadantagrahaṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that in the case of *kumārī gauritarā*, the feminine suffix *ṅī*—which is prescribed before a suffix designated as *gha* by the rule "gharūpakalpapū" (Pāṇini 6.3.43)—does not occur when the word ends in a *gha*-designated suffix, such as *ḍha*, *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ḍha*, *na*, or *sva*. If this is what is being indicated, then [the rule] "khityanavyayasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.66) [is also explained].

The short vowel (*hrasva*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.3.66] would apply only when *khit* follows immediately, and not when a word ending in *khit* follows. Consequently, in examples such as *śunindhaya*, where the word *dhaya* ending in *khit* follows, one might suspect that the shortening would not occur; anticipating this objection, he says: "In the rule *khityanavyayasya*... If the inclusion of the phrase "ending in" (*tadanta*) were not present here as well, then since an indeclinable (*avyaya*) followed immediately by *khit* would be impossible, the shortening would not apply to an indeclinable at all. Thus, the prohibition "not an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*) would be meaningless.

And that prohibition [of the short vowel] in this sūtra indicates that there is the inclusion of the *tadanta* (ending in that) [principle]. Thus, in examples such as *doṣāmanyamahaḥ*, the prohibition by the word *anavyayasya* ("not being an indeclinable") is meaningful for the purpose of preventing the shortening [of the final vowel]. The intended meaning is that the utility [of this rule] lies in the establishment of the short vowel in cases such as *śunindhaya*, where a suffix beginning with *khid* follows.

Regarding *jhrjña.ṭa* and *ṭhasamaḥ sami* (Pāṇini 6.3.93): because the rule *nahivṛti* (Pāṇini 6.3.116) includes the mention of *kvip* within the list beginning with *nañ*, the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*) applies to what begins with that [root]. Now, an objection: by the rule *samaḥ sami* (Pāṇini 6.3.93), when the suffix *kvip* (which ends in no other suffix) follows the root *añc*, the substitution of *sam* for *sam-* is prescribed. An example is *samyaṅ*.

Likewise, by the rule *nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kvau* (Pāṇini 6.3.116), lengthening of the preceding vowel is prescribed when the roots *nah* and others ending in *kvip* follow. Examples include *upānat* and so forth. In that case, the mention of *kvip* in the rule need not be made. Nor should it be argued that in its absence, the two rules would apply even to cases such as *samañcanam* and *upanahanam*.

Because of the governing rule concerning the final member of a compound (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), both of the aforementioned two sūtras apply when the final member (*uttarapada*) takes the form of *añcu* or *nahyādi*. In the case of *samañcanam*, although *añcana* is the final member, there is no fault because *añc* itself is not the final member. Furthermore, the status of being a final member applies to the root *añc* alone only when the suffix *kvip* is present; otherwise, since that verbal root would not even possess the status of a word (*pada*), its being a final member would be impossible.

And so, having raised the objection that the mention of *kvip* is redundant—since the status of being a *kvib*-ending [root] can be obtained by the very force of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in a subsequent word" (*uttarapade*)—he says: "In the case of *añcati*, *nahyati*, etc. Thus, the mention of *kvip* is made for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). It indicates that wherever a root is mentioned in the locative case as a qualifier, the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies even in the absence of an explicit mention of the suffix *al*.

In this way, if the rule *añceḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.95) and the rule *nahivṛtivṛṣi...* (Pāṇini 6.3.116) were qualified by the phrase *uttarapade*, then—by the principle of "specification of the initial" (*tadādividhi*)—the meaning of the sūtra would be: "When a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) begins with a verbal root starting with *añc*, the substitution of *sam* for *sam-* and the lengthening of the vowel of the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) occur. If that were the case, the rules would apply even in examples such as *samañcanam* ("bending together") and *upanahanam* ("binding on"), because the subsequent words *añcanam* and *nahanam* contain the constituent parts *añc* and *nah*. Therefore, the mention of the *kvip*-affix (*kvib-grahaṇa*) was made.

The point is that the two aforementioned rules apply only when followed by *añc* and others ending in *kvip*; thus, there is no fault. As for the purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), it is as follows: in the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*), the term *kṛ*—which qualifies that heading—is understood to mean a subsequent word whose initial constituent is the root *kṛ*. Consequently, the substitution of *s* is established even in forms such as *ayaskāra*, where the suffix *kvip* has been elided. Otherwise, the substitution of *s* would occur only when the root *kṛ* itself ends in *kvip*, as in *ayaskṛt* and similar forms.

By the rules *jhr-jñā-ṭa-ṭha-jana-sana-khanām* (Pāṇini 6.4.42) and *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), there is then elision (*lopa*) for the roots *dhu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *hā* (of *jahāti*), and *sā* before an affix beginning with a vowel that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, as well as before the augment *iṭ*. This [elision] is for the purpose of preventing the subsequent application of *itva* (the substitution of *ī*). Thereafter, *īt*: the words *dhū* and so forth are understood [from the previous rule], and *ī* is substituted for the finals of *dhū* and the others.

By the rules *erliṅi* (Pāṇini 6.4.67), *vānyasya* (6.4.68), *nalyapi* (6.4.69), and *mayateridanyatarasyām* (6.4.80), the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel before the suffix *yat*. Since this result is already established by these rules, the fact that he introduces a heavy (lengthy) rule indicates that even when the operations of the *abhīya* group are not yet established (*asiddha*), there is still a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Furthermore, the mention of *hal* [in the rule] is for the sake of preventing the substitution of *ī* in cases such as *goda*. If this [indication] is accepted, how does the rule find its purpose? Therefore, this Bhāṣya represents the statement of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*).

Regarding the rule *jhrvidṛṭa ṭhajanasanakhanāṃ sanjhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.42), there is a Vārttika which states: *“In the case of the root *san*, the substitution of *ā* takes place by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) over the elision of the nasal.”* This is its meaning: when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *san*, resulting in the form *san-ta*, this rule prescribes the substitution of *ā*. However, since the elision of the nasal would also apply here by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), the principle *“in the case of conflict, that which follows [takes effect]”* (Pāṇini 1.4.2) dictates that the substitution of *ā* alone occurs, due to its subsequent position in the sequence of rules.

"And the form is *sāta*. Now, an objection is raised: "In this case, a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*) is not applicable, because 'where a preceding rule is not established, there is no conflict of rules, due to the absence of the subsequent one.'"

Having raised the objection that, according to this logic, the rule of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules) would not apply even in this case of an *ābhīya* (intervening) operation that is already established, [the author] will state that there is no fault because it is indicated here that the *vipratiṣedha* does indeed occur. In that context, in order to state that the mention of *hal* in the sūtra "ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ hali" (Pāṇini 6.4.66) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he demonstrates the necessity of that indicator by showing its potential uselessness (*vaiyarthyam*) through the passage beginning with "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

The intended meaning here is as follows: In the rule *ghumāsthā*, if the mention of *hal* (consonant) were absent, then even in cases such as *godah* and *kambaladah*, the substitution of *ī* would occur at the stage *godā-a*. However, since the mention of *hal* is present, there is no fault, because the suffix begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) and thus lacks the property of beginning with a consonant (*hal-āditva*). This must be stated.

In the absence of a conflict here, by the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), because the two operations are mutually non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to one another, even when the substitution of *ī* has been applied, that substitution remains non-existent; consequently, by the elision of the *ā* according to *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), the desired form *goda* would be established, rendering the mention of *hal* (consonant) in the rule superfluous. Yet, the inclusion of *hal* indicates that the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) operates even in cases where [an operation] is non-existent (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, since [the rule] is subsequent, *ītva* alone would apply; therefore, the mention of *hal* is for the purpose of preventing that. This is one way [of explaining] its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The second method, however, is as follows: having stated *ītva* without distinction, it can be established that the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) applies as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [rule] when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). For instance, after the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (P. 6.4.64), there is the rule "ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām" (P. 6.4.66), which means that the elision occurs when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kṅit*). This elision is prescribed to supersede *ītva* when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter.

Then [the author says]: "The substitution of *ī* for *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, and so on, occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel. Thus, when the rule is formulated in this way, the established distinction is that the substitution of *ī* for *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, etc., applies before an affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*), whereas there is elision (*lopa*) before an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj*) that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*. Since this distinction is thereby established, the mention of *hal* (consonant) in the original rule would otherwise be redundant; its redundancy serves to indicate that there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here. Consequently, in the case of *godah* ("cow-giver"), because the subsequent rule [for *ī*] would prevail, the elision of *ā* (*ālopa*) would be superseded by the substitution of *ī*; to prevent this, the mention of *hal* becomes meaningful. The purpose, however, is that because it is subsequent to the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*), the substitution of *ā* is established in forms such as *sātaḥ*; such is the meaning of this section.

However, even if the mention of *hal* were not made, since the desired result could be achieved through *lopa* alone—by dividing the rule (*yoga-vibhāga*) for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *ī* in forms such as *godaḥ* according to the method of presenting the preceding sūtra—and since the mention of *hal* would thus have no application to its own portion (*svāṃśe*), this statement from the Bhāṣya is the assertion of a partial view (*ekadeśyukti*) and not the final conclusion (*siddhāntyukti*). Thus he says: "Once [the point] is made known, how [is it so]? This is also clear in the Uddyota. [Regarding the sūtra] *huśnuvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.87): The mention of *hu* and *śnu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *yaṅ-luk* occurs even in the secular language (*bhāṣā*).

By the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "If [the rule] is applied, then forms such as *bebhidīti* and *cecchidīti* are established," it is understood that forms ending in *yaṅ-luk* are indeed ungrammatical (*asādhutā*) in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). Now, one might object: since the word "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) from the preceding rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73) is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule *yaṅo'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the *yaṅ-luk* suffix occurs only in the Vedic language; therefore, the use of forms ending in *yaṅ-luk* would not be correct in the spoken language. Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the correctness of *yaṅ-luk* even in the spoken language by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), stating: "In this context, the mention of *hu* and *śnu* [is the indicator]."

By the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*, it is established that for the root *hu* (to sacrifice), for a stem ending in the suffix *śnu*, and for a multi-syllabic (*anekāc*) stem, a *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the vowel *u* when it is not preceded by a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogapūrva*), provided that a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a vowel follows. Examples include *juhoti*, *dodhavīti*, and *śṛṇoti*. In this context, even without the explicit mention of *hu* and *śnu*, the term *huśnuvoḥ* is understood; for there exists no other multi-syllabic stem ending in *u* before a sārvadhātuka suffix that is distinct from those two.

And thus, the mention of *hu* and *śnu* [in Pāṇini 6.4.87] would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *hu* and *śnu* is for the purpose of excluding forms such as *yoyu* found in Vedic passages like "yuvaṃ yoyuvatīnāṃ vṛṣabham," which are derived from the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive without suffix) and consist of more than one syllable (*anekāc*) preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), ending in the vowel *u*.

By the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), because the *śatṛ* suffix is treated as *ārdhadhātuka*, it lacks the status of *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, that rule [of Pāṇini 6.4.52] does not apply there. Thus, the inclusion of *hu* and *śnu* in that rule would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, being purposeless, the inclusion of *hu* and *śnu* indicates that forms ending in *yaṅluk* are also correct in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).

Furthermore, in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), in forms such as *yoyuvati* ending in the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*), the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*) does not apply; therefore, the inclusion of the term *huśnu* [in Pāṇini 6.4.87] serves its own purpose (*svāṃśe cāritārthya*) by preventing the substitution of *yaṇ* when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix *śatṛ* follows. However, the purpose of this indication (*jñāpana-prayojana*) is that forms such as *bebhidīti* and *cecchidīti*, which end in the elision of *yaṅ*, are grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*) in the spoken language. This is because the *Bhāṣya* provides only these two examples of *yaṅ-luk* forms—namely *bebhidīti* and *cecchidīti*—and thus implies others.

He states that verbal roots (*dhātu*) ending in *yaṅ* with elision (*yaṅluk*) are not valid in the common language (*bhāṣā*), by saying: "Therefore, even in the common language... [referring to the rule] *ata ekah* (Pāṇini 6.4.120). The mention of the roots *phal* and *bhaj* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is established as having already taken effect. The prohibition regarding the roots *śas* and *sidh* is an indicator that the substitution of *e* occurs when there is no difference in form. Because the inclusion of the letter *t* in the rule for the substitution of *at* for *śna* and *as* indicates the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the principle *asiddhavad atra* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), the form *debhatuḥ* is established.

Regarding *jhrvi.ṭa* [the form] *nanu babhaṇatuḥ*: when *bhaṇ-bhaṇ atur* is established, after the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*jaśtva*) for the *abhyāsa* (reduplicated) *bh* is applied by the rule *abhyāse carcā* (Pāṇini 8.4.54). Since the operations of *etva* (substitution of *e* for *a*) and the elision of the *abhyāsa* (*abhyāsalopa*) are to be performed, the former is considered *asiddha* (non-existent/non-effective) with respect to the latter by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 6.4.22). Consequently, the *aṅga* (stem) is not considered to begin with a substitute (*anādeśādi*). Thus, by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye’nādeśāderliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120), in the case of the dual of the *liṭ* (perfect) for the roots *phal* and *bhaj*, [the form becomes] *phelatuḥ*.

When *phal* and *bhaj* have become *phalatuh* and *babhajatuḥ*, and after the application of *halādiśeṣa* and *jaś-tva*, they stand as *phalatuḥ* and *babhajatuḥ*. Since the root begins with a substitute consonant (*ādeśāditva*), the rule *ata ekahalmadhye'nādeśāderliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120) does not apply. Therefore, it must be stated that the explicit mention of the roots *phal* and *bhaj* is for the purpose of establishing the substitution of *etva* (the change of *a* to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*).

If the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) for the abhyāsa (reduplication) were *asiddha*, then, because of that *asiddha* status, the rule "ata ekahalmadhye" would suffice for the establishment of both the *etva* (change to *e*) and the elision of the abhyāsa simply by virtue of the reduplication not being an initial element (*anādeśāditva*). Why, then, is there an explicit mention of those two in the rule "tṛphala"? That very mention serves to indicate that when *etva* and the elision of the abhyāsa are to be applied, the substitution of the abhyāsa is *siddha*.

Furthermore, since the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) is established, the mention of *phali*, *bhak*, and *ji* serves its purpose within its own scope by ensuring the application of *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *i*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*), which would otherwise not apply because they follow an *ādeśa*. However, the actual purpose [of this rule] is that in forms such as *babhaṇatuḥ*, because the *jaś*-substitution of the reduplicated syllable is established, *etva* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur due to the presence of an *ādeśa* at the beginning.

Now, in cases such as *pecatuḥ* and *debhatuḥ*, because the substitutes [for the reduplicated syllable] would be sounds of the same class as the original (*prakṛti*)—namely, a sound of the same class for a *prakṛti*-cari and a *prakṛti*-jaś for a *prakṛti*-jaś—the elision of *e* and the reduplication (*etvābhyāsalopa*) would not occur due to the initial nature of the substitute. To address this, he says: "In the case of *śas* and *didya*... According to the rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* (Pāṇini 6.4.126), the elision of *e* and the reduplication is prohibited for *śas* and *didya*.

In this case as well, because *prakṛticara-* becomes *prakṛticira-* by means of substitution (*ādeśa*), there is an absence of being non-initial (*anādeśāditva*); therefore, since the rules for *etva* (the change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*)—namely, Pāṇini 6.4.120 (*ata ekahalmadhye*)—do not apply, what is the purpose of the prohibition? The fact that the prohibition is indeed stated serves to indicate that when a substitute (*ādeśa*) is identical in form to the original element (*sthānin*), the prohibition "it is non-initial" does not apply to the *etva* and *abhyāsalopa* of that base (*aṅga*) which has such a substitute at its beginning.

And thus, since the prohibition *anādeśe* (in the absence of a substitute) does not apply, the rules for *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) would also apply to the roots *śas* and *dad*. Therefore, the intention is that the mention of *śas* and *dad* in the rule *na śasadadi* is for the purpose of prohibiting those [operations]. The practical utility (*prayojana*), however, is that in forms such as *pecatuḥ*, since the prohibition *anādeśādeḥ* does not apply, the *etva* and *abhyāsalopa* are successfully established.

But even so, one might raise the following objection: when the root *dambh* takes the suffix *liṭ*, resulting in the form *dambh-dambh-atuḥ*, after the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* and the elision of *n* by *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the elision of *n* would be considered *asiddha* by *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22). Consequently, because the vowel *a* would be situated between two conjunct consonants (*saṃyukta-hal*), the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) would not be established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: *śnasor allopaḥ*.

In the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111), the addition of the *tapara* marker (*at*) in the word *at* is intended to prevent the elision of the augment *āṭ* in forms such as *āsan*. One might argue that since the elision of *at* must be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to preceding operations by the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*, the *āṭ* would remain *asiddha* even for the purpose of this elision; thus, the *ākāra* (the letter *ā*) would not be subject to elision anyway. Consequently, the *tapara* marker added to exclude the *ākāra* would be redundant, and its very presence serves to indicate that the status of being *asiddha* is not absolute (i.e., it is *anitya*).

The purpose of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is that, because the substitute (*āṭ*) is not *asiddha*, its elision (*lopa*) should not occur; thus, it serves its own specific function. However, its utility elsewhere is that in forms such as *debhatur*, since the elision of *n* is not *asiddha*, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) are established—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, due to the inclusion of the root *tṝ* in the rule *tṝphalabhaj...* (Pāṇini 6.4.122), which serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur in forms such as *lulavitha*. This is based on the rule *athali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.121).

One might raise the objection that, by the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhathali ca seṭi*, the substitution of *et* (the change of *i* to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) prescribed therein would also apply to *lulavitha*; for once the *ava*-substitution has been made, the vowel *a* would reside between non-conjoined consonants (*asaṃyukta-hal-madhya-stha*), and thus the condition for *etva* would be met. Anticipating this doubt, he says "tṝphala... and so forth; [this applies] even in the case of *teritha*.

When the *guṇa* substitution is applied to the vowel *ṛ*, the substitution of *e* for the vowel *a* is already established by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* (Pāṇini 6.4.120); therefore, the inclusion of the term *tṝ* [in the rule *tṝ-phalabhaja-tapo'taḥ*] would be redundant. However, its inclusion serves to indicate that once the *guṇa* has been applied, the substitution of *e* does not take place for the resulting *a*. Consequently, since the substitution of *e* does not apply in such cases, the inclusion of *tṝ* becomes meaningful. Thus, the intended meaning is that in forms such as *lulavitha*, the substitution of *e* does not occur for the *a* produced by *guṇa*.

In the rule *jhrjñā.ṭa bilvakādibhyaś ca jhrśchasyaṭa* (Pāṇini 6.4.153), the inclusion of *jhrchaṭa* indicates that for elements taught as being in obligatory association (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*), the removal of one necessitates the removal of both. In the rule *jyādādīyasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.160), although the desired form would be established by the continued application of the elision (*lopa*) [from the previous rule], the specific prescription of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) indicates the maxim: "When an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅga*), there is no further application of another operation" (*aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ*). Furthermore, although the form could have been established by the prescription of *akāra*, the prescription of *ākāra* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the principle: "A vowel being taught in its full form (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."

Since the form *kārmastā* would already be established by the rules *kārmastācchīlye* (Pāṇini 6.4.172) and *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), this specific formation (*nipātana*) indicates that the suffixes prescribed for expressing a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*) are also applied to words ending in *aṇ*. These technical rules (*paribhāṣās*) are not explained here because they are well known. Regarding *dāṇḍināyana* (Pāṇini 6.4.174): since the substitution of *t* for the *th* of *han* would already be established by the rule *hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.32) in the case of *bhrauṇahatya*, this specific formation (*nipātana*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *t* is prohibited when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) follows.

Objection: In the sūtra *dāṇḍināyana* and others, words such as *dāṇḍināyana* are taught as irregular formations (*nipātita*). Among them, the word *bhrūṇahatya* is also specified. What, then, is being irregularly formed there? Such a challenge arises. It cannot be argued that the word *bhrūṇahā* (one who kills an embryo) is derived from *bhrūṇahan*, and that in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) of being a killer of an embryo, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class; thus, after the initial vowel-vṛddhi, we have *bhrauṇahanya*, and it is the substitution of *ta* for the *na* that is the irregular formation. [This is because the application of *ṣyañ* would result in the form *bhrāuṇahatya*, not *bhrūṇahatya*.]

Since the substitution of *t* for the *han* root is established even when the suffix *ṣyañ* follows—by the general rule *hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.32), which prescribes the replacement of *t* for *han* when a *ñit* or *ṇit* suffix other than *ciṇ* or *nal* follows—the purposeless repetition (*vaiyarthyam*) of the *t*-substitution in this specific case would otherwise be redundant. Therefore, he says: "only thus" (*ityeveti*). Thus, the specific mention of *t* (the *tatva-nipātana*) indicates that when a *taddhita* suffix follows, the substitution of *t* for *han* by the rule *hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ* does not take place.

Therefore, since the substitution of *t* would not otherwise apply when the suffix *ṣyañ* follows, this [substitution] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), thereby fulfilling its purpose within its own scope. However, its purpose elsewhere is that in forms such as *bhrauṇaghnaḥ* and *vārtraghnaḥ*, where the secondary suffix *aṇ* follows, the substitution of *t* for the *n* of the root *han* does not occur; this is the intended meaning. Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

*Jhrjñā.ṭa āyane* (Sūtra 7.1.2). The inclusion of the marker *cit* in the rule *ghacchau ca* (Sūtra 4.4.117) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitutes *āyan*, etc., occur when they are taught [as part of the suffix]. *Jhrvi.ṭa* Objection: By the rule *āyaneyī* (Sūtra 7.1.2), the substitutes *āyan* and so on are prescribed for the initial elements of suffixes such as *ph*. In that case, when the suffix *phan* is added to the word *naḍa*, resulting in *naḍa-phan*, the word would become devoid of accent by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

Furthermore, in the word *nāḍāyaṇa*, there would be only an udātta accent on the final syllable [by rule], whereas the udātta accent on the vowel *ā* of *āyana* is desired. Suspecting what the means of its accomplishment might be, he says: "In the case of *ghaccha*, the cause is the *cit*-marker. Since the application of the accent occurs at the very stage of the instruction of the suffix, the substitutes such as *phak*, etc., and *āyan*, etc., for the suffixes occur even before the accent is applied. And the accent operates only after the substitution has taken place.

And that [suffix], being *ādyudātta* (having its first syllable accented), results in the vowel *ā* at the beginning of the substitute *āyana* becoming accented. The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this point is the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ghac* in the rule *ghacchau ca*. For instance, when the suffix *ghac* is added to the word *agra*, and the substitution of *iy* for the letter *gh* occurs, the *cit* marker is applied to *ghac* so that the final vowel *ā* in the resulting word *agriya* may be established as accented. This is only possible if the substitution of *iy* for *gh* takes place while the suffix is still in its state of *upadeśa* (original enunciation).

For in that case, the substitution of *iy* would become meaningful only after [the accentuation] by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Furthermore, when the substitution does not occur during the stage of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*), then, since the vowel *ā* in *gha* is acute by the accent of the suffix, the substitution of *iy* for the unaccented *gh* would also be unaccented; the accent of the previously applied *ā* would remain, and thus the word *agriya* would effectively result in being oxytone. Consequently, the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ghac* would be purposeless.

The sense is that, by virtue of that capacity, it is indicated that the substitutes *āyan*, *nā*, and so forth occur precisely in the state of being taught [as the original forms]. Regarding the rule *ṅe-prathamayor* (Pāṇini 7.1.28), the fact that the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) are mentioned here serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe dvitīyāyāṃ ca*.

(Sūtra 7.1.28–29) Regarding *jhr* and *viṭ*: A doubt arises concerning the rule *ṅeprathamayoram* as to whether the term *prathamayoḥ* refers to the two first case endings (*vibhakti*) or to the two first suffixes (*pratyaya*). If the position were that it refers to the two suffixes, then the substitution of *am* would apply only to *su* and *au*. The seed of this doubt, however, is that if the expression *prathamayoḥ* is a feminine designation, then it must refer to the two case endings.

But when there is a reference in the masculine gender, then it is the two *prathama* suffixes that are understood. Since this is so, how is it to be determined here? To that he says: "In this case, of the two case-endings (*vibhakti*)". In the rule "ṅe-prathamayoḥ," it is only the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) that are understood, not the two suffixes (*pratyaya*). The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the rule "dvitīyāyāṃ ca."

The meaning of that rule is that when the second case ending follows, the letter *ā* shall replace [the final phoneme] of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Now, if by the rule "ṅeprathamayoram" the substitution of *am* were prescribed for the two suffixes *su* and *au* (i.e., the nominative endings), then, because there would be no substitution of *am* for the second case, the second case following *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would remain in its unmodified form; consequently, since the substitution of *ā* would already be established by the rule "yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe" (Pāṇini 7.2.86) itself when that [unmodified] case follows, [the present rule would be redundant].

Otherwise, the rule "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*) would be redundant. Therefore, the rule "and in the second case" indicates that in the rule "of *ṅe* and the two first cases" (*ṅeprathamayoḥ*), the term "the two first cases" includes both the first and second case endings. Consequently, since the substitution of *am* is prescribed for the second case ending by that [rule], the case ending following *yuṣmad* and *asmad* will indeed take the form of the substitute *am*.

And since the prohibition "there is no [augment] when there is no specific instruction" (*anādeśe*) would apply to that [suffix], the intention is that the rule "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*) is for the purpose of prescribing the long *ā*. In the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8), the inclusion of the roots *vṛñ* and *vṛṅ* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*, even when based on an affix, is restricted. Now, one might object: let the mention of "kṛt" be omitted from the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti*.

Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that [condition], there would also be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* for the *tiṅ* suffixes beginning with *va*, as in *bibhidiva* and *bibhidima*; for by the rule "kṛsṛbhṛvṛstudrustuśruvo liṭi" (Pāṇini 7.2.13), the prohibition of *iṭ* applies only to those suffixes following roots belonging to the *krī* group, and thus [the prohibition does not apply here].

Because the prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply in such cases as these, one might argue: "That restriction (*niyama*) operates by depending on a specific verbal root (*prakṛti*), whereas the prohibition of *iṭ* [in the rule] 'neḍ vaśi' depends on the affix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, the restriction regarding the roots beginning with *krī* (*krādiniyama*) does not touch upon this prohibition. Consequently, since the prohibition of *iṭ* would also apply in forms like *bibhidiva*, the mention of the term 'kṛt' [in the rule] is necessary to prevent that. This, however, must be rejected.

The restriction regarding the *krādi* group does not have as its scope merely the prohibition of what is characterized by the root (*prakṛti-lakṣaṇa*); rather, it is a restriction stating that if any prohibition of *iṇ*—whether based on the root or based on the suffix—applies to the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, then it applies only to roots beginning with *kṛ*. Otherwise, because the prohibition of *iṇ* would not apply in the case of *bibhidiva*, the mention of *kṛ* [in the rule *kṛtīṅ*] would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, regarding the prohibition of *iṭ* which applies to both the root and the suffix, the rule for the restriction of roots beginning with *kṛ* (*krādiniyama*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because in the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13), the term *vṛ* is used in its general sense to include both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*. The purpose of including both of these is so that the augment *iṭ* does not occur in forms such as *vavṛmahe*.

Furthermore, if the restriction regarding the *krād*-group were to subvert only the prohibition based on the root (*prakṛtyāśraya*) and not that based on the suffix (*pratyayāśraya*), then the prohibition of *iṭ* would already be established by the two rules "neḍ vaśi kṛti" (Pāṇini 7.2.8) and "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11); in that case, the mention of the root *vṛ* would be purposeless. Its inclusion, however, indicates that the prohibition based on the suffix is also suspended.

Furthermore, in the absence of the mention of *vṛ* [in the rule], for both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, by virtue of being distinct from the *krādi* group, the prohibition of *iṭ* based on the suffix—namely, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *neṅ vaśi*—would also be excluded by the restrictive rule that the prohibition of *iṭ* applies only to the *krādi* group. Consequently, in forms such as *vavṛmahe*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would not be established. Therefore, even for the sake of establishing the prohibition of *iṭ* in those cases, the inclusion of *vṛ* in the *krādi* rule is meaningful.

Therefore, since the prohibition of *iṭ* in forms such as *bibhidiva* will follow simply from the restriction regarding the *krād*-group, it is established that it is not logical for the mention of *kṛt* in the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti* to have as its result the non-application of the prohibition of *iṭ* there. Bearing all this in mind, he says: "in the rule *kṛ-sṛ-bhṛ-*. Regarding *ghuṣir aviśabdane* (Pāṇini 7.2.23): since the form [with *ṇic*] would be established by the *curādi* *ṇic* even when meaning "making a sound," the specific mention of "not when meaning making a sound" (*aviśabdane*) indicates that the *ṇic* after *ghuṣ* is optional.

By this, *jughuṣuḥ* (or *puṣyamāṇāḥ*) and *ghuṣyamāṇavāḥ* are established. [Objection: Now, in the rule *ghuṣiraviśabdane*, let the term *aviśabdane* not be stated. For *ghuṣ* is listed in the *bhvādi* class as having the meaning "not making sound" (*aviśabdana*). In the *curādi* class, however, it is listed as *ghuṣir viśabdane*. And that [latter] is [a root] ending in *ṇic*. Since the rule mentions simply *ghuṣi*, only the *bhvādi* root with the meaning "not making sound" is intended to be included, not the one from the *curādi* class.

For in that case, it should have been prescribed as *ghoṣiḥ*. And thus, by the force of the prescription *ghuṣi* alone, there would be an exclusion of the *curādi* root *ghuṣ* which has the meaning of "making known," resulting in the inclusion of only the *bhauvādika* root *ghuṣ* which does not have the meaning of "making known. Anticipating the objection that [the term] *aviśabdane* ("not making known") is therefore redundant, he says: "In the sense of making known," etc. [The word] *siddhaḥ* ("established").

The meaning is that [the rule] is established regarding this portion, namely, *aviśabdane* (in the sense of non-proclamation). Thus, since the term *aviśabdane* would otherwise be redundant, it serves to indicate that the root *ghuṣ*, belonging to the curādigaṇa, optionally takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Furthermore, in the alternative case where the suffix is absent, the inclusion of the curādigaṇa root *ghuṣ*—which ends in a short vowel (*iganta*) and signifies proclamation—is the purpose; for, by being devoid of the causative suffix when signifying proclamation, the authoritative usage *jughuṣuḥ* becomes justified.

In the Bhāṣya, the sentence "Having heard the king’s words, the Puṣyamāṇavas shouted" (*jughuṣuḥ puṣyamāṇavāḥ*) is cited as an authority. *Viśabdana* is the making manifest of one's own intention through speech. Thus, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* when the sense is not that of making manifest, as in the example "the rope has been sounded" (*ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ*). However, with the sense of making manifest, the augment *iṭ* occurs, as in "the sentence has been proclaimed" (*ghuṣitaṃ vākyam*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 7.2.97, which applies after a suffix beginning with *jñā*.

This very [rule] indicates that here there is the continued application up to *map* (*maparyantānuvṛtti*), or it indicates that an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) subverts even internal operations (*antaraṅga*). This is a *paribhāṣā*. The rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the principle that "an operation prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs when that same suffix follows. This too is a *paribhāṣā*. The rule *svāder iñi* (Pāṇini 7.3.8) is an indicator of the following: Final Answer: The final answer is that these rules indicate the continued application up to *map*, the subversion of internal operations by external ones, and the principle that operations prescribed for a root apply when that same suffix follows. I hope it is correct.

The mention of *śva* and others in the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that elsewhere, when *śvan* is mentioned, the mention of "that which begins with it" (*tadādigrahaṇa*) applies. This is for the sake of forms such as *śauvahānam* (the name of a city) and *śauvādaṃṣṭraḥ* (a gem). The meaning of the rule *vi.ṭa ṭhaśvāderiñi* is that when *iñ* follows a word beginning with *śvan*, the *ai* and *au* vowels prescribed by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.4) do not occur. An example is *śvābhastrī*, the descendant of *śvabhastra*.

Now, by the rule "dvārādīnāṃ ca," it is prescribed that for words listed in the *dvārādi* group, there is no *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel; rather, an *aij* augment (*ai* or *au*) is inserted before the semivowels *y* and *v*. And in the *dvārādi* group, the word *śvan* is recited.

And so, although by that [rule] the augment *aij* would apply before the letter *v*, which is a constituent of the word *śvan*, the augment *aij* does not apply in the case of a word whose constituent is the word *śvabhastra*. Thus, suspecting that the prohibition would be purposeless due to the absence of such an application, he says: "The mention of *śva*-etc. in the prohibition. Since the rule concerning *śva*-etc. would otherwise be redundant according to the stated reasoning, it indicates through the inclusion of *śvan* that there is also the inclusion of any word whose constituent is the word *śvan*.

Furthermore, since the word *śvabhastra* is also included by the inclusion of *śvan*, the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca* would require the substitution of *aij* (i.e., *ai* or *au*), and thus the rule *śvāderiñi* was formulated to prohibit that. The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is the establishment of the *aij* substitution in forms such as *śauvahānam* and *śauvādaṃṣṭra*. To explain: in the sense of "that in which dogs are driven away" (*jihate'smin*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *o hāṅ gatau* (Dhp. 1.1023) to form *hānam*. *Śvahānam* is the driving away (*hānam*) of dogs (*śunām*). *Śauvahānam* is derived from that. Similarly for *śauvādaṃṣṭra*. Thus, the *aij* substitution is established.

In the sense that "there is a killing of dogs in this place," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tadasminnastīti deśe tannāmni* (Pāṇini 4.2.67). By the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *aij*. The resulting form is *śauvahāna*. Similarly, *śuno daṃṣṭrā* becomes *śvādaṃṣṭrā*; the lengthening of the vowel is effected by the Vārttika *śuno dantadaṃṣṭrā* (Pāṇini 6.3.130). The suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "produced therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*). Again, by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *aij*. The resulting form is *śauvādaṃṣṭra*.

The point here is that the purpose of including the term *tadādi* ("beginning with that") in the rule should be understood as follows: the application of that rule occurs only when the word *śvan* is included within both [the base and the suffix]. Regarding the rule *jhrjñā.ṭa ṭhaprācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.3.14), since the form for villages of the Easterners would already be established by the mention of "villages of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ grāmāṇām*) alone, the inclusion of the word "cities" (*nagara*) indicates that the mention of "cities" is not included within the mention of "villages."

However, that [interpretation] was refuted in the Bhāṣya on three occasions—namely, under *udīcyagrāmāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.109), *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* (4.2.117), and *dikśabdā grāma* (6.2.103)—due to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the term *nagara* (city) would have to be included in those rules. Furthermore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on *viśiṣṭaliṅga* (2.4.7) that the prohibition of *nagara* in that rule is indeed unnecessary. [Objection: But surely the words *grāma* and *nagara* denote a settlement inhabited by a multitude of people.

In this regard, since the term *grāma* itself would suffice to include a city (*nagara*) as well—given that there is no difference between them in being a settlement for a multitude of people—the inclusion of the word *nagara* in the rule *prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām* might be considered redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "only *prācāṃ grāmāṇām*" (of the villages of the Easterners), thereby indicating that in this grammar, the term *grāma* does not include cities. However, he notes that this interpretation is refuted in the *Bhāṣya*, stating: "But that... because in the three subsequent rules beginning with *udīcyagrāmāt*, the inclusion of cities under the term *grāma* is indeed intended. Thus, that [earlier position] is untenable.

Now, one might object: if it is intended that the mention of "village" (*grāma*) includes the "city" (*nagara*) as well, then—since the prohibition of the city is already obtained by the very prohibition of the village in the rule *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo'grāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.7)—the statement made by the author of the Vārttika that "the prohibition of the city must also be stated" would be unnecessary. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by way of concession, saying: "But in the case of [the rule] *viśiṣṭaliṅga*... etc.

And thus, the meaning is that in that sūtra, the prohibition regarding "nagara" should not have been stated at all. [From the commentary on Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.15: *jñā.ṭa ṭhasaṃkhyāyāssaṃ*]: Since the rule would have been established by the phrase "of a word ending in a measure (*parimāṇa*), provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*"), the explicit mention of *saṃvatsara* indicates that the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) does not include "time" (*kāla*). Consequently, in forms such as *dvivarṣā*, the exclusion based on the rule "*aparimāṇa*" (Pāṇini 4.1.22) does not apply.

Regarding this, [it may be argued]: "By the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.15), the vṛddhi substitution of the final vowel is prescribed for the word *saṃvatsara* following a numeral, as well as for the numeral itself, when they stand as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) before a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with *ñi* or *ñit*. Examples include *dvisāṃvatsarikaḥ* (lasting two years) and *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ* (eighty-two)."

In this regard, let the mention of the word *saṃvatsara* (year) not be made; even in its absence, since the word *saṃvatsara* denotes a measure of time (*kāla*), the lengthening of the final vowel of the second member is established by the rule itself, *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.17). For it might be argued that time (*kāla*) is also a "measure" (*parimāṇa*) because it is the cause for delimiting action (*kriyā*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] states—*parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñeti siddhaḥ*—to indicate that by the inclusion of the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) in the rule, measures in the form of time are not included.

And likewise, in the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ*, since it is impossible for the word *parimāṇa* to include a measurement of time in the form of years, the rule would not apply to provide the vṛddhi of the second member in cases such as *dvisāṃvatsarika*. Therefore, the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasya* [was formulated] to ensure that vṛddhi occurs in such instances.

The mention of the word *saṃvatsara* serves its purpose within its own scope; however, its utility elsewhere is as follows: in cases such as *dvivarṣā*, meaning "one who has been hired for two years," the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *tam adhīṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.80). When this suffix undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *varṣāl luk ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.88), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be required by the rule *dvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.21). However, that application is prohibited by the rule *aparimāṇa-bista-ācita-kambalyebhyo na taddhita-luki* (Pāṇini 4.1.22).

If time (*kāla*) were also considered a measure (*parimāṇa*), then in the case of the word *dvivarṣā*, because it would end in a measure-word, the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp*—which is based on the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words that do not end in a measure-word—would not apply. It is precisely because time is not a measure that the prohibition of *ṅīp* occurs. This is what he expresses by saying: "Therefore, in cases such as *dvivarṣā*," etc. Regarding the rule *ṭhapratyayasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44), the application [of the rule] in examples such as *etikāsu* occurs even when there is an intervention, due to the prohibitive indicator (*jñāpaka*) found in the rule *na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45).

Objection: Now, when the word *etad* is in the feminine, with the addition of *akac*, the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems, the addition of *ṭāp*, and the substitution of *ī* for *a*, the form *etikā* is desired. In that case, because there is an intervention by the vowel *ā*, the letter *k* is not followed by *ṭāp*; thus, the substitution of *ī* [for the *a* before *k*] as prescribed by the rule "pratyayasthātkātpūrvasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.44) would not apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the prohibition in the rule 'na yāsayoḥ'" (Pāṇini 7.3.45). The rule "na yāsayoḥ" is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ī* in cases such as *yakā* and *sakā*.

In that case as well, when the word *yat* and the word *tat* undergo the addition of *akac*, the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement by *a*), and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the vowel *ikāra* would not apply because of the intervention of the letter *ka* between [the original stem-final] and the *a* of *ṭāp*; thus, since the condition of being followed by *ṭāp* (*ṭāpparakatva*) is absent, the prohibition [of *ikāra*] would be purposeless. Therefore, the intention is that this [prohibition] indicates that *itva* occurs even when there is an intervention by the letter *a*. In this context, according to the view that the term *kādi* refers to the mere phoneme *ka*, the rule for *itva* would fail to apply in both instances—*etikā* and *hārikā*—even though there is an intervention by the letter *a*, based on the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam* (that which cannot be separated by anything).

In the view that [the term] refers to a *saṃghāta* (a cluster of sounds), there is no intervention by the vowel *a* at all in cases such as *hārikā*. However, in the case of *etikā*, since the *saṃghāta* ending in *k* is absent, the application of the *it*-augment would not occur; thus, the *it*-augment for words of this class was established in the *Bhāṣya* by means of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45). Kaiyaṭa has explained the phrase "of this class" (*evañjātīyakānām*) as meaning "those which possess the *akac* augment.
