This being the case, the statement that the augment occurs even when there is intervention based on the *jñāpaka* is to be considered problematic, according to Pārthasārathi Bhaṭṭācārya.

Regarding the rule *heracaṅi* (Pāṇini 7.3.56): the prohibition *acaṅi* indicates that elsewhere, when there is an additional suffix *ṇi*, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*) occurs. By this, we have forms such as *prajighāyayiṣati*. Now, an objection is raised: the meaning of the rule *heracaṅi* is simply that the substitution of *ku* for the *ha* of the root *hinoti* occurs after an abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable), but not in the case of *caṅ*. Examples include *jighāya* and so forth. In those cases, the phrase *acaṅi* was included in the rule to prevent the substitution of *ku* for the *ha* in forms like *ajīhayat*. Therefore, [the mention of *ṇi* in the Vārttika] is useless. [Response: It is not useless. [The rule applies] even when there is an additional *ṇi* suffix. For instance, in *prajighāyayiṣati*, the *ha* of the root *hi* undergoes the substitution of *ku* because of the presence of the additional *ṇi* suffix. Thus, the mention of *ṇi* is purposeful.

For instance, the rule is explained as follows: "The substitution of *k* for *h* occurs after that which follows [the reduplication] when the designation *aṅga*, *aḍ*, *addha*, *ṭh*, *ḍa*, or *ga* applies to the cause (the condition) upon which the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) depends. Since, in the case of *prājīhayat*, the status of being an *aṅga* and the status of being a reduplication do not share a common cause (condition), the substitution of *k* for *h* will not occur here. Specifically, in the derivation of *prājīhayat*, the root *hi* is the *aṅga* with respect to the causative suffix (*ṇic*), whereas it is the reduplication with respect to the *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist marker); thus, because the conditions for *aṅga*-hood and reduplication-hood are not identical, the *kutva* substitution does not apply.

And thus, the expression *acaṅi* indicates that the substitution of *k* (kutva) occurs even for a root ending in *ṇi*. This means that although there is a difference in the conditions—since the status of being an *aṅga* is caused by *ṇic* while the reduplication is caused by *caṅ*—the substitution of *k* still takes place. Consequently, since the substitution of *k* would also apply in the case of *prājīhayat*, the term *acaṅi* is stated to prevent it. By this, the substitution of *k* is permitted for a root ending in *ṇi* when followed by any cause for reduplication other than *caṅ*.

Regarding the form *tutujighāyiṣati*, the substitution of *ku* (the change of *h* to *gh*) is established here because the suffix *san* follows a root ending in *ṇic*. This is based on the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stated in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*: "When a base is mentioned, that which has an additional *ṇi* (causative marker) is also included. Furthermore, the long vowel in the rule *jñādṛṭa ṭhajñājanorjñā* (Pāṇini 7.3.79) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the metarule concerning operations within a stem (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*). From the fact that the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛdit* designation in the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), it is indicated that shortening takes precedence over reduplication.

By the *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) in the rule *nāglopi* (Pāṇini 7.4.2), where the term *ag* is used as a *pratyāhāra*, it is understood that elision (*lopa*) is stronger than *vṛddhi*. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the *ṇi* [augment] in the case of *ṇic*. [Objection: But consider the form *mā bhavānaṭiṭat*. Here, from the root *aṭ* with *ṇic*, in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ*, we have the state *aṭ-i-aṭ-i-at*. When *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel occurs, we get *āṭ-i-aṭ-i-at*. Then, by the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), the *ākāra* is shortened to *a*, resulting in *aṭ-i-aṭ-i-at*. Then, by the rule *adāderdvitīyasya*... [the second syllable is reduplicated].

Regarding the rule *sū. 6.1.2* (*ṭeḥ*), when the word *ṭi* is doubled—resulting in the sequence *aṭi ṭi at*—and the *ṇi* is elided, the form *aṭiṭat* is desired. However, that is not achieved. One might object: "In the stage where we have *āṭi at*, since the doubling of the word *ṭi* is obligatory, it would override even the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). Thus, from *āṭiṭi at*, because the first *ṇic* is separated by the subsequent *ṇic*, it lacks the status of being followed by *caṅ*; consequently, the shortening of the penultimate vowel does not apply, and the resulting form would be *āṭiṭat*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the marking of *oṇ* as having an *ṛt* vowel (*ṛdit*)."

By the inclusion of the marker *ṛ* (the *ṛdit* designation) for the root *oṇ*, it is indicated that the rule for shortening (*hrasvatva*) is more powerful than the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Thus, because the shortening is stronger, when the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) has first taken effect, and subsequently the reduplication occurs, the resulting form is indeed *aṭiṭat*. The intention is as follows: when the suffix *luṅ* with the *caṅ* augment is applied to the causative (*ṇijanta*) of the root *oṇ*, we arrive at the stage *oṇi-a-t*. At this point, the rule "ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.1), which prescribes the shortening of the penultimate vowel *o*, would apply. However, to prevent that shortening, the root *oṇṛ* is marked with the *ṛ* (making it *ṛdit*) by the rule "nāglopiśāsvṛditām" (Pāṇini 7.4.2). This rule prohibits shortening for roots that lose a penultimate vowel (*aglopi*), for the root *śās*, and for *ṛdit* roots. Therefore, the *ṛ* marker is added to the root *oṇṛ* specifically to block the application of shortening.

Furthermore, if the doubling were to occur first because of the permanence [of the rule], then, when the doubling of the element *ṇi* results in the form *oṇiṇi at*, the shortening prescribed by the rule "ṇau caṅi" would not take place simply because the first *ṇic* is separated from the *caṅ* affix by the second one, and thus lacks the condition of being immediately preceded by *caṅ*. What, then, would be the purpose of marking it as having an indicatory letter *ṛ* (*ṛdit*)? That very fact of its being so marked indicates that the operation of shortening is more powerful than the doubling.

Furthermore, when the shortening (*hrasva*) has been applied and then the doubling (*dvitva*), the result would be *mā bhavānuṇiṇat*, whereas the desired form is *mā bhavānoṇiṇat*. To achieve that, the substitution of *ṛt* for the root *oṇ* is prescribed. By this, because the prohibition of shortening in the rule *nāglopi* applies, the desired form is established; thus, the rule serves its purpose within its own domain (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*). As for its application elsewhere, the intended meaning is that the previously mentioned form *mā bhavānaṭiṭat* is achieved. Regarding the rule *ṇau caṅi*, there is the Vārttika: "The shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) must be added as an exception (*upasaṃkhyāna*) when *ṇi* follows *ṇic*."

The meaning [of the rule] is that it should be stated that when there is the causative suffix (*ṇic*) following a root already ending in *ṇic*, and then the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with *caṅ* [is applied], the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) occurs. An example shown in the Bhāṣya is: *vīṇām avīvadad devadattena* ("He caused Devadatta to play the lute").

From the causative form of the root *vad* (*vadi*), after applying the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the aorist marker (*luṅ*) with the *caṅ* substitute, we have the form *avād-i-i-at*. In this instance, because the first *ṇic* is separated from the *caṅ* by the second *ṇic*, the condition of being immediately preceded by *caṅ* (*caṅparakatva*) does not exist; thus, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) does not apply. This is prescribed by the author of the Vārttika. Now, one might object: once the second *ṇic* has been elided by the rule "ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there would be no separation [between the first *ṇic* and the *caṅ*], and the shortening would be established by the Sūtra itself.

Nor should it be argued that even when the *ṇi* is elided, there is still an intervention [of the elided element] because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original); for in the case of the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*caṅparanirhrāsa*), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited by the rule: "In the cases of *kvi*, elision (*luk*), the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the shortening of the penultimate vowel in the presence of *caṅ* (*caṅparanirhrāsa*), and the substitution of *ku* (*kutva*). (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.1.58).

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, because the first *ṇic* is elided here, and since that [elided element] is an *ik*, the base (*aṅga*) becomes one whose *ik* has been elided (*aglopi*) immediately after its elision; thus, when the prohibition by the rule "nāglopiśāsvṛditām" (Pāṇini 7.4.2) would apply, shortening is prescribed by a *vārttika* as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). For, due to its priority over the elision, the *vṛddhi* substitution for *ṇic* occurs first, resulting in the vowel *ai*; subsequently, that *ai* is elided, and the *ai* is not an *ak*.

Therefore, since the elision of *ta* (the augment *ṭuk*) results in forms such as *ḍhad*, *ḍhaṭh*, *ḍhaṭha*, *ḍagaṃ*, and so on, the condition "not having an elided *a*" (*nāglopi*) does not apply; consequently, because the prohibition [of shortening] does not take effect, the short vowel would be established by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* alone, making the composition of the Vārttika redundant. To this, he says: "In the rule *nāglopi*... The intention here is as follows: it is made known that the elision (*lopa*) is stronger than the augment (*vṛddhi*). And in that regard, the very rule *nāglopi* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Regarding the statement *amamālat* in the rule *amamālat*, since there is elision of the suffix *ṭi* in the form *ā*, the root becomes *aglopi* (having an elided *a*); thus, by the rule *nāglopi*, the prohibition of the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) is intended. In that context, since the prohibition is already obtained by the phrase *alopinām na* alone, it must be stated that the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *aglopinām* in the rule *nāglopinām na* is for the purpose of prohibiting the shortening of the penultimate vowel even in cases where the stem (*aṅga*) has undergone the elision of the letter *u*, as in *acacāṭat* and similar forms.

In that case, when the *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel *u* has been effected by taking the causative suffix (*ṇic*) as the cause, and subsequently the *ṭi*-portion is elided, there remains only the elision of the vowel *au*, and not the elision of an *aglopa* (an elision of a portion other than the initial). Consequently, even if the *pratyāhāra* [the term *al*] were included [in the rule], the desired result would not be achieved; thus, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* would be purposeless. Yet, the fact that the *pratyāhāra* is indeed included serves to indicate that the elision (*lopa*) is more powerful than the *vṛddhi* substitution.

Consequently, in cases such as *avīvadat*, since the rule [prohibiting *guṇa*] would apply due to the root being *aglopi* (having its penultimate vowel elided) upon the elision of the *ṇi*-suffix, it is necessary to provide an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the shortening of the *upadhā* vowel even when a *ṇic* suffix follows, in order to override that prohibition. Thus he says: "Therefore, [the rule applies] when a *ṇic* follows a *ṇi*. This refers to Pāṇini 6.4.51: *jñā-aniṭi ṇalutvam aglopi* (or more precisely, the context of 7.4.2: *anaglopi*). Regarding the term *aglope*: [The rule 6.4.51 applies] when there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*aglope*).

Since the desired result is already established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the inclusion of the term *aglopin* (that which loses a vowel) is for the purpose of indicating that the elision (*lopa*) of a vowel is also included under the designation *aglopi*. As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*—"From here onwards, the mention of *aglopin* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the absence of *sthānivadbhāva*"—this is merely the opinion of a partial exponent (*ekadeśin*). Now, regarding the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām*: its meaning is that for a root ending in a *ṇic* suffix, for a root denoted by the technical term *śās*, and for roots marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*), there shall be no shortening of the penultimate vowel when followed by a *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist) which itself follows a *ṇic*. In this context, *amamālat* is an example of a root that loses a vowel (*aglopin*).

In the sense of "he made a garland" (*mālām akhyat*), from the word *mālā*, by applying the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (P. 3.1.25), the suffix *ṇic* is added; then, in the *luṅ* tense with *aṭ* and *caṅ*, we have *a-māl-ā-i-a-t*. At this stage, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat* (P. 6.4.155), the final vowel *ā* is elided, resulting in *a-mā-māl-i-a-t*. When the reduplication of the syllable *mā* occurs and we reach the state *a-mamāl-i-a-t*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) is prohibited, because the stem (*aṅga*) contains an elision (*aglopa*) of the form of the letter *ā*.

In this context, because the elision of the *ṭi* (the *ṭi*-portion) is treated as if it were still present by virtue of the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the vowel following the *m* would not be considered an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel). Consequently, the shortening prescribed by the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1) does not apply, and thus the prohibition regarding roots that do not undergo elision (*nāglopī*) would be redundant. To address this, he says: *aglopa*. The mention of *aglopi* is intended to show that even the elision of a whole group of letters (*agvat*) is included under the term *aglopa*.

Therefore, in the case of *atyararājat*—where the sense is "he surpassed the king" (*rājānam atikrāntavān*)—the prohibition of the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva-niṣedha*) is established in the form *ararāj at* through the following process: after the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the aorist marker (*luṅ*), followed by the reduplication marker (*caṅ*), the rule *an* causes the elision of the final syllable (*ṭi*). If *ana* were taken as a whole [meaning "that which has *an*"], it would not be *ak*; therefore, its elision would not be captured by the term *ag-lopa* (elision of *ag*) according to the literal reading of the rule. However, if it is stated that even the elision of something possessing *ag* is included under the term *ag-lopa*, then because the aggregate *an* possesses *ag* in the form of the letter *a*, the stem (*aṅga*) affected by that elision becomes *aglopi*. Consequently, the prohibition of the shortening of the penultimate vowel by the rule *nāglopi* is successfully established.

And thus, although in examples such as *amamalat* the requirement is met through the application of *sthānivadbhāva*, in the case of *atyararājat*, since the elision (*lopa*)—which is a substitute for a combination of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*)—is not an *aj-ādeśa* (a substitute for a vowel), *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply. Therefore, the mention of *aglopi* was made in order to secure the prohibition of the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). The point is that this [mention] is indeed meaningful only if one accepts that even an elision (*lopa*) is included under the term *aglopi*.

With this in mind, Kaiyaṭa stated: "And by the force of the mention of *aglopa*, even the elision of the entire [stem] is understood as *aglopa*, because if only the elision of the suffix were intended, the prohibition would be purposeless. He further said: "In that case, since [the result] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition 'not for those ending in *aglopa*' indicates that from this point onward, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply. Thus, the prohibition "not for those ending in *aglopa*" is said to indicate another underlying meaning.

He states—beginning with the words "from here onwards"—that this [point] has already been understood from that very source, because it was determined in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "acaḥ parasmin" (*Pāṇini 1.1.57*) that a substitute for a consonant (*hal*) or a vowel (*ac*) is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). This is clear in both the *Kaiyaṭa* and the *Uddyota*. Furthermore, the long-vowel pronunciation of *rīṅ* in the sūtra "jñā-dṛ-ṭa-rīṅ-ṛtaḥ" (*Pāṇini 7.4.27*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the *paribhāṣā* regarding the operation within a stem (*aṅgavṛtta-paribhāṣā*). Also, in the sūtra "arti-pipartyos ca" (*Pāṇini 7.4.77*).

Since the rule is already established by the statement "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [the substitution occurs] diversely), the specific mention of the root *ṛ* serves as an indicator that the form is correct even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). [Objection: But surely, for the roots *ṛ* and *pṝ*, which are listed in the *juhotyādi* class, the substitution of the vowel *i* for the reduplicated syllable is prescribed by the rule "artipipatyośca."

In this regard, one might object that since the root *ṛ* belongs to the Vedic language (*chandasa*), the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable is already established by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.78), which means that such a substitution occurs frequently in the Veda; thus, the explicit mention of the root *ṛ* would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he states, "it is established in this very way," in order to indicate that the usage of the root *ṛ* is also grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) in the common language (*bhāṣā*). [The rule] *guṇo yaṅli* (Pāṇini 7.4.82) [then applies].

The mention of *akitaḥ* ("except when preceded by a kit") in the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83) indicates that, in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), subverting rules do not subvert [the present rule]. This is a *paribhāṣā*. [Regarding] *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Sūtra 7.4.83): because of the shortness [of the vowel], the *tva*, *guṇa*, and *vṛddhi* [operations apply]; here, *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable") is a qualifier for the vowels *a*, *ṛ*, *u*, *i*, and *e*. [Objection]: But surely, in the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ*, the term *akitaḥ* is redundant.

Furthermore, in the absence of that [restriction], in forms such as *yaṃyamyate* and *raṃramyate*, where the roots *yam* and *ram* undergo reduplication after the addition of the *yaṅ* suffix, the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*, and the insertion of *nuṭ* by the rule "nugato 'nunāsikāntasya" (Pāṇini 7.4.85), followed by the substitution of *anusvāra* for that *nuṭ*, the forms *yaṃyamyate* and *raṃramyate* are obtained. In this context, the term *akitaḥ* is stated in order to prevent the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Since the *nuṭ* is present, the reduplicated portion is not *akit* (not ending in *k*), and thus there is no fault. And so it is said: [The text continues: ...and so forth.

It should be stated that the inclusion of the term *aki* is purposeful. Because of the hearing of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*, 1.2.28) is brought to mind; and since "a vowel" (*ac*) is a qualifier of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the meaning of the sūtra is: "there is lengthening of a reduplicated syllable ending in a vowel. Furthermore, once the augment *nuK* has been applied, the reduplicated syllable ends in *n* and no longer ends in a vowel; thus, lengthening would not occur anyway. Therefore, the inclusion of *aki* would otherwise be useless.

Thus, from the root *chud*, by the rule "ādeca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the substitution of *ā* occurs; then, when the suffix *liṭ* is applied, after the reduplication of the stem *chā*, because the *tuk* augment (by Pāṇini 6.1.75) is antaranga, we arrive at the form *chāt-chā-atu*. At this stage, by the rule "hrasva" (Pāṇini 7.4.59), it must be stated that the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is substituted. There too, by the mention of the term "short" (*hrasva*), the word "vowel" (*ac*) is brought into the context; and since that [word "vowel"] functions as a qualifier for the reduplicated syllable, the meaning of that rule is: "the short vowel is substituted for a reduplicated syllable ending in a vowel."

Furthermore, when *tuk* is applied, the short vowel (*hrasva*) is not established because the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) no longer ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). Consequently, the form *cacchadatuḥ* would not be obtained. Similarly, in the case of *cacchṛdataḥ*, after the doubling of the root *chṛd* and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the substitution of *a* for the *ṛ*-vowel by the rule "uraṇ raparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.50) would not occur following the application of *tuk* by the rule "che ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.73). This is because the term *ur* in that rule is a qualifier of the reduplicated syllable, and thus the substitution of *a* is prescribed only for a reduplicated syllable ending in an *ṛ*-vowel; once *tuk* is applied, the reduplicated syllable no longer ends in an *ṛ*-vowel.

Likewise, in the case of *cicchādayiṣati*, after the root *chad* has taken the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the desiderative suffix (*san*), and reduplication, and after the application of *halādiśeṣa*—resulting in the form *a-chā-day-iṣati*—the substitution of *tuk* occurs by the rule *che ca*. Consequently, the substitution of *it* by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79) does not apply, because the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) no longer ends in the vowel *a*.

Likewise, regarding the form *cecchidyate*: when the root *chid* takes the *yaṅ* suffix, after doubling (*dvitva*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the change to *c* (*rcatva*), we have *ci a chidyate*. At this stage, by the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73), the *tuk* augment is inserted. One might object that the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82) would not apply here. This is because, through the mention of *guṇa*, the rule *ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) is brought into force; and since that [rule] serves as a qualifier for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the *guṇa* is ordained only for a reduplicated syllable ending in an *ik* vowel. Since the reduplicated syllable in this case does not end in an *ik* vowel, the objection might arise. Anticipating this, he says: "Because of shortness," and so forth.

The intention is this: since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier in the sūtras presented, "of the vowel" (*acaḥ*) and so forth are not qualifiers of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); rather, it is precisely "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) that serves as the qualifier for "of the vowel" (*acaḥ*) and the rest.

The meaning of the rules presented—namely, "the vowel (*ac*) of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) becomes long," "the *ṛ*-vowel of the reduplication becomes *a*," "the *a*-vowel of the reduplication is replaced by *i*," and "the *i* of the reduplication becomes *guṇa*"—is such that short vowels and so forth are established accordingly. Thus, even in the case of *yaṃyamyate*, although the augment *nuK* has been applied, the term *akitaḥ* (not followed by *kit*) is stated for the purpose of prohibiting the application of lengthening to the vowel that is a constituent of the reduplication. Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Pāṇini 8.1.1: *sarvasya dve* (the whole [word] is doubled). By virtue of the evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in the inclusion of the word *kautaskuta* among the *kaska*-type words, the forms such as *paunaḥpunyam* are established even under the view that the doubling occurs twice.

Objection: Under the view that reduplication (*dvirvacana*) prescribed by the rule *sarvasya dve* consists of a double utterance, when the word *punaḥ* is reduplicated, one expects the forms *paunaḥpunyam*—derived from *punaḥpunaḥ* (meaning "that which occurs repeatedly") with the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*)—and *paunaḥpunikam*—derived with the suffix *ṭhañ* according to *kālaṭṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11) in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*). However, these forms would not be established [under the view of double utterance].

Anticipating the objection that—since the rule established by the mention of "compound" (samāsa) restricts the designation *prātipadika* only to meaningful composite groups that are compounds, and since the composite group "punah-punah" lacks the status of a *prātipadika*, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) governed by the heading *prātipadika* would be untenable—he says: "In the list beginning with *kaska-*, etc. (*kaskādiṣu*).

Since the word *kutastu* is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), the suffix *aṇ* cannot be applied to it; thus, the reading of *kautaskutaḥ* as ending in *aṇ* would be inconsistent. Therefore, this [reading] indicates that a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) may be produced even from a non-stem that has been reduplicated. Consequently, there is no fault—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the rule *jātu-apūrvam* (Pāṇini 8.1.47): in the context of the rule *āho utāho* (Pāṇini 8.1.49), because of the mention of the immediately preceding [word] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the mention of *apūrva* is a qualifier of *jātu*, and not of a verbal form (*tiṅanta*).

In that case as well, the term *apūrva* (never-before-occurring) is understood by way of recurrence from the previous rule. Now, regarding the rule *jātvapūrvam*, there arises a doubt: does the word *apūrva* mean "that which has no prior [occurrence]" (*avidyamāna-pūrva*), and if so, is it a qualifier of *jātu* or a qualifier of the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)? In the first alternative, the meaning would be: "A verbal suffix following *jātu*—provided that *jātu* is never before [used with that verb]—is not unaccented. An example would be *jātu bhokṣyase*.

In the second alternative, the meaning is that due to the word *jātu*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that is not preceded by another word is not unaccented. Having raised the doubt as to which of these two alternatives is authoritative, he says: "Or rather, *āho* or *utāho*. This is the intention: by the rule "After *āho* or *utāho*" (Pāṇini 8.1.49), it is understood that a finite verb following immediately after *āho* or *utāho* is not subject to suppression of accent (*nihanyate*). The examples are *āho bhuṅkte* and *utāho bhuṅkte*. In that case as well, the term *apūrvam* ("not preceded") is carried over from the rule "After *jātu*, [a verb] not preceded [by another word]" (Pāṇini 8.1.47).

If this [term *apūrva*] were a qualifier of the finite verb (*tiṅanta*), then it would follow that a finite verb not preceded by anything would occur only immediately after *āho* or *utāho*. Consequently, in the example "āho devadattaḥ pacati," since the finite verb would already be preceded by something, the prohibition of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) would not apply, and thus the inclusion of the term *anantara* ("immediately following") in the rule "āho utāho" would be redundant. Yet, since that term was indeed included, it indicates that *apūrva* is not a qualifier of the finite verb, but rather a qualifier of the cause (*nimitta*).

And so, since it has been stated that after *apūrva*, *āho*, or *utāho*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not unaccented, although the word *āho* in the example *deva āho bhuṅkte* (O God, eat! is excluded because it is preceded by another word, the finite verb in *āho devadattaḥ pacati* (Ah, Devadatta cooks! would not be excluded as it is likewise preceded by another word. Therefore, the term *anantara* ("immediately following") is included to exclude such cases. By this, it is determined that in the rule *jātvapūrvam*, the phrase *apūrvam* is a qualifier of the cause (*nimitta*) *jātu* itself, and not of the finite verb.

Thus ends the eighth chapter. By the compassionate gaze of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa as well as of the gurus, the best of the wise, and through the grace of Śrī Pārthasārathi, this commentary has been completed without any obstacle. Born in the agrahāra known as Nāvalpāka, which is adorned by a multitude of learned men, the crest-jewel of the four systems of philosophy, named Rāmānujācārya—the son of the wise Kṛṣṇatāta—has composed this exposition for the easy understanding of beginners.
